# On Manin’s Conjecture for Châtelet surfaces

**Authors:** Katharine Woo Address: Department of Mathematics, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305 Email address: katywoo@gmail.com

## Abstract

We resolve Manin’s conjecture for all Châtelet surfaces over $\mathbb{Q}$ .

#### Contents

- 1 Introduction

- 2 Outline

- 3 Background and notation

- 4 Upper bounds

- 5 Initial reductions

- 6 The cuspidal contribution – the finite image case

- 7 The cuspidal contribution – the Grössen case

- 9 Level of distribution

- 10 Large moduli and Hooley’s $\Delta$ -function

- 11 The asymptotics

- 12 Analysis of the leading constant

- References

## 1. Introduction

Let $\Delta\in\mathbb{Q}^{\times}$ satisfy $\sqrt{-\Delta}\not\in\mathbb{Q}$ , and let $f(z)\in\mathbb{Q}[z]$ be a separable polynomial of degree $3$ or $4$ . A Châtelet surface $X_{\Delta,f}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is defined as a proper smooth model of the affine surface:

$$ x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=f(z). $$

The purpose of this paper is to prove Manin’s conjecture for all Châtelet surfaces, including when $\Delta<0.$

Châtelet surfaces were first studied by Châtelet in [6, 7], who was interested in parameterizing their rational points over number fields (see [15]). Later, these surfaces were the first examples of surfaces that are not homogeneous spaces for which the Hasse principle, weak approximation, and other interesting problems about rational points were resolved. For certain pairs $(\Delta,f(z))$ , $X_{\Delta,f}$ may fail the Hasse principle due to a Brauer-Manin obstruction. In [10, 11], Colliot-Thélène, Sansuc, and Swinnerton-Dyer show that the Brauer-Manin obstruction is the only possible cause of why such a surface may fail the Hasse principle; these results hold not only over $\mathbb{Q}$ , but over any number field.

We first present Manin’s conjecture, as applied to Châtelet surfaces. There exists a map $\psi:X_{\Delta,f}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{4}$ , whose image is a singular del Pezzo surface of degree four (as described by Browning in [4]). This map then induces a height function on $X_{\Delta,f}$ by pulling back the natural height $H$ on $\mathbb{P}^{4}$ via $\psi.$ We define the point-counting function:

$$ \tilde{N}(X_{\Delta,f},B)=\#\{x\in X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q}):H(x)\leq B\}. $$

Manin’s conjecture, originally written as [1, Conjecture C’] by Batyrev and Manin and stated over $\mathbb{Q}$ explicitly by Browning as [5, Conjecture 2.3], predicts the behavior of $\tilde{N}(X_{\Delta,f},B)$ as $B\rightarrow\infty$ ; additionally, in [43], Peyre gives an interpretation of the constant in terms of local densities and the Brauer group. In the following conjecture, the exponent is worked out in [4, Lemma 1] by Browning.

#### Conjecture 1.1 (Manin’s conjecture for Châtelet surfaces).

Let $\Delta\in\mathbb{Q}^{\times}$ satisfy that $\sqrt{-\Delta}\not\in\mathbb{Q}$ and let $f(z)\in\mathbb{Z}[z]$ be a separable polynomial of degree 3 or 4 that decomposes as a product of $r$ irreducible polynomials $f=f_{1}\ldots f_{r}$ . Let $X_{\Delta,f}/\mathbb{Q}$ be a Châtelet surface defined by $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=f(z)$ . Assume that $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset$ . Then as $B\rightarrow\infty$ ,

$$ \tilde{N}(X_{\Delta,f},B)\sim C_{\Delta,f}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}, $$

where $C_{\Delta,f}>0$ and

$$ \rho_{\Delta,f}=2+\#\{1\leq i\leq r:\sqrt{-\Delta}\in\mathbb{Q}[z]/(f_{i}(z))\}. $$

#### Remark 1.2.

This formulation of Manin’s conjecture over $\mathbb{Q}$ is equivalent to the same statement under the assumption that $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})$ is Zariski-dense, thanks to the fact that if $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset$ then $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})$ is Zariski-dense. Indeed by [11, Proposition 9.8.(iii)], if $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset$ then $X_{\Delta,f}$ is birational to a geometrically integral nonconical cubic surface in $\mathbb{P}^{3}$ with a pair of conjugate singular points. Then by [17, Theorem A] of Coray and Tsfasman, $X_{\Delta,f}$ must be unirational and thus $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})$ is Zariski-dense.

Moreover, the question of when $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset$ is settled by the seminal result of Colliot-Thélène, Sansuc, and Swinnerton-Dyer [11]; it demonstrates that $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$ if and only if there is either a Brauer-Manin obstruction or a local obstruction to the existence of rational points. Furthermore, as discussed in [11], a Brauer-Manin obstruction to the Hasse principle may occur only when $f(z)$ is the product of two irreducible quadratics. There is a finite and effective computation for determining when $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset;$ this computation uses auxiliary varieties that we will introduce in (1.2).

Numerous instances of Manin’s conjecture for Châtelet surfaces have been resolved. In [4], Browning established an upper bound of the correct order of magnitude for Châtelet surfaces with $\Delta>0.$ In [37], Iwaniec and Munshi derive a lower bound when $f(z)$ is an irreducible cubic polynomial and $\Delta$ can be either positive or negative. In their seminal result, de la Bretèche, Browning, and Peyre [23] introduced the use of the torsor method, among other tools, to prove Manin’s conjecture for $x^{2}+y^{2}=f(z)$ when $f$ decomposes as a product of distinct linear factors. Later, de la Bretèche and Browning [20] showed Manin’s conjecture for the case that $\Delta=1$ and $f(z)$ contains an irreducible cubic factor. In [25], the asymptotic for Manin’s conjecture is established for $x^{2}+y^{2}=f(z)$ where $f$ is an irreducible quartic or a product of two irreducible quadratic factors over $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ by de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum; these factorization cases are often regarded as the trickiest cases. Finally, Destagnol [28] resolved Manin’s conjecture for $\Delta=1$ by proving the asymptotic for $x^{2}+y^{2}=f(z)$ where $f$ is a product of two linearly independent linear factors and an irreducible quadratic factor, the remaining unknown factorization. In the above cases, the techniques are amenable to replacing $x^{2}+y^{2}$ with any positive-definite quadratic form of class number one.

Châtelet surfaces belong to a wider class of surfaces; indeed, Châtelet surfaces are singular del Pezzo surfaces of degree four. Manin’s conjecture was established by Batyrev and Tschinkel [2] for all del Pezzo surfaces of degree $\geq 7$ and nonsingular del Pezzo surfaces of degree 6, as these are toric varieties. Additionally, Manin’s conjecture is known for many more examples of del Pezzo surfaces of lower degree, as is discussed by Browning in [5, Chapter 2].

In [4, Lemma 2], Browning shows that

$$ \tilde{N}(X_{\Delta,f},B)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\#\Big\{((x,y),(u,v),t)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{+}:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)\\
\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1,\max(|tu^{2}|,|tv^{2}|,|x|,|y|)\leq B\Big\}, $$

where $F(u,v)$ denotes the homogenization of $f(z)$ . We modify this height function slightly to better suit our techniques. Define:

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},B):=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\#\Big\{((x,y),(u,v),t)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{+}:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)\\
\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1,\max(|tu^{2}|,|tv^{2}|,\|x\pm y\sqrt{-\Delta}\|)\leq\nu_{\Delta,f}B\Big\}, $$

where $\|.\|$ denotes the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb{C}$ and

$$ \nu_{\Delta,f}=\begin{cases}\left(\max_{\mathbf{y}\in[-1,1]^{2}}|F(\mathbf{y})|\right)^{1/2},&\Delta>0\\
1,&\Delta<0.\end{cases} $$

This new height is bounded up to a constant (depending on $\Delta$ and $f$ ) both above and below by the natural height on $X_{\Delta,f}$ induced by $\psi$ and hence $N(X_{\Delta,f},B)\asymp\tilde{N}(X_{\Delta,f},B)$ ; however, this choice simplifies our computations.

#### Theorem 1.3.

Let $\Delta\in\mathbb{Z}$ be a squarefree integer satisfying that $\sqrt{-\Delta}\not\in\mathbb{Q}$ . Let $f(z)\in\mathbb{Z}[z]$ be a separable polynomial of degree 3 or 4. Let $X_{\Delta,f}/\mathbb{Q}$ be the corresponding Châtelet surface. Then as $B\rightarrow\infty$ , there exists a constant $c_{\Delta,f}$ such that

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},B)=c_{\Delta,f}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}+O_{\Delta,f}(B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1-10^{-10}}). $$

Moreover, if $c_{\Delta,f}$ is zero then there is a Brauer-Manin obstruction or a local obstruction to rational points on $X_{\Delta,f}.$

#### Corollary 1.4.

Manin’s conjecture holds for all Châtelet surfaces over $\mathbb{Q}.$

#### Remark 1.5.

Observe that if there is a Brauer-Manin obstruction or a local obstruction to the existence of rational points on $X_{\Delta,f}$ , then we automatically know that $N(X_{\Delta,f},B)=0$ . Hence, Theorem 1.3 can be upgraded to $c_{\Delta,f}=0$ if and only if there is a Brauer-Manin or local obstruction.

In Theorem 1.3, we do not assume a priori that $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset.$ Our proof of the aforementioned asymptotic result gives an explicit, albeit complicated, expression for $c_{\Delta,f}$ . Notably, $c_{\Delta,f}$ is closely related to auxiliary varieties; these varieties appear in the work of Colliot-Thélène, Coray, and Sansuc in [9] when $f(z)$ is the product of two irreducible quadratics. Since our expression for $c_{\Delta,f}$ is complicated, we determine when it vanishes but do not pursue an adelic interpretation along the lines of Peyre’s prediction [43]. In Appendix A, we show that the constant matches Peyre’s prediction in a simple, but novel case.

Let $f(z)=f_{1}(z)\ldots f_{r}(z)$ be a decomposition into irreducible factors and let $\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{r}\in\mathbb{Q}^{\times}$ satisfy that $\alpha_{1}\cdots\alpha_{r}=1$ . We define the auxiliary variety:

$$ X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},\ldots,f_{r},\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{r}}:=\{(z,(x_{i},y_{i})_{i=1}^{r}):x_{i}^{2}+\Delta y_{i}^{2}=\alpha_{i}f_{i}(z)\neq 0\}. $$

The relationship between $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}$ and $X_{\Delta,f}$ will be expanded upon further in §12. For now, let us define the following condition:

- (A) There exists a tuple $(\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r})\in(\mathbb{Q}^{\times})^{r}$ satisfying $\alpha_{1}\cdots\alpha_{r}=1$ such that

$$ X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q}_{v})\neq\emptyset $$

for all places $v$ of $\mathbb{Q}$ .

We will show that if condition (A) holds then our constant $c_{\Delta,f}$ is nonzero (see Proposition 12.5). Additionally, if $f(z)$ is irreducible, then a consequence is that $c_{\Delta,f}$ is nonzero if there are no local obstructions to rational points on $X_{\Delta,f}$ .

In this way, Theorem 1.3 gives an analytic proof of the existence of many rational points on $X_{\Delta,f}$ via direct counting if condition (A) holds. Now, by the work of Colliot-Thélène, Coray, and Sansuc, and an application of Harari’s “formal lemma” [32], one can interpret condition (A) in terms of the Brauer-Manin obstruction and local obstructions of $X_{\Delta,f}$ . In particular, this allows us to conclude that if $c_{\Delta,f}$ is zero, then $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$ as well.

Finally, we remark on the possible application of these techniques to achieve an analytic proof of weak approximation for $X_{\Delta,f}$ . That $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}$ is a binary quadratic form corresponding to principal ideals is not of much relevance to our proof; indeed one can recreate the entire argument with a positive-definite or indefinite binary quadratic form. Adding arbitrary congruence conditions on $(u,v)$ will also be of little consequence for the analytic techniques. These points will be expanded on and are necessary ingredients in forthcoming work on del Pezzo surfaces of degree one, where both arbitrary congruence conditions and arbitrary positive-definite binary quadratic forms are required. So, at least in the case when $f(z)$ is irreducible, the methods can be adapted to establish weak approximation for $X_{\Delta,f}$ .

Finally, we highlight the new ingredients that allow us to push beyond $\Delta=1$ . In §2, we provide a detailed outline of our proof. First, we decompose our count into contributions from Eisenstein series and cusp forms. Consider the following function for $\Delta$ a positive squarefree integer:

$$ \theta(z)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}I\subset\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})}\\
I\textrm{ is principal}\end{subarray}}\exp(2\pi iz\cdot N(I)). $$

This function is a modular form of weight one and has a decomposition into Eisenstein and cuspidal components. If $\Delta=1$ , then the fact that $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ has class number one implies that $\theta(z)$ is purely Eisenstein, i.e. the cuspidal part is zero. We will find that in general the cuspidal contribution is negligible in comparison with the Eisenstein contribution.

When $\Delta<0$ , i.e. the indefinite case, a similar picture forms with careful analysis; the main additional obstacle in this case is that $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ has an infinite unit group. To mitigate this difficulty, we restrict our point-count to mildly-short boxes and intervals of length scaled by $\ell=\log(B)^{-10^{-10}}.$ This restriction allows us to estimate accurately the count

$$ \#\{|x\pm y\sqrt{-\Delta}|\leq B:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)\} $$

and convert our sum into a question about principal ideals $I$ with norm $t^{2}F(u,v).$ Of course, summing over short intervals and boxes complicates our estimates and sometimes adds an extra factor of $\ell^{-O(1)}$ , where this exponent can be made explicit. Fortunately, the error terms achieved by previous results on Manin’s conjecture, whose techniques we mimic, achieve savings of $\log(B)^{-10^{-5}}$ which will be more powerful than $\ell^{-O(1)}.$ Once the sum is written in terms of principal ideals of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ , we can again decompose the count in terms of Eisenstein and cuspidal contributions as before; this is equivalent to decomposing the Maass form into Eisenstein and cuspidal ingredients.

Second, we demonstrate that the cuspidal contribution is always negligible in comparison with the Eisenstein contribution. Let $C(z)$ denote the cuspidal part of $\theta(z)$ and let $\lambda_{C}(n)$ denote its Fourier coefficients. Our cuspidal contribution reduces to estimating sums of the form

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}\left|\lambda_{C}(t^{2}F(u,v))\right|, $$

and of the form

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{d\mid t}\mu(d)\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}\lambda_{C}\left(t^{2}F(u,v)/d^{2}\right). $$

In the first case, we study correlation sums of the absolute values of its Fourier coefficients $\lambda_{C}(n)$ along polynomial values; although we sacrifice cancellation in the sign of $\lambda_{C}(n)$ , we still gain a saving of a power of log. In particular, we use a Nair-type sieve [42] to reduce the problem to computing the first few Sato-Tate moments of the corresponding $L$ -functions (see Rankin’s [44] work on the moments of the Ramanujan $\tau$ -function). We remark that this method was used by Holowinsky [35] to study correlation sums of Fourier coefficients of cusp forms with quadratic polynomials. Heath-Brown [34] also used this technique to study the equidistribution of solutions to certain Châtelet surfaces and his work inspired our proof techniques. While this technique handles most cases, there are delicate issues concerning the cuspidality of the base change lift of $C(z)$ to the splitting field of $f(z)$ ; in these cases, the absolute values are too expensive of a sacrifice.

Fortunately, in the above exceptional cases, we can appeal to the more robust method of handling the second sum. We determine that since $C(z)$ is a cusp form, we can derive savings for the sum

$$ \sum_{d\leq X}\mu(d)\sum_{t\leq X/d}\lambda_{C}(at^{2}). $$

Moreover, our cusp forms are induced from class group characters of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta}).$ This extra structure allows us to track explicitly the dependency in the above bound on $a$ . Thus, we can derive a polylogarithmic saving on

$$ \sum_{|u|,|v|\leq B^{1/2}}\sum_{d\leq B/\max(|u|,|v|)^{2}}\mu(d)\sum_{t\leq B/d\max(|u|,|v|)^{2}}\lambda_{C}(t^{2}F(u,v)). $$

The inner sum is controlled by the poles of the symmetric square $L$ -function of $C(z)$ (see [45] for a discussion of the poles); if there is no pole, then the desired cancellation follows from the inner sum. If $C(z)$ is dihedral and the symmetric square $L$ -function has a pole, then an asymptotic for the inner sum is well-understood and the cancellation follows from the Möbius sum.

For the Eisenstein contribution, we follow the methods of [23, 20, 25, 28, 33] that resolved the $\Delta=1$ case. The third new feature is that for more general $\Delta$ , due to Gauss genus theory (see [30]), the Eisenstein Fourier coefficients now contain an extra summation over genus characters. This extra complication can still be handled by the aforementioned techniques for the $\Delta=1$ case and we achieve an explicit expression for the leading constant $c_{\Delta,f}.$

The fourth and last new ingredient is the analysis of the vanishing of the leading constant $c_{\Delta,f}$ . This is resolved in §12 and involves the auxiliary varieties introduced in (1.2). In particular, our leading term brings us to a non-negative sum which is approximately of the form

$$ \sum_{(\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r})/\sim}\prod_{p}\mu_{p}(X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})). $$

where if $\mu_{p}(X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q}_{p}))\geq 0$ is zero then $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})=\emptyset.$ Here, the sum over $(\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r})/\sim$ is over a sufficient and finite set of auxiliary varieties. Consequently, we show that if $c_{\Delta,f}=0$ then there is a local obstruction for every auxiliary variety.

## 2. Outline

In this section, we outline our proof strategy; our goal is to highlight the new techniques and convey the essential ideas, without the technical detail provided in the rest of the paper. By leaving out some of the more notationally-heavy complications, we hope to provide a clear roadmap for the rest of the paper. We warn the reader that in this section some of the claims are vague (and will be made precise in later sections) and some are technically false (but morally true and the modifications needed to correct the statements will be given later).

Let us start with the case when $\Delta>0$ . If $\Delta=1$ , Theorem 1.3 is known; so assume that $\Delta>1$ (for example, we can take $\Delta=5$ ). The main challenge to overcome is when $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ has class number greater than one. From our definition (1.1), we see that:

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},B)=\sum_{0\leq t\leq B}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}r_{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}}(t^{2}F(u,v)), $$

where $r_{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}}(n)=\#\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=n\}.$ Consider the binary theta series

$$ \theta(z)=\sum_{n}r_{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}}(n)\exp(2\pi inz)=\sum_{x,y}\exp(2\pi iz(x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}), $$

which is a modular form of weight one in $M_{1}(\Gamma_{0}(-\Delta),\chi)$ (see [36, §22.3]), where $\chi$ denotes the real quadratic character for $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta}).$ We can decompose $\theta(z)$ in terms of its Eisenstein and cuspidal contributions $\theta(z)=E(z)+C(z)$ . Note that since $\theta(z)$ is a weight one modular form, the Fourier coefficients of the Eisenstein component and the cuspidal component are expected to be of the same magnitude.

The Fourier coefficients of the Eisenstein part can be written explicitly in terms of genus characters, i.e. the class group character of order $\leq 2$ . As such, we have a nice description of the Fourier coefficients of the Eisenstein part:

$$ \lambda_{E}(n)\approx(1\star\chi)(n):=\sum_{d\mid n}\chi(d). $$

For the cuspidal part, we can write $\lambda_{C}(n)$ as a fixed linear combination of Fourier coefficients $\lambda_{\Psi}(n)$ , where $\Psi$ is the automorphic cuspidal representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$ given by a class group character $\psi$ of order $\geq 3$ . The critical fact that we can restrict to those $\psi$ of order $\geq 3$ follows from Gauss genus theory for binary quadratic forms, as discussed by Fomenko in [30]. We can describe these coefficients $\lambda_{\Psi}(n)$ explicitly:

$$ \lambda_{\Psi}(n)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{a}\subset\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})}\\
N(\mathfrak{a})=n\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{a}). $$

From this decomposition of $r_{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}}(n)$ , we can see that Theorem 1.3 follows from gaining asymptotics on

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}(1\star\chi)(t^{2}F(u,v)) $$

and sufficient upper bounds on

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}\lambda_{\Psi}(t^{2}F(u,v)). $$

Note that we have left out the $\gcd$ -conditions here.

Before analyzing the two sums above, let us discuss what happens when $\Delta<0$ . There are two challenges involved in the indefinite case: again, we run into issues when $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ has class number greater than one; we also must handle the fact that there are infinitely many solutions to the equation $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=1.$ To handle the second issue, we restrict to counting in short boxes.

Let $\ell,L=w(B)$ , a small value going slowly to zero as $B\rightarrow\infty.$ We eventually take $w(B)=\log(B)^{-10^{-10}}.$ Define the box

$$ \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L):=\mathbf{x}_{0}+[0,L]^{2}, $$

and the interval

$$ \mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell):=\{\exp(2\pi i\theta^{\prime}):\theta^{\prime}\in[\theta,\theta+\ell]\}. $$

Then we consider the restricted counting function:

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)):=\#\left\{((x,y),(u,v),t)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{+}:\begin{array}[]{cc}x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v),\\
(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\\
\|x\pm y\sqrt{-\Delta}\|\leq B,\\
\arg(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})\in\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell),\\
\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1\end{array}\right\}. $$

In other words, we restrict $(u,v)$ to a mildly shorter box $(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ and constrain the argument $\arg(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})\in\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell).$ Here we define the argument as

$$ \arg(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})=\frac{|x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}|}{|x-y\sqrt{-\Delta}|}\bmod|\varepsilon|^{2}, $$

where $\varepsilon$ is the fundamental unit to Pell’s equation $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=1.$ Our strategy is to produce an asymptotic for $N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell))$ ; this asympotic would then recover an estimate for $N(X_{\Delta,f},B)$ by splitting the region $\{|x|,|y|\leq B,|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}\}$ into short boxes and arguments in $\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)$ , and then summing over $\mathbf{x}_{0}$ and $\theta$ . This computation is done in §5.7.

By restricting to the shorter box and interval, we can make precise the count

$$ \#\{|x\pm y\sqrt{-\Delta}|\leq B:x^{2}+y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v),\arg(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})\in\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)\}. $$

In particular, we can find an explicit constant

$$ \kappa(\mathbf{x}_{0},\theta)=c_{\Delta}\cdot\max(-\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|,0)\cdot\frac{|\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)|}{4\pi} $$

satisfying that

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell))=(\kappa(\mathbf{x}_{0},\theta)+O(w(B)))\\
\times\sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)}\#\{I\subset\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta}):I\textrm{ a principal ideal and }N(I)=t^{2}F(u,v)\}\\
+E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)), $$

where $E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell))$ is a linear combination of remainder terms of the form

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}|\lambda_{\Xi}(t^{2}F(u,v))| $$

for $\Xi$ a cuspidal automorphic representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$ given by an unitary nontrivial Hecke Grössencharacter $\xi$ on $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ of infinite order (see Definition 3.2).

For the main term, we again use a decomposition into Eisenstein and cuspidal components. In particular, we can express

$$ \#\{I\subset\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta}):I\textrm{ principal and }N(I)=n\}=\frac{1}{|C|}\sum_{\psi\in\hat{C}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{a}\subset\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})}\\
N(\mathfrak{a})=n\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{a}), $$

where $C$ is the class group of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta}).$ Again, from Gauss’s genus theory, the Eisenstein contribution comes from the class group characters of order $\leq 2$ ; the Fourier coefficient for the Eisenstein part is approximately

$$ \lambda_{E}(n)\approx(1\star\chi)(n). $$

Similarly, the cuspidal Fourier coefficient is a linear combination of sums $\lambda_{\Psi}$ where $\Psi$ is the representation given by $\psi$ a class group character of order $\geq 3.$ This matches the process completed in the positive definite case.

In the end, Theorem 1.3 reduces to estimating the sum

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)}(1\star\chi)(t^{2}F(u,v)), $$

and providing a suitable upper bound on the sums

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}\lambda_{\Xi}(t^{2}F(u,v)), $$

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}|\lambda_{\Xi}(t^{2}F(u,v))|. $$

where $\Xi$ is the representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$ induced by a Hecke character $\xi$ . Additionally, (2.3) will only be used when $\xi$ is a class group character of order $\geq 3$ (and hence has finite image), whereas (2.4) only occurs when $\xi$ is a Hecke Grössencharacter (which has infinite image). We remark that it is likely that with more careful analysis we could remove the absolute values in (2.4); however, we achieve the necessary savings with the absolute values added.

Our method for estimating the Eisenstein contribution follows closely the previous approaches when $\Delta=1$ ; indeed, when $\Delta=1$ , $\theta(z)=E(z)$ and so the whole sum is contained in the Eisenstein part. We particularly mimic the proofs of de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum in [25] and the proof of Heath Brown in [33]. However, we must consider when $(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ lies in a short box – fortunately, all of the techniques are either amenable to this issue or we achieve a savings that is far larger than the loss incurred from summing over $|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}$ instead of the smaller region.

Using estimates on lattice points in convex regions, we establish a near-optimal level of distribution result for squarefree binary forms in §9. Write $F(x,y)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}F_{i}(x,y)$ as the decomposition into irreducible forms. We show that

$$ \sum_{d_{i}\leq D_{i}}\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
d_{i}\mid F_{i}(u,v)\end{subarray}}1-\frac{BL^{2}}{t}\cdot\frac{\#\{\mathbf{x}\bmod d_{1}\cdots d_{r}:d_{i}\mid F_{i}(\mathbf{x})\}}{(d_{1}\cdots d_{r})^{2}}\right|\ll D+\sqrt{\frac{BD}{t}}\exp(\sqrt{\log\log(B)}), $$

where $D=D_{1}\ldots D_{r}.$ This result allows us to take $D\leq\frac{B}{t}\log(B/t)^{-\varepsilon}$ for any $\epsilon>0$ and still obtain a reasonable bound. This level of distribution result is obtained in [25] for $F(x,y)$ irreducible or a product of two irreducible quadratics; we closely follow their techniques. Also, Marasingha [39] studies a general level of distribution result for squarefree binary forms and achieves a savings for $D\leq\frac{B}{t}\log(B/t)^{-A}$ for any large enough integer $A>0$ . We remark that if $F(x,y)$ has linear factors then the shape of the above bound is slightly different.

This step is the primary obstacle to studying $F(x,y)$ of higher degree; for $\deg(F)\leq 3$ , the level of distribution is sufficient and for $\deg(F)=4$ , it is almost sufficient (up to a power of $\log(B)$ ). For $\deg(F)>4$ , the level of distribution would be a power of $B$ away from necessary and this gap can not be covered by the argument as written below.

The other main input into our proof comes directly from de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum in [22] when $F(x,y)$ is irreducible or the product of two irreducible quadratics; we describe their idea in detail in §10 and discuss how to handle other factorizations of $F(x,y)$ . Define the twisted Hooley $\Delta$ -function:

$$ \Delta(n,\chi):=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}D\in\mathbb{R}\\
0\leq v\leq 1\end{subarray}}\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\mid n\\
d\in[D,e^{v}D]\end{subarray}}\chi(d)\right|. $$

Applying Nair’s sieve and [22, Theorem 1.1], we achieve that for $D\geq\frac{B}{t}\log(B/t)^{-10^{-5}},$

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}\\
\exists d_{i}\sim D_{i}:d_{i}\mid F_{i}(u,v)\end{subarray}}\Delta(F(u,v),\chi)\ll\frac{B}{t}\cdot\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2-10^{-5}}. $$

Note that since we take $L=w(B)=\log(B)^{-10^{-10}}$ , this bound is still $\ll\frac{BL^{2}}{t}\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2-10^{-7}}.$ This procedure handles the large moduli.

Together, these results allow us to re-express the Eisenstein contribution as:

$$ BL^{2}\sum_{t\leq B}\frac{1}{t}\sum_{(a_{i})\bmod\Delta}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1+\chi(a_{i}))\cdot\#\{\mathbf{x}\bmod\Delta:F_{i}(\mathbf{x})\equiv a_{i}\bmod\Delta\}\\
\times\sum_{d_{i}\leq D_{i}}\frac{\chi(d_{1}\ldots d_{r})\cdot\#\{\mathbf{x}\bmod d_{1}\cdots d_{r}:d_{i}\mid F_{i}(\mathbf{x})\}}{(d_{1}\cdots d_{r})^{2}}\\
+O\left(\sum_{t\leq B}\frac{B}{t}\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2-10^{-5}}\right). $$

However, the above expression is an oversimplification – in particular, it assumes that $(1\star\chi)(n)$ is a totally multiplicative function, which it is not. Instead, we must substitute the identity that

$$ (1\star\chi)(mn)=\sum_{c\mid\gcd(m,n)}\mu(c)\chi(c)(1\star\chi)(n/c)(1\star\chi)(m/c). $$

Consequently, we re-express our main term as:

$$ \sum_{(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)}(1\star\chi)(F(u,v))=\sum_{(c_{1},\ldots,c_{r})}^{\prime}\mu(c_{1}\cdots c_{r})\chi(c_{1}\cdots c_{r})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
c_{i}\mid F_{i}(u,v)\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1\star\chi)(F_{i}(u,v)/c_{i}). $$

Here the sum over $(c_{1},\ldots,c_{r})$ is restricted to a finite set of possible vectors where the entries divide the pairwise resultants of the irreducible factors of $f(z)$ .

Proceeding as before with our level of distribution result and bounds on the large moduli with the twisted Hooley $\Delta$ -function, our main term is actually of the form:

$$ BL^{2}\sum_{(c_{1},\ldots,c_{r})}^{\prime}\mu(c_{1}\cdots c_{r})\chi(c_{1}\cdots c_{r})\sum_{t\leq B}\frac{1}{t}\cdot\sum_{(a_{i})\bmod\Delta}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1+\chi(a_{i}))\#\{\mathbf{x}\bmod\Delta:F_{i}(\mathbf{x})\equiv c_{i}a_{i}\bmod\Delta\}\\
\times\sum_{d_{i}\leq D_{i}}\frac{\chi(d_{1}\cdots d_{r})\#\{\mathbf{x}\bmod c_{1}\cdots c_{r}\cdot d_{1}\cdots d_{r}:c_{i}d_{i}\mid F_{i}(\mathbf{x})\}}{(c_{1}\cdots c_{r}\cdot d_{1}\cdots d_{r})^{2}}. $$

Before analyzing this leading term further, let us discuss the cuspidal contribution.

First, we start with the finite image case. To study (2.3), we first change the order of summation:

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}\lambda_{\Xi}(t^{2}F(u,v))=\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq B^{1/2}}\sum_{t\leq B/\max(|u|,|v|)^{2}}\lambda_{\Xi}(t^{2}F(u,v)). $$

At this point, we need to address a previous false claim about cuspidal contribution in (2.3) – because we are counting those $(x,y)$ such that $\gcd(x,y,t)=1$ , we need to restrict our sum to ideals satisfying that $N(I)=t^{2}F(u,v)$ where $I=\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{t}$ , $\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1$ . In other words, our sum (2.3) should be of the form:

$$ \sum_{|u|,|v|\leq B^{1/2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\end{subarray}}\xi(\mathfrak{a})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/\max(|u|,|v|)^{2}\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\xi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}. $$

Now, since $\xi^{2}$ is a nontrivial class group character, we achieve a power saving upper bound in the sum over ideals $\mathfrak{t}$ . In particular, we claim that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/\max(|u|,|v|)^{2}\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\xi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}\ll\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\mid\mathfrak{a}}\left(1+\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{2/3}}\right)\cdot\left(\frac{B}{\max(|u|,|v|)^{2}}\right)^{5/6}. $$

The above is a consequence of the prime ideal theroem with nontrivial Hecke characters.

To complete our analysis of the finite image cuspidal contribution, we apply a generalization of Nair’s sieve for non-negative multiplicative functions along polynomial values by de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum [24]. In particular, this sieve gives us that

$$ \sum_{|u|,|v|\leq B^{1/2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\end{subarray}}\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\mid\mathfrak{a}}\left(1+\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{2/3}}\right)\\
\ll B\cdot\exp\left(\sum_{p\leq B^{1/2}}\frac{\#\{x\bmod p:f(x)=0\bmod p\}}{p}\cdot\left((1\star\chi)(1+p^{-2/3})-1\right)\right)\ll B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}. $$

Using partial summation, we achieve that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/\max(|u|,|v|)^{2}\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\xi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/N(\mathfrak{t}))^{1/2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\xi(\mathfrak{a})\ll B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}. $$

This is negligible compared to the main term of size $B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}.$

We can also view this sum more generally through the perspective of the Fourier coefficients of cusp forms. Let $C(z)$ be a weight one cusp form with central character $\chi$ ; the gcd condition $\gcd(x,y,t)=1$ leads us to the sum

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{d\mid t}\mu(d)\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}\lambda_{C}\left(\frac{t^{2}F(u,v)}{d^{2}}\right)=\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq B^{1/2}}\sum_{d\leq B/\max(|u|,|v|)^{2}}\mu(d)\sum_{t\leq B/(d\max(|u|,|v|)^{2})}\lambda_{C}(t^{2}F(u,v)). $$

This naturally brings us to analyzing the sum

$$ \sum_{d\leq X}\mu(d)\sum_{n\leq X/d}\lambda_{C}(an^{2}) $$

and wanting to track the dependency on $a$ above. Using Perron’s formula, we can rewrite the above in terms of $L(s,\text{sym}^{2}(C))$ and $\zeta(s)^{-1}$ . Since $C(z)$ is a cusp form, $L(s,\text{sym}^{2}(C))$ can have at most a pole of order one at $s=1$ (see [45] for a criteria for when there is a pole); thus, $L(s,\text{sym}^{2}(C))\zeta(s)^{-1}$ converges at $s=1$ . This allows us to derive a bound

$$ \sum_{d\leq X}\mu(d)\sum_{n\leq X/d}\lambda_{C}(an^{2})\ll\mathfrak{S}_{a}X\log(X)^{-10}, $$

where $\mathfrak{S}_{a}$ is a finite product over the primes dividing $a$ . When $C(z)$ is induced by a class group character, we have explicit bounds on $\mathfrak{S}_{a}$ ; in particular, the following holds for primes $p$ :

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{p}=\begin{cases}2+O(1/p^{2/3}),&\chi(p)=1,\\
O(1/p^{2/3}),&\chi(p)=-1.\end{cases} $$

Plugging the asymptotic above in and applying Nair’s sieve as before, we achieve that the contribution from the cuspidal components with finite image is bounded by

$$ \ll B\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq B^{1/2}}\frac{\mathfrak{S}_{F(u,v)}}{\max(|u|,|v|)^{2}}\log(B/\max(|u|,|v|)^{2})^{-10}\ll B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}. $$

This is again negligible compared to the main term of size $B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}.$

In the Grössencharacter case, i.e. (2.4), we aim to acheive a small power of $\log(B)$ savings from the absolute values of the Fourier coefficients of $\Xi$ . For this argument, we apply the same version of Nair’s sieve above with our non-negative multiplicative function now taken to be $|\lambda_{\Xi}(n)|$ . Consequently, we have that

$$ \sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}|\lambda_{\Xi}(t^{2}F(u,v))|\ll\frac{B}{t}\cdot\prod_{p\ll B/t}\left(1+\frac{(|\lambda_{\Xi}(p)|-1)\cdot\#\{x\bmod p:f(x)\equiv 0\bmod p\}}{p}\right). $$

To understand the above product, we study the sum

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{p}\subset\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})}\\
N(\mathfrak{p})\ll B/t\end{subarray}}\frac{\#\{x\bmod N(\mathfrak{p}):f(x)\equiv 0\bmod N(\mathfrak{p})\}}{2N(\mathfrak{p})}\cdot|\xi(\mathfrak{p})+\xi(\mathfrak{p})^{-1}|. $$

One can show that when $p$ splits in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ ,

$$ |\lambda_{\Xi}(p)|-1\leq\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}\lambda_{\Xi^{2}}(p). $$

When $p$ does not split in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ , by definition $|\lambda_{\Xi}(p)|-1=-1$ . Using (2.7), we can reduce (2.6) to analyzing

$$ \left(\frac{-1}{4}+\frac{3}{4}(\rho_{\Delta,f}-2)\right)\log\log(B/t)+O(1)+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{p}\subset\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})}\\
N(\mathfrak{p})\ll B/t\end{subarray}}\frac{\xi^{2}(\mathfrak{p})\#\{x\bmod N(\mathfrak{p}):f(x)\equiv 0\bmod N(\mathfrak{p})\}}{N(\mathfrak{p})}. $$

It remains to understand the final sum. At this point, we recall that we only analyze this sum $\Xi$ is induced by a Grössencharacter $\xi$ , and hence $\xi^{2}$ is nontrivial. We must then lift the nontrivial Hecke character $\xi^{2}$ to $K_{f}$ , the splitting field of $f(z)$ over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ , to understand the sum above; in other words, we need to understand the base change of $\xi^{2}$ to $K_{f}$ . This new Hecke character $\tilde{\xi}=\xi^{2}\circ N_{K_{f}/\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})}$ on $K_{f}$ is necessarily nontrivial since $\xi$ had infinite order; it is, however, not true that the base change of $\xi$ to $K_{f}$ is always nontrivial if we remove the assumption that $\xi$ has infinite order.

The prime ideal theorem for Hecke Grössencharacters determines that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{p}\subset\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})}\\
N(\mathfrak{p})\ll B/t\end{subarray}}\frac{\xi^{2}(\mathfrak{p})\#\{x\bmod N(\mathfrak{p}):f(x)\equiv 0\bmod N(\mathfrak{p})\}}{N(\mathfrak{p})}=o(\log\log(B/t)). $$

Consequently, for such character $\xi$ ,

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}|\lambda_{\Xi}(t^{2}F(u,v))|\ll\sum_{t\leq B}\frac{B}{t}\cdot\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2-1/5}\ll B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1-1/5}. $$

We remark that this approach was given in [34] by Heath-Brown and our approach is strongly inspired by his work. We also note that our savings here is large enough to overcome the fact that we have moved from summing over $(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ to $|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}$ as long as $w(B)\leq\log(B)^{-1/49}.$

We would like to highlight that this approach to the Grössencharacter case can also be used to approach (2.3) in most cases. In particular, we only require that the base change of $\xi^{2}$ to $K_{f}$ to be a nontrivial Hecke character to achieve a small polylogarithmic savings; this lift will be acceptable unless $K_{f}$ is not independent from the Hilbert class field of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta}).$

Finally, we comment on how this technique can be applied to a wider class of cusp forms. For instance, let $C(z)\in S_{1}(\Gamma_{0}(-\Delta),\chi)$ be a cusp form and consider the sum

$$ \sum_{|u|,|v|\leq X}|\lambda_{C}(t^{2}F(u,v))|\ll\frac{B}{t}\cdot\prod_{p\ll B/t}\left(1+\frac{(|\lambda_{C}(p)|-1)\cdot\#\{x\bmod p:f(x)\equiv 0\bmod p\}}{p}\right). $$

We have again applied Nair’s sieve here. We can replace (2.7) with Hecke relations:

$$ |\lambda_{C}(p)|-1\leq-\frac{1}{18}+\frac{4}{9}\lambda_{\text{sym}^{2}(C)}(p)-\frac{1}{18}\lambda_{\text{sym}^{4}(C)}(p). $$

We can then proceed with the argument above under the assumption of certain analytic properties of the base change of $\text{sym}^{2}(C)$ and $\text{sym}^{4}(C)$ to $K_{f}$ . In summary, the savings in this bound, despite the addition of absolute values around the Fourier coefficients, comes from the early Sato-Tate moments of $C(z)$ and its base change to $K_{f}$ . This idea will be expanded upon in forthcoming work.

Finally, we return to the Eisenstein contribution, i.e. the main term and how we determine when $c_{\Delta,f}$ is zero. Let us define $\xi(s;f,\chi)$ to be the following Dirichlet series for $\Re(s)>1:$

$$ \xi(s;f,\chi)=\sum_{d_{i}}\frac{\chi(d_{1}\cdots d_{r})\#\{x\bmod d_{1}\cdots d_{r}:d_{i}\mid f_{i}(x)\}}{(d_{1}\cdots d_{r})^{s}}. $$

For every irreducible factor $f_{i}(z)$ of $f(z)$ , let us take $K_{i}=\mathbb{Q}[z]/f_{i}(z)$ . Then we will see that

$$ \xi(s;f,\chi)=A_{\Delta,f}(s)\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{r}L_{K_{i}}(s,\chi),\hskip 28.45274ptA_{\Delta,f}(1)\neq 0 $$

where $L_{K_{i}}(s,\chi)$ is the quadratic twist of the Dedekind zeta function $\zeta_{K_{i}}(s)$ by $\chi$ and $A_{\Delta,f}(s)$ converges for $\Re(s)>3/4$ . We will see that the order of the pole at $s=1$ of $L_{K_{i}}(s,\chi)$ is one if $\sqrt{-\Delta}\in K_{i}$ and zero otherwise. As a consequence, $\xi(s;f,\chi)$ has a pole of order $\rho_{\Delta,f}-2$ at $s=1$ .

Since $\xi(s;f,\chi)$ is intimately tied to our sum over $d_{i}\leq D_{i}$ in our main term (2.5), we find that (2.5) can be re-written as

$$ BL^{2}\log(B)\sum_{(c_{1},...,c_{r})}^{\prime}\mu(c_{1}\cdots c_{r})\chi(c_{1}\cdots c_{r})\sum_{(a_{i})\bmod\Delta}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1+\chi(a_{i}))\#\{\mathbf{x}\bmod\Delta:F_{i}(\mathbf{x})\equiv c_{i}a_{i}\bmod\Delta\}\\
\times\textrm{Res}_{s=1}\xi(s;f,\chi)\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}\times\prod_{p\mid c_{1}\cdots c_{r}}\mathfrak{S}_{p}, $$

where $\mathfrak{S}_{p}$ are local factors. It should be noted that $c_{1}\cdots c_{r}$ itself must divide the product of resultants $\prod_{i\neq j}\textrm{Res}(f_{i},f_{j})$ and so this is a finite product.

In §12, we will show that if

$$ \sum_{a_{i}\bmod\Delta}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1+\chi(a_{i}))\cdot\#\{\mathbf{x}\bmod\Delta:F_{i}(\mathbf{x})\equiv c_{i}a_{i}\bmod\Delta\}=0 $$

then for some $p\mid\Delta$ , $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},c_{1},...,c_{r}}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})=\emptyset$ (the expression above is an oversimplification, but we later notate the more complicated relevant expression as $\bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c})$ ). We remark that the true (more complicated) computation involves a sum over genus characters as well. After some manipulations, we further see that if the contribution from a particular tuple $(c_{1},\dots,c_{r})$ to the sum above is zero, then for some $p\mid c_{1}\dots c_{r}\Delta$ , we indeed have that $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},\dots,f_{r},c_{1},\dots,c_{r}}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})=\emptyset.$ Moreover, we show that these are all of the possible local obstructions to $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},c_{1},...,c_{r}}$ and that the finite set of $(c_{1},...,c_{r})$ in the restricted sum are the only ones necessary to consider.

Consequently, we have the following statement: if our leading constant $c_{\Delta,f}$ is zero then for every vector $(c_{1},...,c_{r})$ , there is a local obstruction to rational points on the torsor $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},c_{1},...,c_{r}}$ . Finally, the results of Colliot-Thélène, Coray, and Sansuc [9, 12] and Harari’s “formal lemma”[32] (see Theorem 12.2) allows us to interpret this result in terms of the Brauer-Manin obstruction; specifically, if the leading constant $c_{\Delta,f}=0$ then there is either a Brauer-Manin obstruction or local obstruction to rational points on $X_{\Delta,f}$ . We remark that in §12.1 we discuss in detail the case when $f(z)$ is irreducible and there is only one auxiliary variety – $X_{\Delta,f}$ itself; in this case, our leading constant is a single product. In Appendix A, we show that in the case that $\Delta>0$ is prime and $f(z)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ , this product is the expected product of local densities.

## 3. Background and notation

### 3.1. Notation

First, let us establish the notation that we will use for the remainder of the paper.

- • $f$ will always denote a single variable polynomial and $F$ a binary form,

- • $f(z)=f_{1}...f_{r}(z)$ is the decomposition of $f(z)$ into irreducible polynomials,

- • $d\sim D$ if $d\in[D,2D]$ ,

- • $e(\alpha)=\exp(2\pi i\alpha)$ ,

- • $e_{p}(\alpha)=\exp(2\pi i\alpha/p),$

- • $\log_{k}(x)=\log\log\log...\log(x)$ where there are $k$ -iterated logarithms,

- • If $\mathbf{v}=(v_{i})$ denotes a vector, then the lower-case unbolded letter $v$ denotes the product of the entries of $\mathbf{v}$ ,

- • $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ is the quadratic field extension generated by $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}$ ,

- • $N(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})=x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}$ ,

- • $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ is the ring of integers of $K$ ,

- • $I$ , $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{p},\mathfrak{t},\mathfrak{k}$ will denote ideals of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ ,

- • $\mathcal{U}$ will denote the ring of units inside of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ ,

- • $C$ will denote the class group of $K$ ,

- • $\hat{C}$ will denote the group of class group characters of $K$ , which can also be viewed as Hecke characters of $K$ ,

- • $\chi$ will denote the real quadratic character such that $\zeta_{K}(s)=\zeta(s)L(s,\chi)$ , and we will denote the modulus of the character as $-\Delta;$ in other words,

$$ -\Delta:=\begin{cases}4\Delta,&\Delta>0,\\ -\Delta,&\Delta<0,\end{cases} $$

- • We define the $\Delta$ -part of an integer $n$ as:

$$ p_{-\Delta}(n)=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\textrm{ prime}\\ p^{e}\|n\\ p\mid-\Delta\end{subarray}}p^{e}. $$

We also define the part of $n$ coprime to $\Delta$ as

$$ p_{\neg-\Delta}(n)=n/p_{-\Delta}(n)=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\textrm{ prime}\\ p^{e}\|n\\ p\nmid-\Delta\end{subarray}}p^{e}, $$

- • $K_{f_{i}}$ denotes splitting field of $f_{i}$ over $K$ and $K_{f}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}K_{f_{i}}$ ,

- • $\mathfrak{P}$ will denote a prime ideal on $\mathcal{O}_{K_{f}}$ ,

- • For a binary form $F(u,v)$ , we denote

$$ \varrho_{F}(n):=\#\{(u,v)\bmod n:F(u,v)\equiv 0\bmod n\} $$

and the related count

$$ \varrho_{F}^{*}(n):=\#\{(u,v)\bmod n:\gcd(u,v,n)=1,F(u,v)\equiv 0\bmod n\}. $$

We also consider the single-variable version of this local count:

$$ \varrho_{f}(n):=\#\{x\bmod n:f(x)\equiv 0\bmod n\}. $$

- • We define the Dirichlet series for $\Re(s)>1$ : (3.1)

$$ \xi(s;f,\chi)=\prod_{p}\left(1+\frac{\chi(p)\varrho_{f}(p)}{p^{s}}\right). $$

We also introduce some notation specific to the indefinite case, i.e. when $\Delta<0$ . In this case, $K$ is a real quadratic field.

#### Definition 3.1.

Let $(x_{0},y_{0})$ denote the fundamental solution to Pell’s equation $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=1$ . Then we write $\varepsilon=x_{0}+y_{0}\sqrt{-\Delta}$ as the fundamental unit. Every element of $u\in\mathcal{U}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}$ will satisfy that for some $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ ,

$$ u=\varepsilon^{k}. $$

Next, let us fix $(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}$ . Then we define two new variables:

$$ \alpha=x+y\sqrt{-\Delta},\textrm{ }\overline{\alpha}=x-y\sqrt{-\Delta}. $$

Then we say that $(x,y)$ (or $\alpha$ ) is minimal if $x\geq 0$ and

$$ 1\leq\left|\frac{\alpha}{\overline{\alpha}}\right|\leq|\varepsilon^{2}|. $$

We note that for any principal ideal $I$ , there will be an unique minimal generator $(x,y)$ such that $(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})=(\alpha)=I$ . We denote the minimal element of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ equivalent to $(x,y)$ up to a unit as $(x,y)\bmod\varepsilon$ . We may also denote this element as $\alpha\bmod\varepsilon.$

Finally, let us define our Hecke Grössencharacter $\Psi$ that will detect the “argument” of $\alpha$ , as alluded to in the outline. This definition is inspired by the choice of Grössencharacter taken by Heath-Brown in [34].

#### Definition 3.2.

Define the Hecke character $\Psi$ on principal ideals $I=(\alpha)$ to be:

$$ \Psi(I)=\textrm{sgn}(\alpha\overline{\alpha})\exp\left(\pi i\cdot\frac{\log|\alpha|-\log|\overline{\alpha}|}{\log|\varepsilon|}\right). $$

$\Psi$ can then be lifted trivially to the set of all ideals of $\mathcal{O}_{K}.$

#### Remark 3.3.

Note that $\Psi$ is indeed well-defined on ideals as the following holds:

$$ \log|\varepsilon\alpha|-\log|\overline{\varepsilon\alpha}|=2\log|\varepsilon|+\log|\alpha|-\log|\overline{\alpha}|. $$

Additionally, we know that $|\Psi(\mathfrak{a})|=1$ for any ideal $\mathfrak{a}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K},$ so $\Psi$ is a nontrivial unitary Hecke Grössencharacter.

### 3.2. Hooley’s $\Delta$ -function

Next, we recall the definition and state our notation for the following arithmetic functions:

#### Definition 3.4.

The divisor function will be denoted as

$$ \tau(n):=\sum_{d\mid n}1. $$

#### Definition 3.5.

Hooley’s $\Delta$ -function is defined as

$$ \Delta(n):=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}D\in\mathbb{R},0\leq v\leq 1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\mid n\\
d\in[D,e^{v}D]\end{subarray}}1. $$

We note that the average of $\tau(n)$ satisfies

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}\tau(n)\sim X\log(X). $$

On the other hand, the average of the $\Delta$ -function has a small saving:

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}\Delta(n)\ll X\log(X)^{o(1)}. $$

This feature is particularly useful in our level of distribution result proved in §9, since we will need to be careful about tracking any and all powers of $\log(X)$ . We will use the following case of a more general theorem proved by de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum in [27].

#### Theorem 3.6 (de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum, [27, (1.7)]).

Let $f\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be an irreducible polynomial. Then the following bound holds:

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}\Delta(n)\varrho_{f}(n)\ll_{f}X\log\log(X)^{5/2}. $$

Next, we introduce the twisted Hooley $\Delta$ -function by the quadratic character $\chi$ .

#### Definition 3.7.

The Hooley $\Delta$ -function twisted by $\chi$ is defined as

$$ \Delta(n,\chi):=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}D\in\mathbb{R}\\
0\leq v\leq 1\end{subarray}}\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\mid n\\
d\in[D,e^{v}D]\end{subarray}}\chi(d)\right|. $$

Observe that $\Delta(n,\chi)\leq\Delta(n)\leq\tau(n)$ for all $n$ .

#### Remark 3.8.

We also note that the following inequalities hold:

$$ \Delta(n)\geq\sup_{D\in\mathbb{R}}\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\mid n\\
d\sim D\end{subarray}}1\right|=:\Delta_{2}(n), $$

$$ \Delta(n,\chi)\geq\sup_{D\in\mathbb{R}}\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\mid n\\
d\sim D\end{subarray}}\chi(d)\right|=:\Delta_{2}(n,\chi). $$

This falls from the fact that $2\leq e^{v}$ for some $0\leq v\leq 1.$

In [22], de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum showed that the average of $\Delta(n,\chi)^{2}$ is smaller than the average of the divisor function. Moreover, this bound also holds for correlations of $\Delta(n,\chi)^{2}$ with the number of local solutions of a polynomial.

#### Theorem 3.9 (de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum, [22, Theorem 1.1]).

For $\chi$ a nonprincipal quadratic character mod $M$ and $f\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ a polynomial irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-M})$ . Then, the following bound holds for an explicit constant $c_{f,M}>0$ :

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}\Delta(n,\chi)^{2}\varrho_{f}(n)\ll_{\chi,F}X\exp(c_{f,M}\sqrt{\log_{2}(X)\log_{3}(X)}). $$

### 3.3. A sieve on binary forms

We will often need a sieve for averages of non-negative multiplicative functions along polynomial values. The concept for this sieve was first introduced by Nair in [42] for the average of multiplicative functions along single-variable polynomials; later, this work was generalized by Nair and Tenenbaum in [41].

#### Theorem 3.10 (Nair [42]).

Let $f\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be a squarefree polynomial with no fixed prime divisors. Let $g$ be a non-negative multiplicative function that is uniformly bounded on prime values. Then we have that

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}g(|f(n)|)\ll_{g}X\prod_{p\leq X}\left(1-\frac{\varrho_{f}(p)}{p}\right)\exp\left(\sum_{p\leq X}\frac{g(p)\varrho_{f}(p)}{p}\right). $$

This sieve was first generalized to binary forms by de la Bretèche and Browning [19] for irreducible forms. The most general version for binary forms was established by de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum in [24], and this is the result that we shall use.

Define $M_{k}(A,B,\epsilon)$ to be a class of sub-multiplicative functions in $k$ variables satisfying for $G\in M_{k}(A,B,\epsilon)$ ,

$$ G(a_{1},...,a_{k})\leq\min(A^{\Omega(a_{1}...a_{k})},B(a_{1}...a_{k})^{\epsilon}). $$

We note that $\tau(n),\Delta(n),\Delta(n,\chi)$ all belong to $M_{1}(2,B(x)=x,\epsilon).$

#### Theorem 3.11 (de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum, [24, Theorem 1.1]).

Assume $G\in M_{k}(A,B,\epsilon)$ for a fixed $A,B\geq 1$ . Let $F(x,y)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}F_{i}(x,y)$ be a squarefree product of primitive binary forms. Fix $\alpha>0$ and assume that $Y\geq X^{\alpha}$ and $x_{0},y_{0}\in[X,2X]$ . Then we have that

$$ \sum_{x,y\in[x_{0},x_{0}+Y]\times[y_{0},y_{0}+Y]}G(|F_{1}(x,y)|,...,|F_{k}(x,y)|)\ll_{A,B,\alpha}Y^{2}E(X+Y)\prod_{p\leq X+Y}\left(1-\frac{\varrho_{F}(p)}{p^{2}}\right), $$

where we define

$$ E(X+Y)=\sum_{s=s_{1}...s_{k}\leq X+Y}G(s_{1},...,s_{k})\frac{\#\{x,y\bmod s:s_{i}\mid F_{i}(x,y)\forall i\}}{s^{2}}. $$

In particular, if $g(n)$ is a non-negative multiplicative function bounded by $\tau(n)$ and $F(x,y)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}F_{i}(x,y)$ is a squarefree primitive binary form, then we have that

$$ \sum_{x,y\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}g(F_{i}(x,y))\ll X^{2}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\prod_{p\leq X}\left(1+\frac{\varrho_{F_{i}}(p)(g(p)-1)}{p^{2}}\right). $$

Sometimes, we will wish to apply the following corollary of Theorem 3.11 where we specify certain divisors of $F(x,y)$ :

#### Corollary 3.12.

Let $F(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y]$ be an irreducible primitive binary form and $g\in M_{1}(A,B,\epsilon)$ . We say that $g(t)=0$ if $t\not\in\mathbb{Z}$ . Then we have that

$$ \sum_{x,y\leq X}g(|F(x,y)/c|)\ll_{A,B}\frac{X^{2}(A^{\deg(F)}\cdot\deg(F))^{\Omega(c)}}{c}\prod_{p\ll X}\left(1+\frac{\varrho_{F}(p)(g(p)-1)}{p^{2}}\right). $$

#### Proof.

We rearrange our sum as:

$$ \sum_{x,y\leq X}g(|F(x,y)/c|)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\bmod c\\
c\mid F(\alpha)\end{subarray}}\sum_{x,y\ll X/c}g(|F_{\alpha}(x,y)/c|), $$

where we define $F_{\alpha}(x,y)=F(cx+\alpha_{1},cy+\alpha_{2}).$ Since $c\mid F(\alpha)$ , we have that $F_{\alpha}(x,y)/c$ is itself an irreducible binary form with integer coefficients. Moreover, $F_{\alpha}(x,y)/c=c^{e_{\alpha}}\tilde{F}_{\alpha}(x,y)$ for some primitive binary form $\tilde{F}_{\alpha}$ and power $e_{\alpha}\leq\deg(F)$ . So, we use submultiplicativity and apply Theorem 3.11 to the inside sums. Hence, we have the relation:

$$ \sum_{x,y\ll X/c}g(|F_{\alpha}(x,y)/c|)\ll\frac{X^{2}A^{e_{\alpha}\Omega(c)}}{c^{2}}\prod_{p\ll X}\left(1+\frac{\varrho_{F_{\alpha}/c}(p)(g(p)-1)}{p^{2}}\right). $$

Since $g\in M_{1}(A,B,\epsilon)$ , we can see the contribution from the primes $p\mid c$ is bounded by $A^{\omega(c)}$ . So, let us assume from now on that $p\nmid c$ . Now, we consider

$$ \varrho_{F_{\alpha}/c}(p)=\#\{\mathbf{x}\bmod p:F_{\alpha}(x,y)/c\equiv 0\bmod p\}=\#\{\mathbf{x}\bmod p:F(cx+\alpha_{1},cy+\alpha_{2})\equiv 0\bmod p\}. $$

For $p\nmid c$ , we know that $c$ is invertible in $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ and thus we get that $\varrho_{F_{\alpha}/c}(p)=\varrho_{F}(p).$

So, our original sum can be bounded by

$$ \sum_{x,y\leq X}g(|F(x,y)/c|)\ll X^{2}\cdot\frac{A^{\deg(F)\cdot\Omega(c)}}{c^{2}}\cdot\prod_{p\ll X}\left(1+\frac{\varrho_{F}(p)(g(p)-1)}{p^{2}}\right)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\bmod c\\
c\mid F(\alpha)\end{subarray}}1. $$

Finally, we recall that $\varrho_{F}(c)\leq c\deg(F)^{\omega(c)}$ . So, we have our desired bound.

∎

### 3.4. Upper bounds on fixed sizes of divisors

We introduce two lemmas that bound the contribution of large divisors of a polynomial. These results will be particularly useful in §10.

First, we write a result that bounds the number of integers with particularly large divisors; the following formulation was stated in [33] by Heath-Brown.

#### Lemma 3.13 (Heath-Brown, [33, Lemma 5.1]).

There exists an explicit constant $\eta>0$ such that

$$ \#\{m\ll X:\exists d\sim D,d\mid m\}\ll\frac{X}{\log(D)^{\eta}}. $$

Next, we introduce a modification of the above lemma for binary forms that was proved by de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum in [25].

#### Lemma 3.14 (de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum, [25, (7.41)]).

Let $F(x,y)$ be a binary quartic. Then there exists an explicit constant $\eta>0$ such that

$$ \#\{|x|,|y|\leq X:\exists d\sim D:d\mid F(x,y)\}\ll X^{2}\cdot\left(\frac{X^{2}/D+D/X^{2}+\log\log(X)}{\log(D)^{\eta}}\right). $$

We remark that in both of the cases above $\eta$ is explicit and greater than 1/1000.

### 3.5. Dirichlet series and Rankin-Selberg $L$ -functions

In this subsection, we will discuss the connection between $\xi(s;f,\chi)$ , and a quadratic twist of a Dedekind zeta function. First, we want to establish another similar Dirichlet series that will appear in our computations later. Recall from the notation section that for a vector $\mathbf{d}=(d_{1},\ldots,d_{r})$ , we write the product of the entries as $d=d_{1}\cdots d_{r}.$ Let $\Re(s)>1$ and define the following

$$ \xi(s;F,\chi)=\sum_{d_{i}=1}^{\infty}\frac{\chi(d)\varrho_{F}^{*}(\mathbf{d})}{d^{2s}}. $$

For vectors $(p_{1},\ldots,p_{r})$ with prime entries $p_{i}$ , we know that $\varrho_{F}^{*}((p_{i}))\leq 4^{r}$ ; so, $\xi(s;F,\chi)$ converges for all $\Re(s)>1$ . We also note that we have an Euler product for $\xi(s;F,\chi)$ :

$$ \prod_{p}\Bigg(1+\frac{\chi(p)}{p^{s}}\cdot(\varrho_{F}^{*}((p,1,\ldots,1))+\ldots+\varrho_{F}^{*}((1,\ldots,p)))\\
+\frac{\chi(p)^{2}}{p^{2s}}\cdot(\varrho_{F}^{*}((p,p,1,\ldots,1))+\ldots+\varrho_{F}^{*}((1,\ldots,p,p)))+\ldots\Bigg). $$

This expansion allows us to see that

$$ \xi(s;F,\chi)=S_{F,\chi}(s)\prod_{p}\left(1+\frac{\chi(p)}{p^{s}}\cdot(\varrho_{F}^{*}((p,1,\ldots,1))+\ldots+\varrho_{F}^{*}((1,\ldots,p)))\right), $$

where $S_{F,\chi}(s)$ converges for $\Re(s)>1/2.$

We note that at all but finitely many primes $p$ , we have that

$$ \varrho_{F}^{*}((p,1,\ldots,1))+\ldots+\varrho_{F}^{*}((1,\ldots,p))=\varrho_{f}(p)=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\varrho_{f_{i}}(p). $$

Here we recall from §3.1 that $\varrho_{f}(p)=\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x)=0\bmod p\}$ . Thus, we get that

$$ \xi(s;F,\chi)=R_{f,\chi}(s)S_{F,\chi}(s)S_{f,\chi}(s)\prod_{i=1}^{r}\xi(s;f_{i},\chi), $$

where we have that $R_{f,\chi}(s)$ a product over finitely many primes $p\mid F(1,0)$ and $S_{f,\chi}(s)$ converges for $\Re(s)>1/2.$ Now, this tells us that $\xi(s;F,\chi)$ has a pole at $s=1$ if and only if $\xi(s;f,\chi)$ has a pole at $s=1$ . The pole at $s=1$ of both of these functions will be determined by the pole of a quadratic twist of a Dedekind zeta function.

Define the field $L_{f_{i}}=\mathbb{Q}[z]/f_{i}(z)$ . Let us consider the $\zeta$ -function of $L_{f_{i}}$ :

$$ \zeta_{L_{f_{i}}}(s)=\prod_{\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{L_{f_{i}}}}\left(1+N(\mathfrak{P})^{-s}+N(\mathfrak{P})^{-2s}+\ldots\right). $$

It is known that $\zeta_{L_{f_{i}}}(s)$ has a meromorphic continuation to $\mathbb{C}$ , a functional equation, and a simple pole at $s=1$ . Since $\deg(f_{i})\leq 4$ , we know that the Galois group of $L_{f_{i}}$ is solvable. Thus, by the resolution of Dedekind’s conjecture for solvable groups by Uchida [47] and van der Waall [48], we have that

$$ \zeta_{L_{f_{i}}}(s)=\zeta(s)\prod_{\pi_{j}}L(s,\pi_{j}), $$

where $\pi_{j}$ are nontrivial irreducible representations and $L(s,\pi_{j})$ are entire.

Next, we can view the Dirichlet $L$ -function $L(s,\chi)$ as a $L$ -function of a nontrivial irreducible representation, which we denote by $\chi$ as well. Then the quadratic twist of $\zeta_{L_{f_{i}}}(s)$ by $\chi$ is given by:

$$ L(s;f_{i}\times\chi)=L(s,\chi)\prod_{\pi_{j}}L(s,\pi_{j}\times\chi). $$

We then have the following Dirichlet series and Euler product expansions for $\Re(s)>1:$

$$ L(s;f_{i}\times\chi)=\sum_{\mathfrak{A}\subset\mathcal{O}_{L_{f_{i}}}}\chi(N(\mathfrak{A}))N(\mathfrak{A})^{-s}=\prod_{\mathfrak{P}}\left(1+\chi(N(\mathfrak{P}))N(\mathfrak{P})^{-s}+\chi(N(\mathfrak{P}))^{2}N(\mathfrak{P})^{-2s}+\ldots\right). $$

Note that since $L_{f_{i}}=\mathbb{Q}[z]/f_{i}(z)$ , the following relation is true:

$$ \varrho_{f_{i}}(p)=\#\{\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{L_{f_{i}}}:N(\mathfrak{P})=p\}. $$

This tells us that

$$ \xi(s;f_{i},\chi)=S_{L_{f_{i}},\chi}(s)L(s;f_{i}\times\chi), $$

where $S_{L_{f_{i}},\chi}(s)$ converges for $\Re(s)>1/2.$ Thus, we get the following lemma:

#### Lemma 3.15.

The Dirichlet series $\xi(s;F,\chi)$ and $\xi(s;f,\chi)$ have meromorphic continuations to $\Re(s)>1/2.$ Additionally, assume that $L(s;f_{i}\times\chi)$ has a pole of order $m_{i}$ at $s=1$ . Then the order of the pole at $s=1$ of both $\xi(s;F,\chi)$ and $\xi(s;f,\chi)$ is given by $m_{1}+\ldots+m_{r}$ .

#### Corollary 3.16.

The order of the pole of $\xi(s;F,\chi)$ and $\xi(s;f,\chi)$ at $s=1$ is $\rho_{\Delta,f}-2,$ where $\rho_{\Delta,f}$ is defined in Conjecture 1.1.

#### Proof.

It suffices to show that the order of the pole at $s=1$ of $L(s;f_{i}\times\chi)$ is given by

$$ \begin{cases}1,&\sqrt{-\Delta}\in L_{f_{i}}\\
0,&\textrm{else.}\end{cases} $$

Since $\chi$ is nontrivial and $\pi_{j}$ are nontrivial irreducible representations, $L(s;f_{i}\times\chi)$ has a pole if and only if $\pi_{j}=\chi$ for some $j$ . This phenomenon occurs if and only if $\sqrt{-\Delta}\in\mathbb{Q}[z]/(f_{i}(z))=L_{f_{i}}.$ ∎

### 3.6. Theta series and class group characters

In this subsection, we will discuss the connection between this problem and modular forms, as alluded to in §2. Note that if $C$ is the class group of $K$ , then

$$ \mathbf{1}_{\mathfrak{a}\textrm{ is principal}}=\frac{1}{|C|}\sum_{\psi\in\hat{C}}\psi(\mathfrak{a}). $$

Consequently, we get that

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})=n}\mathbf{1}_{\mathfrak{a}\textrm{ is principal}}=\frac{1}{|C|}\sum_{\psi\in\hat{C}}\sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})=n}\psi(\mathfrak{a}). $$

On the other hand, consider the following function:

$$ \theta(z)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{a})=n\\
\mathfrak{a}\textrm{ is principal}\end{subarray}}e(z\cdot N(\mathfrak{a})). $$

As commented in [36, Equation (22.55)], for $\Delta>0$ , $\theta(z)$ will be a Mellin transform of an Epstein zeta function and will be a modular form of weight one in $M_{1}(\Gamma_{0}(-\Delta),\chi).$ In fact, if $\Delta>0$ , then this is a recognizable theta series:

$$ \theta(z)=\sum_{x,y}e(z\cdot(x^{2}+\Delta y^{2})). $$

Since $\theta(z)\in M_{1}(\Gamma_{0}(-\Delta),\chi)$ , we can decompose it into its Eisenstein and cuspidal part. We present the following explicit decomposition of the Fourier coefficients, as shown by Blomer in [3, Lemma 2.2] for $\Delta>0$ . This decomposition is also discussed by Fomenko in [30].

#### Lemma 3.17.

Let $\theta(z)=E(z)+C(z)$ , where $E(z)$ is an Eisenstein series and $C(z)$ is a cusp form. Let $\lambda_{E}(n)$ (resp. $\lambda_{C}(n)$ ) denote the Fourier coefficients of $E(z)$ (resp. $C(z)$ ). Then we have that

$$ \lambda_{E}(n)=\frac{1}{|C|}\sum_{\text{ord}(\psi)\leq 2}\sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})=n}\psi(\mathfrak{a}), $$

$$ \lambda_{C}(n)=\frac{1}{|C|}\sum_{\text{ord}(\psi)\geq 3}\sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})=n}\psi(\mathfrak{a}). $$

Additionally, Iwaniec discusses in [38, §12.5] how to express the Eisenstein term in even more detail when $K$ is a quadratic field. Because we are working with binary quadratic forms, the Eisenstein component contains not only the trivial component, but the contribution from all of the genus characters. Furthermore, we can describe these genus characters explicitly. Let $q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta$ and $\gcd(q_{1},q_{2})=1$ . Then all of our genus characters are of the form:

$$ \psi(\mathfrak{p})=\chi_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathfrak{p})=\begin{cases}\chi_{q_{1}}(N(\mathfrak{p})),&\mathfrak{p}\nmid q_{1},\\
\chi_{q_{2}}(N(\mathfrak{p})),&\mathfrak{p}\nmid q_{2}.\end{cases} $$

These correspond to a basis of Eisenstein series with Fourier coefficients given by

$$ \varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\chi_{q_{1}}(d)\chi_{q_{2}}(n/d), $$

with $\chi_{q_{1}},\chi_{q_{2}}$ real quadratic characters satisfying $\chi_{q_{1}}\chi_{q_{2}}=\chi$ when $\gcd(n,-\Delta)=1.$ Note that the trivial character corresponds to $q_{1}=1$ and $q_{2}=-\Delta.$ Thus, we get that

$$ \lambda_{E}(n)=\frac{1}{|C|}\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(n). $$

Here the restricted sum is due to the fact that while all genus characters are of the form $\chi_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathfrak{p})$ , not all decompositions $q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta$ with $\gcd(q_{1},q_{2})=1$ correspond to genus characters.

In particular, let

$$ |\Delta|=\prod_{i=1}^{r}p_{i}. $$

Then the genus field is given by

$$ K(\sqrt{p_{1}^{*}},\ldots,\sqrt{p_{r}^{*}}) $$

where if $p_{i}$ is an odd prime then

$$ p_{i}^{*}=\begin{cases}p,&p\equiv 1\bmod 4,\\
-p,&p\equiv 3\bmod 4,\end{cases} $$

and when $p_{i}=2$ ,

$$ 2^{*}=\begin{cases}1,&\Delta\equiv 1\bmod 4,\\
-4,&\Delta\equiv 3\bmod 4,\\
8,&\Delta\equiv 2\bmod 8,\\
-8,&\Delta\equiv-2\bmod 8.\end{cases} $$

The genus characters included in the restricted sum for $\lambda_{E}(n)$ are therefore those that correspond to characters of the genus field. We will apply the above decompositions in §5.

## 4. Upper bounds

In this section, we will establish some upper bounds for $N(X_{\Delta,f},B)$ that are necessary for our proof. First, we recall that an upper bound of the correct order of magnitude was established by Browning [4] for the positive-definite case.

#### Theorem 4.1 (Browning, [4]).

Assume that $\Delta>0$ is a nonsquare integer. Then as $B\rightarrow\infty$ , we have that

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},B)\ll B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}. $$

We will need a similar upper bound for this counting function on short boxes $N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1})$ ; more explicitly, we will need upper bounds on

$$ S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1}):=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\#\Big\{((x,y),(u,v),t)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{+}:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v),\\
0<t\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)}),(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\|x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}\|,\|x-y\sqrt{-\Delta}\|\leq\nu_{\Delta,f}B,\\
\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1\Big\}. $$

In the above sum, we have already removed the large torsors – this process will occur in §5.1 before our applications of the lemmas below.

#### Lemma 4.2.

Assume that $\Delta>0$ is a nonsquare integer. If $L\gg\exp(-(\log(B))^{1/3})$ , then we have that

$$ S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1})\ll L^{2}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1} $$

#### Proof.

We first expand the definition of $S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1})$ :

$$ S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1})\ll\sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\end{subarray}}\#\{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v),\gcd(x,y,t)=1\}, $$

Our first step is to rewrite this inner count with a sum over ideals. Consider the principal ideal $I=(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})$ . Since $\gcd(x,y,t)=1$ and $N(I)=t^{2}F(u,v)$ , we know that for any prime $p$ dividing $t$ , we must have that $(p)=\mathfrak{p}\overline{\mathfrak{p}}$ splits in $K$ and that $(p)$ does not divide $I$ . As a result, we can write

$$ I=\mathfrak{t}^{2}\mathfrak{a} $$

where $N(\mathfrak{t})=t$ , $N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)$ , and $\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1.$ Additionally, we have that $\gcd(t,I,\overline{I})=1,$ which occurs if and only if $\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1.$ Here we write that $\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b})=1$ if $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{b}$ do not share any common prime ideal factors. We point out that from now on we use the convention that $N(\mathfrak{t})=t$ .

So, we can bound the above sum by:

$$ S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1})\ll\sum_{N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B}\sum_{(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)}\#\{\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\}. $$

Next, we can bound this sum of ideals as follows:

$$ \#\{\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=n\}\ll(1\star\chi)(n), $$

and henceforth replace $\#\{\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\}$ by $(1\star\chi)(F(u,v))$ in the sum above.

Note that $(1\star\chi)(n)$ is a non-negative multiplicative function that is bounded by $\tau(n)$ . Applying Theorem 3.11, we get the following upper bound:

$$ \displaystyle S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1}) \displaystyle\ll\sum_{N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B}\sum_{(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)}(1\star\chi)(F(u,v)) \displaystyle\ll\sum_{N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B}\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{t})}\cdot BL^{2}\prod_{p\ll B/t}\left(1+\frac{\varrho_{f}(p)\chi(p)}{p}\right). $$

We recognize this product over primes as the factors in the Euler product of $\xi(s;f,\chi)$ . Since $\xi(s;f,\chi)$ has a pole of order $\rho_{\Delta,f}-2$ at $s=1$ (Corollary 3.16), we achieve that

$$ \displaystyle S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1}) \displaystyle\ll L^{2}B\sum_{N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B}\frac{1}{t}\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2} \displaystyle\ll L^{2}\cdot B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}. $$

∎

For the indefinite case, we can similarly achieve an optimal upper bound.

#### Lemma 4.3.

Assume that $\Delta<0$ is an integer. If $L\gg\exp(-(\log(B))^{1/3})$ , then we have that

$$ S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1})\ll\left(\left|\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{\log|\varepsilon|}\right|+O(1)\right)L^{2}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}. $$

#### Proof.

We first expand the definition of $S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1}):$

$$ S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1})\ll\sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}\bmod\varepsilon\\
x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)\end{subarray}}\#\{k\in\mathbb{Z}:|\varepsilon^{k}\alpha|,|\overline{\varepsilon}^{k}\overline{\alpha}|\leq B\}. $$

Consider the count of units

$$ \#\{k\in\mathbb{Z}:|\varepsilon^{k}\alpha|,|\overline{\varepsilon}^{k}\overline{\alpha}|\leq B\}. $$

We can see that

$$ |\varepsilon^{k}\alpha|\leq B\iff k\leq\frac{\log(B)}{\log|\varepsilon|}-\frac{\log|\alpha|}{\log|\varepsilon|}. $$

Since $\alpha$ is minimal, we have by definition that

$$ 1\leq\frac{|\alpha|}{|\overline{\alpha}|}=\frac{|\alpha|^{2}}{\alpha\overline{\alpha}}\leq|\varepsilon|^{2}. $$

Because $\alpha\overline{\alpha}=t^{2}F(u,v)$ , we can see that

$$ \frac{\log|\alpha|}{\log|\varepsilon|}=\frac{\log|t^{2}F(u,v)|}{2\log|\varepsilon|}+O(1). $$

On the other hand, since $(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ , we have that

$$ \frac{\log|t^{2}F(u,v)|}{2\log|\varepsilon|}=\frac{\log(B)}{\log|\varepsilon|}+\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{2\log|\varepsilon|}+O(L). $$

Thus, we have that

$$ |\varepsilon^{k}\alpha|\leq B\iff k\leq\left|\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{2\log|\varepsilon|}\right|+O(1). $$

A similar computation with $|\overline{\varepsilon}^{k}\overline{\alpha}|$ reveals an analogous lower bound. So, we have that

$$ \#\{k\in\mathbb{Z}:|\varepsilon^{k}\alpha|,|\overline{\varepsilon}^{k}\overline{\alpha}|\leq B\}=\left|\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{\log|\varepsilon|}\right|+O(1). $$

Plugging this in above, we can see the following:

$$ \displaystyle S(X_{\Delta,f}, \displaystyle\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1})\ll\left(\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{\log|\varepsilon|}+O(1)\right)\sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\end{subarray}}\#\{\alpha\bmod\varepsilon:\alpha\overline{\alpha}=t^{2}F(u,v)\} \displaystyle\ll\left(\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{\log|\varepsilon|}+O(1)\right)\sum_{N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B}\sum_{(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)}\#\{\mathfrak{a}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}:N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\}. $$

Now, as in the positive-definite case, we can again use the following bound:

$$ \#\{N(\mathfrak{a})=n\}\ll(1\star\chi)(n). $$

So, we can apply Theorem 3.11:

$$ \displaystyle S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1}) \displaystyle\ll\left(\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{\log|\varepsilon|}+O(1)\right)\sum_{N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B}\sum_{(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)}(1\star\chi)(t^{2}F(u,v)) \displaystyle\ll\left(\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{\log|\varepsilon|}+O(1)\right)\sum_{N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B}\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{t})}\cdot BL^{2}\prod_{p\ll B/t}\left(1+\frac{\varrho_{f}(p)\chi(p)}{p}\right) \displaystyle\ll\left(\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{\log|\varepsilon|}+O(1)\right)L^{2}B\sum_{N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B}\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{t})}\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2} \displaystyle\ll\left(\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{\log|\varepsilon|}+O(1)\right)L^{2}\cdot B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}. $$

Again, we have used that the product over primes is related to $\xi(s;f,\chi)$ , which has a pole of order $\rho_{\Delta,f}-2$ at $s=1$ (Corollary 3.16).

∎

#### Remark 4.4.

Intuitively, we expect for a generic $\alpha$ that

$$ \#\{k\in\mathbb{Z}:|\varepsilon^{k}\alpha|,|\overline{\varepsilon}^{k}\overline{\alpha}|\leq B\}=O(1). $$

However, we also expect that for certain $\alpha$ , this quantity can be as large as $\log(B)$ . This discrepancy is now hidden in the $\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|/\log|\varepsilon|$ term, as $\mathbf{x}_{0}$ ranges over values in $[-1,1]^{2}$ . For most $\mathbf{x}_{0}$ , $|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|$ is of approximately constant size, but for a small subset of $\mathbf{x}_{0}$ , the value $|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|$ can be quite small.

## 5. Initial reductions

In §2, we discussed that a key ingredient in our proof is a restriction to short boxes and the use of Hecke Grössencharacters. In this section, we will demonstrate explicitly why these tools are crucial for our method. First, we recall some notation. Let $\mathbf{x}_{0}\in[-1,1]^{2}$ and $L$ be length to be determined later. Recall that we denote:

$$ \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L):=\mathbf{x}_{0}+[0,L]^{2}. $$

### 5.1. Removal of large torsors

We will first remove the contribution from the large torsors – when $t\in[B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)}),B]$ .

#### Lemma 5.1.

Assume that $\Delta$ is a squarefree integer and $\sqrt{-\Delta}\not\in\mathbb{Q}$ . Define the contribution from large $t$ as:

$$ L(X_{\Delta,f},B):=\#\Big\{((x,y),(u,v),t)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{+}:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v),\\
|u|,|v|\in(B/t)^{1/2},\|x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}\|,\|x-y\sqrt{-\Delta}\|\leq\nu_{\Delta,f}B,\\
t\in[B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)},B],\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1\Big\}. $$

Then we have the upper bound:

$$ L(X_{\Delta,f},B)\ll B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-3/2}. $$

#### Proof.

Fix a $t\in[B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)}),B]$ for now. First, assume that $\Delta>0$ ; then, we have that

$$ \#\{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v):|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2},\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1\}\\
\ll\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}\#\{\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=t^{2}F(u,v)\}\ll(1\star\chi)(t)\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}\#\{\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\}. $$

The above comes from the initial analysis of the sum in Lemma 4.2. Since $\#\{\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=n\}\ll(1\star\chi)(n)$ and this is a non-negative multiplicative function, we apply Theorem 3.11 to achieve

$$ \displaystyle\#\{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v): \displaystyle|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2},\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1\} \displaystyle\ll\frac{B\cdot(1\star\chi)(t)}{t}\prod_{p\ll B/t}\left(1+\frac{\varrho_{f}(p)\chi(p)}{p}\right)\ll\frac{B\cdot(1\star\chi)(t)}{t}\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}. $$

Next, consider when $\Delta<0$ . We claim that the same upper bound holds for a fixed large $t$ . In Lemma 4.3, we saw that

$$ \#\{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v):|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2},\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1\}\\
\ll\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha=x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}\bmod\varepsilon\\
x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)\end{subarray}}\#\{k\in\mathbb{Z}:|\varepsilon^{k}\alpha|,|\overline{\varepsilon}^{k}\overline{\alpha}|\leq B\}\\
\ll(1\star\chi)(t)\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}\left(\frac{\log(B)}{\log|\varepsilon|}-\frac{\log|t^{2}F(u,v)|}{2\log|\varepsilon|}+O(1)\right)\#\{N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\}\\
\ll\frac{B\cdot(1\star\chi)(t)}{t}\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}+\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}\left(\frac{\log(B)}{\log|\varepsilon|}-\frac{\log|t^{2}F(u,v)|}{2\log|\varepsilon|}\right)\#\{N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\}. $$

Since $|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}$ , we have that $t^{2}F(u,v)=B^{2}F(\mathbf{y})$ for some $\mathbf{y}\in[-1,1]^{2}$ . So, we get that

$$ \frac{\log(B)}{\log|\varepsilon|}-\frac{\log|t^{2}F(u,v)|}{2\log|\varepsilon|}=-\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{y})|}{2\log|\varepsilon|}. $$

Assume that $1\geq L_{t}\geq(t/B)^{1/3}$ and divide $[-1,1]^{2}$ into boxes of sidelength $L_{t}$ . Then for $\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L_{t})$ , we have that

$$ -\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{y})|}{2\log|\varepsilon|}=-\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{2\log|\varepsilon|}+O(L_{t}). $$

Then if we sum over $(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L_{t})$ :

$$ \left(-\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{\log|\varepsilon|}+O(1)\right)\sum_{(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L_{t})}\#\{N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\}\\
\ll\left(-\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{\log|\varepsilon|}+O(1)\right)\cdot\frac{BL_{t}^{2}\cdot(1\star\chi)(t)}{t}\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}. $$

Here we have used that $\#\{N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\}\ll(1\star\chi)(F(u,v))$ and Theorem 3.11.

For our final step in the indefinite case, we sum over $\mathbf{x}_{0}\in[-1,1]^{2}$ spaced $L_{t}$ apart. We can see that

$$ \#\{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v):|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2},\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1\}\\
\ll\frac{B\cdot(1\star\chi)(t)}{t}\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}+\frac{B\cdot(1\star\chi)(t)}{t}\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}\sum_{\mathbf{x}_{0}}\left(-\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{2\log|\varepsilon|}+O(L_{t})\right)L_{t}^{2}\\
\ll\frac{B\cdot(1\star\chi)(t)}{t}\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}\left(1+\int_{[-1,1]^{2}}-\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{y})|}{2\log|\varepsilon|}d\mathbf{y}+O(L_{t})\right). $$

Since this integral converges and $L_{t}\in[(t/B)^{1/3},1]$ , we derive that when $\Delta<0$ :

$$ \#\{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v):|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2},\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1\}\\
\ll\frac{B\cdot(1\star\chi)(t)}{t}\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}. $$

Thus, this bound holds independent of the sign of $\Delta.$

Finally, we sum over the values of $t$ , achieving that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{t\in[B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)}),B]} \displaystyle\#\{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v):|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2},\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1\} \displaystyle\ll\sum_{t\in[B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)}),B]}\frac{B\cdot(1\star\chi)(t)}{t}\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2} \displaystyle\ll\sum_{N(\mathfrak{t})\in[B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)}),B]}\frac{B}{N(\mathfrak{t})}\ll B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-3/2}. $$

This completes the proof of this lemma. ∎

Comparing this to Theorem 1.3, it is clear that this is an error term; hence, it is safe to assume from here on that $t\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})$ .

### 5.2. Short boxes and intervals

From now on, we take $t\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})$ and fix a short box and short interval. Let us recall for $\theta\in[0,1]$ and $\ell\leq 1$ a length to be determined later, we defined the interval:

$$ \mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell):=\{e(\theta^{\prime}):\theta^{\prime}\in[\theta,\theta+\ell]\}\subset S^{1}. $$

Let us define the following point-counting functions: if $\Delta>0$ , we write

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1}):=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\#\Big\{((x,y),(u,v),t)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{+}:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v),\\
(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\|x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}\|,\|x-y\sqrt{-\Delta}\|\leq B\cdot\max_{\mathbf{y}\in[-1,1]}|F(\mathbf{y})|^{1/2},\\
t\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)}),\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1\Big\}. $$

If $\Delta<0$ , we write

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)):=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\#\Big\{((x,y),(u,v),t)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{+}:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v),\\
(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\Psi(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})\in\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell),|x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}|,|x-y\sqrt{-\Delta}|\leq B,\\
t\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)}),\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1\Big\}. $$
