We remark that restricting $\Psi(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})\in\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)$ allows us to control the argument of $\alpha=x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}.$ Similarly, taking $(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ for $L=o(1)$ gives us precision on the value of $t^{2}F(u,v).$

In the next few sections, we will establish the following estimates on $N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),I(\theta,\ell))$ .

#### Proposition 5.2.

Assume $\Delta>0$ is a squarefree integer and $\sqrt{-\Delta}\not\in\mathbb{Q}$ , and let $B$ be a sufficiently large number. Let $\mathbf{x}_{0}\in[-1,1]^{2}$ and $L\gg\log(B)^{-10^{-10}}$ . Then there exists a constant $c_{\Delta,f}$ such that as $B\rightarrow\infty,$

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1})=L^{2}\cdot c_{\Delta,f}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}(1+O(\log(B)^{-10^{-10}})). $$

Moreover, if $c_{\Delta,f}=0$ then there is a Brauer-Manin obstruction or a local obstruction, i.e. $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset.$

#### Proposition 5.3.

Assume $\Delta<0$ is a squarefree integer and $\sqrt{-\Delta}\not\in\mathbb{Q}$ , and let $B$ be a sufficiently large number. Let $\mathbf{x}_{0}\in[-1,1]^{2}$ , $\theta\in[0,1]$ , and $\ell,L\gg\log(B)^{-10^{-10}}.$ Then we have that there exists a constant $b_{\Delta,f}$ such that as $B\rightarrow\infty$ ,

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell))=\kappa(\mathbf{x}_{0},\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell))\cdot b_{\Delta,f}\cdot L^{2}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}(1+O(\log(B)^{-10^{-10}})), $$

where we define

$$ \kappa(\mathbf{x}_{0},\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell))=\max(-\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|/\log|\varepsilon|,0)\cdot\frac{|\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)|}{4\pi}. $$

Moreover, if $b_{\Delta,f}$ is zero then there is a Brauer-Manin obstruction or a local obstruction, i.e. $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset.$

#### Remark 5.4.

We reiterate that in §12 we will show that if these constants $c_{\Delta,f}$ and $b_{\Delta,f}$ are zero then for every relevant vector $\mathbf{c}$ , there is a local obstruction to rational points on the variety $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\mathbf{c}}$ as defined in (1.2).

### 5.3. Decomposition of the positive-definite case

For this subsection, let us assume that $\Delta>0$ . We do not genuinely need short boxes in this situation.

Note that in (5.2), the conditions that $\|x\pm y\sqrt{-\Delta}\|=\sqrt{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}}\leq B\cdot(\max_{\mathbf{y}\in[-1,1]}|F(\mathbf{y})|)^{1/2}$ holds trivially. Thus, we get that

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\sum_{0<t\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\#\{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v):\gcd(x,y,t)=1\}. $$

Our first step is to rewrite this inner sum with a sum over ideals; we repeat the argument discussed in §4 for this. Consider the principal ideal $I=(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})$ . Since $\gcd(x,y,t)=1$ and $N(I)=t^{2}F(u,v)$ , we know that for any prime $p$ dividing $t$ , we must have that $(p)=\mathfrak{p}\overline{\mathfrak{p}}$ splits in $K$ and that $(p)$ does not divide $I$ . As a result, we can write

$$ I=\mathfrak{t}^{2}\mathfrak{a} $$

where $N(\mathfrak{t})=t$ , $N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)$ , and $\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1.$ Additionally, we have that $\gcd(t,I,\overline{I})=1,$ which occurs if and only if $\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1.$ Here we write that $\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b})=1$ if $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{b}$ do not share any common prime ideal factors.

Consequently, we can rewrite the sum as:

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1})=\frac{|\mathcal{U}|}{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\mathbf{1}_{\mathfrak{t}^{2}\mathfrak{a}\textrm{ is principal}}. $$

Recall that the group of units $\mathcal{U}$ is finite in this case. From (3.3), we know that we can rewrite the above sum with class group characters:

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1})=\frac{|\mathcal{U}|}{2|C|}\sum_{\psi\in\hat{C}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{a}). $$

Following Lemma 3.17, we split the above sum into its Eisenstein and cuspidal parts. In particular, let us define for $\psi\in\hat{C}$ satisfying $\text{ord}(\psi)\geq 3$ :

$$ E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{a}). $$

We can see that

$$ \sum_{\text{ord}(\psi)\geq 3}E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi) $$

will be the contribution to $N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1})$ given by the cuspidal class group characters; this be shown in §6 to be an error term.

For the Eisenstein contribution, i.e. the genus characters as described in §3.6, we must make an appropriate modification to deal with the condition $\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1.$ For this we note that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{a})=n\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\chi_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathfrak{a})=\sum_{\mathfrak{k}\mid\overline{\mathfrak{t}}}\mu(\mathfrak{k})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{a})=n/N(\mathfrak{k})\end{subarray}}\chi_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{k})=\sum_{\mathfrak{k}\mid\overline{\mathfrak{t}}}\mu(\mathfrak{k})\chi_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathfrak{k})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{a})=n/N(\mathfrak{k})\end{subarray}}\chi_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{k}). $$

From now on, we will denote the norm of $\mathfrak{k}$ as $N(\mathfrak{k})=k.$ Since $\mathfrak{k}\mid\mathfrak{t}$ and so $\gcd(\mathfrak{k},\Delta)=1,$ it follows from the definition of $\chi_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathfrak{a})$ given in [36, §12.5] that $\chi_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathfrak{k})=1.$ So, for a genus character parameterized by $q_{1},q_{2}$ satisfying $q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta$ and $\gcd(q_{1},q_{2})=1$ , we define:

$$ M_{q_{1},q_{2}}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L))=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\mathfrak{k}\mid\overline{\mathfrak{t}}}\mu(\mathfrak{k})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(F(u,v)/k)\\
=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{k})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{k},\overline{\mathfrak{k}})=1\end{subarray}}\mu(\mathfrak{k})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/k\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/kt)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(F(u,v)/k), $$

where the Fourier coefficients of the corresponding Eisenstein series are when $\gcd(n,-\Delta)=1$ :

$$ \varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(n)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\mid n\end{subarray}}\chi_{q_{1}}(d)\chi_{q_{2}}(n/d). $$

#### Remark 5.5.

We note (and will expand in detail further in §8.2) that

$$ \varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(n)\approx(1\star\chi)(n). $$

This function $(1\star\chi)$ is the one studied by de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum in [25] to prove the case of $x^{2}+y^{2}=f(z)$ for $f$ an irreducible binary quartic. As such, the analysis from the Eisenstein part will strongly match how previous authors have proved the asymptotic for $\Delta=1$ .

We can now write that:

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1})=\frac{|\mathcal{U}|}{2|C|}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta\end{subarray}}^{\prime}M_{q_{1},q_{2}}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L))+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\psi\in\hat{C}\\
\text{ord}(\psi)\geq 3\end{subarray}}O(E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)). $$

Above, the restricted sum is as in (3.5) and corresponds to those pairs $(q_{1},q_{2})$ to do indeed give genus characters for $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta}).$

### 5.4. Decomposition of the indefinite case

For this subsection, assume that $\Delta<0$ . In this case, the group of units $\mathcal{U}$ is infinite and generated by the fundamental unit $\varepsilon$ . We wish to count:

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell))=\\
\frac{1}{2}\cdot\sum_{t\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}\bmod\varepsilon\\
x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)\\
\Psi(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})\in\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)\\
\gcd(x,y,t)=1\end{subarray}}\#\{k\in\mathbb{Z}:|\varepsilon^{k}\alpha|,|\overline{\varepsilon}^{k}\overline{\alpha}|\leq B\} $$

Our goal is to express the above sum in terms of $M_{q_{1},q_{2}}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L))$ and $E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)$ (and similar functions). To do so, we must first estimate this count $\#\{k\in\mathbb{Z}:|\varepsilon^{k}\alpha|,|\overline{\varepsilon}^{k}\overline{\alpha}|\leq B\}$ and remove the condition that $\Psi(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})\in\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell).$

#### 5.4.1. Counting the number of units

To estimate the count $\#\{k\in\mathbb{Z}:|\varepsilon^{k}\alpha|,|\overline{\varepsilon}^{k}\overline{\alpha}|\leq B\},$ we apply bounds similar to the proofs of Lemma 4.3 and Lemma 5.1. Note that $|\varepsilon^{k}\alpha|\leq B$ if and only if

$$ k\leq\frac{\log(B)}{\log|\varepsilon|}-\frac{\log|\alpha|}{\log|\varepsilon|}. $$

Since $\Psi(\alpha)\in\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)$ and $\alpha$ is minimal, we know that

$$ \frac{\log|\alpha|-\log|\overline{\alpha|}}{\log|\varepsilon|}=\frac{2\log|\alpha|}{\log|\varepsilon|}-\frac{\log|\alpha\cdot\overline{\alpha}|}{\log|\varepsilon|}\in[\theta,\theta+\ell]. $$

Recall that $\alpha\cdot\overline{\alpha}=x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v).$ Since $(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ , we know that $t^{2}F(u,v)=B\cdot(F(\mathbf{x}_{0})+O(L)).$ So, we can replace this term with

$$ \frac{\log|\alpha\cdot\overline{\alpha}|}{\log|\varepsilon|}=\frac{\log|t^{2}F(u,v)|}{\log|\varepsilon|}=\frac{2\log(B)}{\log|\varepsilon|}+\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{\log|\varepsilon|}+O_{\varepsilon}(L). $$

Combining all of these factors together, we get that

$$ k\leq-\frac{\theta}{2}-\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{2\log|\varepsilon|}+O(\ell+L). $$

A similar computation with $|\overline{\varepsilon}^{k}\overline{\alpha}|\leq B$ reveals that we also need

$$ k\geq-\frac{\theta}{2}+\frac{\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|}{2\log|\varepsilon|}+O(\ell+L). $$

Thus, we get that

$$ \#\{k\in\mathbb{Z}:|\varepsilon^{k}\alpha|,|\overline{\varepsilon}^{k}\overline{\alpha}|\leq B\}=\max(-\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|/\log|\varepsilon|,0)+O(\ell+L). $$

#### Remark 5.6.

Since $\mathbf{x}_{0}\in[-1,1]^{2}$ , we expect $\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|/\log|\varepsilon|$ to often be negative.

Plugging (5.7) in, we have that

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell))=\left(\max(-\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|/\log|\varepsilon|,0)+O(\ell+L)\right)\\
\times\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}\bmod\varepsilon\\
x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)\\
\Psi(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})\in\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)\\
\gcd(x,y,t)=1\end{subarray}}1. $$

#### 5.4.2. Applying the Erdős-Turán inequality

In this subsection, we remove the condition that $\Psi(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})\in\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell);$ we follow the proof structure set out by Heath-Brown in [34]. We recall the following application of the Erdős-Turán inequality [29], as written in [40, Theorem 1]:

#### Lemma 5.7 (Erdős-Turán, [29]).

Let $\mathcal{A}_{t}(n)=\{x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}\bmod\varepsilon:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=n,\gcd(x,y,t)=1\}$ and $\mathcal{I}\subset S^{1}$ . Then we have that as $n\rightarrow\infty$ and for any $H\geq 1$ ,

$$ \sum_{x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbf{1}_{\Psi(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})\in\mathcal{I}}-\frac{|\mathcal{I}|}{2\pi}\cdot\#\mathcal{A}\ll H^{-1}\#\mathcal{A}\\
+\sum_{1\leq h\leq H}\left(\frac{1}{H+1}+\min(|\mathcal{I}|,(\pi h)^{-1})\right)\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}\in\mathcal{A}\\
\gcd(x,y,t)=1\end{subarray}}\Psi(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})^{h}\right|. $$

Applying the above to (5.8), we achieve that:

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell))=\frac{|\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)|}{4\pi}\cdot\left(\max(-\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|/\log|\varepsilon|+O(\ell+L)\right)\\
\times\left(M^{\prime}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L))(1+O(\ell^{-1}H^{-1}))+O\left(\ell^{-1}\sum_{1\leq h\leq H}\frac{1}{h}A^{\prime}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h)\right)\right), $$

where we define

$$ M^{\prime}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)):=\sum_{t\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}\bmod\varepsilon\\
x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)\\
\gcd(x,y,t)=1\end{subarray}}1, $$

$$ A^{\prime}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h)=\sum_{t\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\Bigg|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}\bmod\varepsilon\\
x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)\\
\gcd(x,y,t)=1\end{subarray}}\Psi(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})^{h}\Bigg|. $$

Let us take $H=\log(B)^{5}.$ Lemma 4.3 tells us that

$$ M^{\prime}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L))\ll L^{2}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}. $$

Hence, we can see that

$$ \ell^{-1}H^{-1}M^{\prime}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L))\ll\ell^{-1}L^{2}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-6} $$

will be more than a sufficient error term. So, it remains to better understand $M^{\prime}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L))$ and $A^{\prime}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h).$

#### Remark 5.8.

We would like to point out that there is an extra set of absolute values in the definition of $A^{\prime}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h)$ compared to $E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)$ , despite them both being error terms that come from the cuspidal contribution. This leads us to requiring different types of analysis on each sum.

#### 5.4.3. Class group characters

We again apply the results of §3.6 and rewrite the above expressions in terms of class group characters. Consider the following sum for $0\leq h\leq H$ :

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}\bmod\varepsilon\\
x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)\\
\gcd(x,y,t)=1\end{subarray}}\Psi(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})^{h}. $$

Since every principal ideal $I=(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})$ with $N(I)=t^{2}F(u,v)$ will have a unique generator $x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}$ that is minimal, we can write the above sum as:

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(I)=t^{2}F(u,v)\\
I\textrm{ is principal}\\
\gcd(x,y,t)=1\end{subarray}}\Psi(I)^{h}. $$

Next, we again note that since we require $\gcd(x,y,t)=1$ , we must have that for any prime $p$ dividing $t$ , the ideal $(p)=\mathfrak{p}\overline{\mathfrak{p}}$ splits and we can not have $(p)$ dividing $I$ . Thus, we can write

$$ I=\mathfrak{t}^{2}\mathfrak{a}, $$

where $N(\mathfrak{t})=t$ , $N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)$ , and $\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1.$ So, we can write the above sum as

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})=t\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\Psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2h}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\Psi(\mathfrak{a})^{h}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{\mathfrak{t}^{2}\mathfrak{a}\textrm{ is principal}}. $$

Applying (3.3), the above sum is equivalent to:

$$ \frac{1}{|C|}\sum_{\psi\in\hat{C}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})=t\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\Psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2h}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\Psi(\mathfrak{a})^{h}\psi(\mathfrak{a}). $$

From Lemma 3.17, we can decompose further the contributions from the Eisenstein and cuspidal parts. Let us start with the main term given by $M^{\prime}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L))$ above; in particular, we have that

$$ M^{\prime}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L))=\frac{1}{|C|}\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}M_{q_{1},q_{2}}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L))+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\psi\in\hat{C}\\
\text{ord}(\psi)\geq 3\end{subarray}}O(E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)), $$

In the above decomposition, $M(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L))$ and $E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)$ are defined in (5.5) and (5.4).

On the other hand, for $A^{\prime}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h)$ , we add in the corresponding absolute value signs. In particular, define for $1\leq h\leq H=\log(B)^{5}$ and $\psi\in\hat{C}$ :

$$ A(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h,\psi)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sigma(F(u,v),\Psi^{h}\psi;\overline{\mathfrak{t}}), $$

where we have defined $\sigma(n,\psi;t)$ as

$$ \sigma(n,\psi;\mathfrak{t}):=\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{a})=n\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{t})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{a})\right|. $$

Lemma 3.17 tells us that

$$ A^{\prime}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h)\leq\sum_{\psi\in\hat{C}}A(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h,\psi). $$

### 5.5. Unifying the positive-definite and indefinite notation

Let us summarize our findings. For $\Delta>0$ , we saw that

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),S^{1})=\frac{|\mathcal{U}|}{2|C|}\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}M_{q_{1},q_{2}}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L))+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\psi\in\hat{C}\\
\text{ord}(\psi)\geq 3\end{subarray}}O(E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)). $$

On the other hand, for $\Delta<0$ , we had the relation when $H=\log(B)^{5}$

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell))=\frac{|\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)|}{4\pi}\cdot(\max(-\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|/\log|\varepsilon|,0)+O(\ell+L))\\
\times\Bigg(\frac{1}{|C|}\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}M_{q_{1},q_{2}}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L))+O(B\log(B)^{\varrho_{\Delta,f}-6})\\
+\frac{1}{|C|}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\psi\in\hat{C}\\
\text{ord}(\psi)\geq 3\end{subarray}}O(E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi))+\ell^{-1}\sum_{1\leq h\leq H}\frac{1}{h}\sum_{\psi\in\hat{C}}O(A(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h,\psi))\Bigg). $$

Thus, to prove Proposition 5.2 and Proposition 5.3, it will suffice to prove the following results for our cuspidal and Eisenstein parts.

#### Proposition 5.9 (The cuspidal contribution – the finite image case).

Let $L\gg\log(B)^{-1/10}$ . For $\text{ord}(\psi)\geq 3$ , we have that

$$ E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)\ll_{\Delta,f}L^{2}\cdot B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1-\frac{1}{3}}. $$

#### Proposition 5.10 (The cuspidal contribution – the Grössencharacter case).

Let $L\gg\exp(-\log(B)^{1/3})$ . For $1\leq h\leq\log(B)^{5}$ and $\psi\in\hat{C}$ , we have that

$$ A(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h,\psi)\ll_{B,\Delta,f}L^{2}\cdot B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1-1/5}. $$

#### Proposition 5.11 (The Eisenstein contribution).

Let us assume that $L\gg\log(B)^{-10^{-10}}.$ There exists a constant $C_{q_{1},q_{2},f}$ such that as $B\rightarrow\infty$ , we have that

$$ M_{q_{1},q_{2}}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L))=C_{q_{1},q_{2},f}L^{2}\cdot B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}(1+O(\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1-10^{-8}})). $$

#### Remark 5.12.

We will further discuss $C_{q_{1},q_{2},f}$ in §11 and §12 – in particular, we relate $C_{q_{1},q_{2},f}$ to Brauer-Manin and local obstructions to the Hasse principle. However, it turns out that it is simpler to classify directly when $c_{\Delta,f}$ of Theorem 1.3 is zero, as it will become necessary to consider the sum over genus characters

$$ \sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}C_{q_{1},q_{2},f}. $$

#### Remark 5.13.

We can see that the above two propositions that our size constraints on the length of our short boxes $L$ and short intervals $\ell$ come from the Eisenstein term. Additionally, we can see that the necessity to look at short boxes and intervals comes only from the case when $\Delta<0$ and $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}$ is indefinite (as it was used in §5.3 to estimate $\#\{k\in\mathbb{Z}:|\varepsilon^{k}\alpha|,|\varepsilon^{-k}\overline{\alpha}|\leq B\}$ ). Our condition in Proposition 5.10 that $L\gg\exp(-\log(B)^{1/3})$ comes simply by the desire to have $(B/t)^{1/2}|\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)|\gg 1.$ The condition $L\gg\log(B)^{-1/10}$ in Proposition 5.9 allows us to compare $L^{2}B$ and $LB$ against the corresponding savings.

### 5.6. Interpretation with cusp forms

At this point, let us point out that if $\xi$ is a Hecke character of $K$ , then there is a corresponding automorphic representation $\Xi$ of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$ . Moreover, the Fourier coefficients of $\Xi$ will be given by

$$ \lambda_{\Xi}(n)=\sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})=n}\xi(\mathfrak{a}). $$

Since any class group character is a Hecke character, and $\Psi$ is by definition a Hecke character, we can interpret $E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)$ and $A(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h,\psi)$ in terms of these cuspidal automorphic representations $\Xi$ .

First, let $\Xi$ be the automorphic representation for $\Psi^{h}\psi$ for $h\geq 1$ . Then we will see that $A(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h,\psi)$ is upper bounded by the sum:

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}|\lambda_{\Xi}(F(u,v))|. $$

In Proposition 5.10, we will achieve our savings despite the absolute values placed around the Fourier coefficients – this savings will come from studying the first few Sato-Tate moments of $\Xi$ .

Second, let $\Phi$ be the automorphic representation for the class group character $\psi$ with $\text{ord}(\psi)>2$ . Our error term $E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)$ can then be written as (approximately):

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\end{subarray}}\sum_{d\mid t}\mu(d)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\lambda_{\Phi}\left(\frac{t^{2}F(u,v)}{d^{2}}\right). $$

This viewpoint will be expanded on in §6.1. In Proposition 5.9, we achieve our saving by the sum over $\mathfrak{t}$ and $d$ and optimal upper bounds on the contribution from the sum over $(u,v)$ . It is important in this argument that unlike $A(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h,\psi)$ , there are no absolute values.

### 5.7. Proof of the asymptotic for Theorem 1.3

In both cases, Lemma 5.1 allows us to reduce the problem to estimating:

$$ S(X_{\Delta,f},B):=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\#\Big\{((x,y),(u,v),t)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{+}:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v),\\
|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2},\|x\pm y\sqrt{-\Delta}\|\leq\nu_{\Delta,f}B,\\
0<t\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)}),\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1\Big\}. $$

For this sum, we split into short intervals. We choose $L=\lceil\log(B)^{10^{-10}}\rceil^{-1}$ . If $\Delta>0$ , take $\ell=1$ and so $\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)=S^{1}$ ; if $\Delta<0$ , we let $\ell=\lceil\log(B)^{-10^{-10}}\rceil$ . Let $\mathbf{x}_{0}$ and $\theta$ then range over the corresponding dividing of the box $[-1,1]^{2}$ and interval $[0,1].$ We know that

$$ S(X_{\Delta,f},B)=\sum_{\mathbf{x}_{0}}\sum_{\theta}N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)). $$

If $\Delta>0$ , we apply Proposition 5.2:

$$ \displaystyle S(X_{\Delta,f},B) \displaystyle=c_{\Delta,f}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}(1+O(\log(B)^{-10^{-10}}))\cdot\sum_{\mathbf{x}_{0}}L^{2} \displaystyle=4\cdot c_{\Delta,f}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}(1+O(\log(B)^{-10^{-10}})). $$

This completes the positive-definite case.

On the other hand, if $\Delta<0$ , we apply Proposition 5.3 to achieve:

$$ \displaystyle S(X_{\Delta,f},B) \displaystyle=b_{\Delta,f}B\log(B)^{\varrho_{a,f}-1}(1+O(\log(B)^{-10^{-7}}))\cdot\sum_{\mathbf{x}_{0}}\sum_{\theta}\kappa(\mathbf{x}_{0},\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)) \displaystyle=b_{\Delta,f}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}(1+O(\log(B)^{-10^{-7}}))\cdot\sum_{\mathbf{x}_{0}}\sum_{\theta}L^{2}\cdot\ell\cdot\max(-\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|/\log|\varepsilon|,0). $$

Recall that if $b_{\Delta,f}=0$ then there is a Brauer-Manin or local obstruction.

Finally, we can see that this sum can be approximated by the integral:

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{x}_{0}}\sum_{\theta}L^{2}\cdot\ell\cdot\max(-\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|/\log|\varepsilon|,0)\\
=\int_{-1}^{1}\int_{-1}^{1}\int_{0}^{1}\max(-\log|F(x,y)|/\log|\varepsilon|,0)d\theta dxdy+O(\log(B)^{-10^{-10}}). $$

Since this integral is a constant only depending on $f$ and $\varepsilon$ (which only depends on $\Delta$ ), we can write this expression as $d_{\Delta,f}+O(\log(B)^{-10^{-10}}).$ Moreover, it is clear that $d_{\Delta,f}>0$ . Plugging this back into $S(X_{\Delta,f},B)$ , we have that

$$ S(X_{\Delta,f},B)=b_{\Delta,f}d_{\Delta,f}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}(1+O(\log(B)^{-10^{-10}})). $$

Taking $c_{\Delta,f}=b_{\Delta,f}d_{\Delta,f}$ finishes the proof. ∎

### 5.8. Proof of Corollary 1.4

Note that we have restricted in Theorem 1.3 to when $\Delta\in\mathbb{Z}$ is squarefree and $f(z)\in\mathbb{Z}[z]$ , whereas the general definition for Châtelet surfaces allows $\Delta\in\mathbb{Q}$ and $f(z)\in\mathbb{Q}[z]$ . Consider the initial surface:

$$ x^{2}+\Delta_{0}y^{2}=f_{0}(z) $$

for $\Delta_{0}\in\mathbb{Q}$ a nonsquare and $f_{0}(z)\in\mathbb{Q}[z]$ . After clearing denominators, we can see that rational points on the above surface will be in direct bijection with the rational points on the surface:

$$ (Qx)^{2}+\Delta_{1}y^{2}=f_{1}(z) $$

for $Q,\Delta_{1}\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $f_{1}(z)\in\mathbb{Z}[z]$ . After modifying the height function accordingly (by a factor of $Q$ ), we can see that the problem of counting rational points on this surface is equivalent to counting rational points (with the modified height function) on the surface

$$ x^{2}+\Delta_{1}y^{2}=f_{1}(z) $$

for $\Delta_{1}\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $f_{1}(z)\in\mathbb{Z}[z]$ .

Next, if $\Delta_{1}$ is not squarefree, we can write $\Delta_{1}=\Delta\delta^{2}.$ Hence, our surface can be written as

$$ x_{1}^{2}+\Delta(\delta y)^{2}=f_{1}(z). $$

After modifying the height function by a factor of $\delta,$ we can see that counting rational points on the above surface is equivalent to counting rational points on

$$ x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=f(z), $$

where $f(z)=f_{1}(z)\in\mathbb{Z}[z]$ . Thus, Theorem 1.3 indeed resolves Manin’s conjecture for all Châtelet surfaces over $\mathbb{Q}.$

## 6. The cuspidal contribution – the finite image case

In this section, we prove Proposition 5.9. Let us recall the definition of $E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)$ from (5.4):

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{a}). $$

We also recall that $\psi$ is a class group character of order $\geq 3$ . As described in the outline, we aim to change the order of summation and achieve savings from the sum over $\mathfrak{t}$ ; however, our situation is slightly complicated by the fact that we are summing over short-ish boxes $\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L).$

Let $\epsilon(B)$ to be determined later. We say that $t\sim_{\epsilon}T$ if $t\in[T,T(1+\epsilon(B))].$ Consider the space:

$$ D(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)=\cup_{T_{i}}(B/T_{i})^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L), $$

where $T_{i}$ ranges over the “dyadic interals of difference $(1+\epsilon(B))$ ” up to $B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)}).$ First, we claim that almost all of the points $(u,v)$ counted in $E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)$ are in $D(\mathbf{x}_{0},L).$

#### Lemma 6.1.

Assume $\epsilon(B)<L$ . Let $(u,v)$ be in $(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ for some $t$ , but not contained in $D(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ . Then $(u,v)$ is $O(\epsilon(B))$ close to the corners of the box $\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ . In other words, either

$$ (u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}(x_{0},y_{0}+L)+[0,O(\epsilon(B))]^{2} $$

or

$$ (u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}((x_{0}+L,y_{0}))+[0,O(\epsilon(B))]^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ , we know that

$$ \frac{t^{1/2}}{B^{1/2}}(u,v)\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L). $$

We also know that if $T_{1}\leq t\leq T_{2}$ , then

$$ \frac{T_{1}^{1/2}}{B^{1/2}}(u,v)\not\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\frac{T_{2}^{1/2}}{B^{1/2}}(u,v)\not\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L). $$

Let us assume that $u\leq v$ . Then we must have that $\frac{T_{1}^{1/2}}{B^{1/2}}u<x_{0}$ and $\frac{T_{2}^{1/2}}{B^{1/2}}v>y_{0}+L.$ Thus, we get that $\frac{t^{1/2}}{B^{1/2}}u-x_{0}\leq O(\epsilon(B)\cdot\frac{t^{1/2}}{B^{1/2}}u)$ . Similarly, we achieve that $y_{0}+L-\frac{t^{1/2}}{B^{1/2}}v=O(\epsilon(B)\cdot\frac{t^{1/2}}{B^{1/2}}v).$ ∎

Next, we justify changing the order of summation for $E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi).$

#### Lemma 6.2.

Let us define

$$ D(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)=\sum_{T_{i}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/T_{i})^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)}\psi(\mathfrak{a})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\sim_{\epsilon}T_{i}\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}. $$

Here the sum over $T_{i}$ is a sum over powers of $(1+\epsilon(B))$ up to $B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)}).$ Assume that $\epsilon(B)=o(L)$ . Then we can bound

$$ |E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)-D(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)|\ll L\epsilon(B)B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1} $$

#### Proof.

First, we compare $D(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)$ to an intermediate sum:

$$ I(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)=\sum_{T_{i}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/T_{i})^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)}\psi(\mathfrak{a})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\sim_{\epsilon}T_{i}\\
(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}. $$

Assume $(u,v)\in(B/T_{i})^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ , but $(u,v)\not\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ for some $t\in[T_{i},(1+\epsilon(B))T_{i}]$ . Since $\epsilon(B)\leq L$ , we can isolate such points as satisfying that they are within $O(\epsilon(B))$ of the edges of $(B/T_{i})^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ . Thus, we have that (using the trivial bound $|\psi^{2}(\mathfrak{t})|\leq 1$ )

$$ \displaystyle|D(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)-I(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)| \displaystyle\ll\sum_{T_{i}}\epsilon(B)T_{i}\cdot\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/T_{i})^{1/2}\partial\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)+O(\epsilon(B))\end{subarray}}(1\star\chi)(F(u,v)) \displaystyle\ll\epsilon(B)\sum_{T_{i}}T_{i}\cdot\frac{B}{T_{i}}\cdot L\epsilon(B)\cdot\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2} \displaystyle\ll L\epsilon(B)^{2}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}\cdot\frac{\log(B)}{\epsilon(B)}\ll L\epsilon(B)B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}. $$

Here we have used Theorem 3.11 as before with the non-negative multiplicative function $(1\star\chi)(n)$ . Also, observe that $(B/T_{i})^{1/2}(\partial\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)+O(\epsilon(B))\supset(B/T_{i})^{1/2}\partial\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)+O(\epsilon(B))$ and the larger one has area $BT_{i}^{-1}L\epsilon(B).$ Here we have used that there are $\ll\log(B)/\epsilon(B)$ such values of $T_{i}$ .

Next, we want to compare $I(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)$ and $E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)$ . We can see that

$$ I(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in D(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)}\psi(\mathfrak{a})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})=t\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}, $$

whereas we have that

$$ E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in\cup_{t}(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)}\psi(\mathfrak{a})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})=t\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}. $$

Thus, the difference is summing over exactly those $(u,v)$ not contained in $D(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ . Thus, we have that

$$ \displaystyle|I(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi) \displaystyle-E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)| \displaystyle\ll\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}((x_{0},y_{0}+L)+O(\epsilon(B)))\\
\cup(B/t)^{1/2}((x_{0}+L,y_{0})+O(\epsilon(B)))\end{subarray}}(1\star\chi)(F(u,v)) \displaystyle\ll\sum_{N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})}\epsilon(B)^{2}\cdot\frac{B}{t}\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2} \displaystyle\ll B\epsilon(B)^{2}\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}. $$

Again, we have applied Theorem 3.11 on the sum over $(u,v)$ with the non-negative multiplicative function $(1\star\chi)(n).$ ∎

Finally, we wish to bound $D(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)$ . Now, we place the absolute values:

$$ D(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)\leq\sum_{T_{i}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/T_{i})^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)}\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\sim_{\epsilon}T_{i}\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}\right|. $$

#### Lemma 6.3.

For $T\gg_{K}1$ , and $\psi^{2}\neq 1$ , the following bound holds:

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq T\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}\ll_{K}\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\mid\mathfrak{a}}\left(1+\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{2/3}}\right)T^{5/6}. $$

#### Corollary 6.4.

Let $\epsilon(B)=o(1)$ . Then we have that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\sim_{\epsilon}T\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}\ll_{K}\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\mid\mathfrak{a}}\left(1+\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{2/3}}\right)T^{5/6}. $$

The above corollary comes from noting that since $\epsilon(B)=o(1)$ ,

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\sim_{\epsilon}T\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq(1+\epsilon)T\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})<T\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}\\
\ll_{K}\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\mid\mathfrak{a}}\left(1+\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{2/3}}\right)((1+\epsilon)T)^{5/6}+\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\mid\mathfrak{a}}\left(1+\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{2/3}}\right)T^{5/6}\ll_{K}\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\mid\mathfrak{a}}\left(1+\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{2/3}}\right)T^{5/6}. $$

#### Proof of Lemma 6.3.

Define the Dirichlet series:

$$ \xi_{\mathfrak{a}}(s,\psi^{2}):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{b}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{b},\overline{\mathfrak{b}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathbf{a},\overline{\mathfrak{b}})=1\end{subarray}}\frac{\psi(\mathfrak{b})^{2}}{N(\mathfrak{b})^{s}}. $$

This series converges absolutely for $\Re(s)>1$ . We note that

$$ \xi_{\mathfrak{a}}(s,\psi^{2})=\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\mid\mathbf{a}}\left(1-\frac{\psi(\mathfrak{p})^{2}}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{s}}\right)\cdot\xi(s,\psi^{2}), $$

where we define

$$ \xi(s,\psi^{2}):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{b}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{b},\overline{\mathfrak{b}})=1\end{subarray}}\frac{\psi(\mathfrak{b})^{2}}{N(\mathfrak{b})^{s}}. $$

We can relate $\xi(s,\psi^{2})$ to a Hecke $L$ -function as such:

$$ \xi(s,\psi^{2})\cdot\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}I\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}\\
I\textrm{ principal}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{N(I)^{s}}=\xi(s,\psi^{2})\zeta(2s)=L_{K}(s,\psi^{2}):=\sum_{\mathfrak{b}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}}\frac{\psi(\mathfrak{b})^{2}}{N(\mathfrak{b})^{s}}, $$

where $L_{K}(s,\psi^{2})$ is a Hecke L-function. Thus, we have that

$$ \xi_{\mathfrak{a}}(s,\psi^{2})=f_{\mathbf{a}}(s)L_{K}(s,\psi^{2}), $$

where

$$ f_{\mathbf{a}}(s)=\zeta(2s)^{-1}\cdot\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\mid\mathfrak{a}}\left(1-\frac{\psi(\mathfrak{p})^{2}}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{s}}\right). $$

Consequently, $\xi_{\mathbf{a}}(s,\psi^{2})$ is analytic for $\Re(s)>1/2$ (since $\psi^{2}\neq 1$ , $L_{K}(s,\psi^{2})$ converges at $s=1$ ).

Let us consider the following weighted sum:

$$ S(T)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq T\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}(T-N(\mathfrak{t})). $$

By Perron’s formula, we have that for any $\sigma>1$ the following holds:

$$ S(T)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\sigma-i\infty}^{\sigma+i\infty}f_{\mathfrak{a}}(s)\zeta(2s)L_{K}(s,\psi^{2})\frac{T^{1+s}}{s(s+1)}ds. $$

Take $1/2<\alpha<1$ . Let us shift the contour above to the line $\Re(s)=\alpha$ . Since $\psi^{2}\neq 1$ , we know that $L(s,\psi^{2})$ will not have a pole at $s=1$ . Thus, we have that the above is

$$ \displaystyle S(T) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\alpha-i\infty}^{\alpha+i\infty}f_{\mathbf{a}}(s)\zeta(2s)L_{K}(s,\psi^{2})\frac{T^{1+s}}{s(s+1)}ds \displaystyle\ll_{\alpha}\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\mid\mathfrak{a}}\left(1+\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{\alpha}}\right)T^{1+\alpha}\int_{\alpha-i\infty}^{\alpha+i\infty}|L_{K}(s,\psi^{2})|\frac{ds}{s(s+1)}. $$

Now, for $\Re(s)=\alpha$ , the convexity bound gives us that

$$ |L_{K}(s,\psi^{2})|\ll_{K}|s|^{\frac{1-\alpha}{2}+\epsilon}. $$

So, we have that the inner integral is bounded above by

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(\alpha+|t|)^{\frac{1-\alpha+\epsilon}{2}-2}dt<\infty, $$

which converges to a constant depending on $\alpha$ . Thus, we have that

$$ S(T)\ll_{\alpha}\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\mid\mathfrak{a}}\left(1+\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{\alpha}}\right)T^{1+\alpha}. $$

Next, we use the following trick. Consider the difference

$$ S(T+T^{\prime})-S(T)=T^{\prime}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq T\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2}+O_{K}\left(T^{\prime 2}\right) $$

where the error term comes from the ideals with $N(\mathfrak{t})\in(T,T+T^{\prime}]$ and the trivial bound $|\psi^{2}|\leq 1$ . Applying the above bound (6.1), we also have that

$$ S(T+T^{\prime})-S(T)\ll_{\alpha}\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\mid\mathfrak{a}}\left(1+\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{\alpha}}\right)(T+T^{\prime})^{1+\alpha}. $$

Let us take $\beta=\frac{1+\alpha}{2}$ ; since $1/2<\alpha<1$ , we have that $3/4<\beta<1$ . Then we can see that by comparing the above bounds and taking $T^{\prime}=T^{\beta}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq T\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t})^{2} \displaystyle\ll T^{\prime}+\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\mid\mathfrak{a}}\left(1+\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{\alpha}}\right)T^{1+\alpha}T^{\prime-1} \displaystyle\ll\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\mid\mathfrak{a}}\left(1+\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{\alpha}}\right)T^{\beta}. $$

This brings us to our final choices of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ . Let us choose $\alpha=2/3$ and $\beta=5/6.$ These provide us with the final bound.

∎

Now, let us plug this into our estimates for $D(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)$ . This gives us that:

$$ D(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)\leq\sum_{T_{i}}T_{i}^{5/6}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/T_{i})^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}(1\star\chi)(F(u,v))\cdot\prod_{p\mid F(u,v)}(1+1/p^{2/3}). $$

Applying Nair’s sieve (Theorem 3.11) to the inner sum, we get that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{(u,v)\in(B/T_{i})^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)} \displaystyle(1\star\chi)(F(u,v))\prod_{p\mid F(u,v)}(1+p^{-2/3}) \displaystyle\ll\frac{BL^{2}}{T_{i}}\exp\left(\sum_{p\ll B/T_{i}}\frac{\varrho_{f}(p)}{p}\cdot\left((1\star\chi)(p)\cdot(1+p^{-2/3})-1\right)\right) \displaystyle\ll\frac{BL^{2}}{T_{i}}\exp\left((\rho_{\Delta,f}-2)\log\log(B/T_{i})+\sum_{p\ll B/T_{i}}\frac{2\varrho_{f}(p)}{p^{5/3}}\right) \displaystyle\ll\frac{BL^{2}}{T_{i}}\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}. $$

Thus, we have that

$$ \displaystyle D(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)\ll L^{2}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}\sum_{T_{i}}T_{i}^{-1/6}. $$

We note that this inner sum is a geometric series, since $T_{i}$ is summed over powers of $(1+\epsilon(B))$ up to $B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})$ :

$$ \sum_{T_{i}}T_{i}^{-1/6}=\sum_{k=0}^{K}(1+\epsilon(B))^{-k/6}<\frac{1}{1-(1+\epsilon(B))^{-1/6}}, $$

where $K=(\log(B)-\sqrt{\log(B)})/\log(1+\epsilon(B)).$ Now we know that

$$ \frac{1}{1-(1+\epsilon(B))^{-1/6}}\ll\epsilon(B)^{-1}. $$

So, we get that

$$ D(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)\leq\epsilon(B)^{-1}BL^{2}\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}. $$

Finally, we choose $\epsilon(B)$ . Let us take $\epsilon(B)=\log(B)^{-1/2}$ . So, we get that

$$ D(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)\ll BL^{2}\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-3/2}. $$

On the other hand, by Lemma 2.2,

$$ |E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)-D(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)|\ll LB\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-3/2}. $$

Hence,

$$ E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)\ll LB\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-3/2}+BL^{2}\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-3/2}. $$

Since $L\gg\log(B)^{-10^{-1}}$ , we can also safely say that

$$ E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi)\ll L^{2}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1-1/3}. $$

This concludes the proof of Proposition 5.9.∎

### 6.1. Interpretation with cusp forms

Now, let us reframe the above proof using the cusp form interpretation of our sum $E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);0,\psi).$ We consider the expression after our change of variables (Lemma 6.2),

$$ D(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);\psi)=\sum_{T_{i}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/T_{i})^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t}^{2}\mathfrak{a})=t^{2}F(u,v)\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\\
N(\mathfrak{t})\sim_{\epsilon}T_{i}\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{t}^{2}\mathfrak{a}). $$

Let $\Xi$ denote the cuspidal automorphic representation on $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$ given by $\psi$ ; since $\psi$ is a class group character, the representation $\Xi$ has finite image. By replacing the condition $\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1$ with a Möbius sum over divisors of $N(\mathfrak{t})$ , the above is equivalent to

$$ \sum_{T_{i}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/T_{i})^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\sim_{\epsilon}T_{i}\end{subarray}}\sum_{d\mid t}\mu(d)\lambda_{\Xi}\left(\frac{t^{2}F(u,v)}{d^{2}}\right)\\
=\sum_{T_{i}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/T_{i})^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{d\leq T_{i}}\mu(d)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\sim_{\epsilon}T_{i}/d\end{subarray}}\lambda_{\Xi}(t^{2}F(u,v)). $$

We will return to this sum at the end of the section, but for now let us consider the sum

$$ \sum_{d\leq X}\mu(d)\sum_{t\leq X/d}\lambda_{\Xi}(at^{2}). $$

Let $C(z)$ denote a holomorphic cusp form in $S_{k}(\Gamma_{0}(-\Delta),\chi)$ and $\lambda_{C}(n)$ denote its normalized Fourier coefficients. Let us take $c$ to be a constant such that $|\lambda_{C}(p)|\leq c$ for all primes $p$ . We claim that the following bound holds, independent of whether of not $C(z)$ is dihedral.

#### Lemma 6.5.

Let $C(z)\in S_{k}(\Gamma_{0}(-\Delta),\chi)$ and assume that $|\lambda_{C}(p)|\leq c$ for all primes $c$ . Then we have the bound

$$ \sum_{d\leq X}\mu(d)\sum_{t\leq X/d}\lambda_{C}(at^{2})\ll(c+1)^{\omega(a)}X\log(X)^{-40c}. $$

#### Remark 6.6.

The exponent of $40c$ is fairly arbitrary, but we choose a number for concreteness that will suffice in future bounds.

#### Proof.

We define the weighted sum:

$$ S(X):=\sum_{d\leq X}d\mu(d)\sum_{t\leq X/d}\lambda_{C}(at^{2})(X/d-t). $$

From Perron’s formula, we know that for $\sigma>1$ ,

$$ S(X)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\sum_{d\leq X}d\mu(d)\int_{\sigma-i\infty}^{\sigma+i\infty}\xi(s;a,C)\cdot\frac{(X/d)^{s+1}}{s(s+1)}ds, $$

where we define the Dirichlet series

$$ \xi(s;a,C):=\sum_{n}\frac{\lambda_{C}(an^{2})}{n^{s}}. $$

We now relate the above Dirichlet series to the $L$ -function $L(s,\text{sym}^{2}(C))$ . Define $\alpha_{p}$ and $\beta_{p}$ such that

$$ 1-\lambda_{C}(p)p^{-s}+\chi(p)p^{-2s}=(1-\alpha_{p}p^{-s})(1-\beta_{p}p^{-s}). $$

Let us define

$$ g_{a}(s):=\prod_{p^{e}\|a}\left(\lambda_{C}(p^{e})+\lambda_{C}(p^{e+1})p^{-s}+...\right)\left(1-\alpha_{p}^{2}p^{-s}\right)\left(1-\beta_{p}^{2}p^{-s}\right)\left(1-\chi(p)p^{-s}\right). $$

Then we have the relation for $\Re(s)>1$ :

$$ \xi(s;a,C)=g_{a}(s)L(2s,\chi^{2})^{-1}L(s,\text{sym}^{2}(C)). $$

In particular, $\xi(s;a,C)$ and $L(s,\text{sym}^{2}(C))$ share the same order of the pole at $s=1$ . We refer the reader to Shimura’s [45] classificaton of when $L(s,\text{sym}^{2}(C))$ has a pole at $s=1$ ; in our proof, it will turn out that there is cancellation independent of if $C(z)$ is dihedral or not.

Let us bring back the Möbius sum. We can see that

$$ S(X)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\sigma-i\infty}^{\sigma+i\infty}\xi(s;a,C)\frac{X^{s+1}}{s(s+1)}\cdot\sum_{d\leq X}\frac{\mu(d)}{d^{s}}ds. $$

Take $\sigma=1+\frac{1}{\log(X)}>1$ , we know that for any $A>0$ ,

$$ \sum_{d\leq X}\frac{\mu(d)}{d^{s+1}}=\zeta(s)^{-1}\left(1+O(\log(X)^{-A})\right). $$

Thus, we have that for any $A^{\prime}>0$ ,

$$ S(X)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\sigma-i\infty}^{\sigma+i\infty}g_{a}(s)L(2s,\chi^{2})^{-1}L(s,\text{sym}^{2}(C))\zeta(s)^{-1}\frac{X^{s+1}}{s(s+1)}ds+O\left(\sup_{\Re(s)=\sigma}|g_{a}(s)|\cdot X^{2}\log(X)^{-A^{\prime}}\right). $$

Next, we want to add cutoffs at $\sigma+iD$ and $\sigma-iD$ for $D$ to be determined later. This gives us that the integral above is equal to

$$ \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\sigma-iD}^{\sigma+iD}\xi(s;a,C)\zeta(s)^{-1}\frac{X^{s+1}}{s(s+1)}ds+O\left(\sup_{\Re(s)=\sigma}|g_{a}(s)|\cdot\frac{X^{2}\log(X)^{2}}{D}\right) $$

Finally, let us shift our line of integration to $\Re(s)=\alpha$ for some $\alpha>1-\log(D)^{-8}$ ; in other words, we stay within a zero free region for $\zeta(s)$ . We note that if $L(s,\text{sym}^{2}(C))$ has a pole at $s=1$ , then it is a simple pole and will be cancelled by the zero of $\zeta(s)^{-1}$ . If $L(s,\text{sym}^{2}(C))$ is holomorphic at $s=1$ , then again $\xi(s;a,C)\zeta(s)^{-1}$ will be holomorphic at $s=1$ . Thus, we get the formula

$$ S(X)=O\left(\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\Im(s)=\pm D\\
\alpha\leq\Re(s)\leq\sigma\end{subarray}}|g_{a}(s)|\cdot\frac{X^{2}\log(X)^{2}}{D}\right)+O\left(X^{2-\log(D)^{-8}}\int_{\alpha-iD}^{\alpha+iD}\frac{|\xi(s;a,C)||\zeta(s)|^{-1}}{|s||s+1|}ds\right). $$

Recall that the convexity bound [36, (5.8),(5.20)] gives us that

$$ |\xi(s;a,C)|\ll|g_{a}(s)|(|s|+1)^{1-\alpha}. $$

We also know from [46, (3.6.5)] that since $\Re(s)=\alpha>1-\log(D)^{-8}$ , we have that

$$ |\zeta(s)|^{-1}\ll\log(|s|+3)^{7}. $$

Thus, in this region,

$$ \int_{\alpha-iD}^{\alpha+iD}\frac{|\xi(s;a,C)||\zeta(s)|^{-1}}{|s||s+1|}ds\ll\sup_{\Re(s)=\alpha}|g_{a}(s)|. $$

Thus, we have that

$$ S(X)\ll\sup_{\alpha\leq\Re(s)\leq\sigma}|g_{a}(s)|\cdot\left(\frac{X^{2}\log(X)^{2}}{D}+X^{2-\log(D)^{-9}}\right). $$

Take $D=\log(X)^{101c}$ and $A^{\prime}=101c$ . Consequently, we have that

$$ S(X)\ll\sup_{\alpha\leq\Re(s)\leq\sigma}|g_{a}(s)|X^{2}\log(X)^{-99c}. $$

Finally, we need to remove our weight. Let $Y<X$ be determined later and consider

$$ S(X+Y)-S(X)=\sum_{d\leq X+Y}d\mu(d)\sum_{t\leq(X+Y)/d}\lambda_{C}(at^{2})((X+Y)/d-t)-\sum_{d\leq X}d\mu(d)\sum_{t\leq X/d}\lambda_{C}(at^{2})(X/d-t). $$

Rearranging the expression, we get that

$$ S(X+Y)-S(X)=Y\sum_{d\leq X}\mu(d)\sum_{t\leq X/d}\lambda_{C}(at^{2})\\
+\sum_{d\leq X}d\mu(d)\sum_{X/d<t\leq(X+Y)/d}\lambda_{C}(at^{2})((X+Y)/d-t)\\
+\sum_{X<d\leq X+Y}d\mu(d)\sum_{t\leq(X+Y)/d}\lambda_{C}(at^{2})((X+Y)/d-t). $$

Since $Y<X$ , the last sum only contains $t=1$ and hence is bounded by

$$ \ll|g_{a}(1)|X\cdot\left|\sum_{X\leq d\leq X+Y}\mu(d)\right|. $$

Consider the second sum. Note that since $t>X/d$ , we have that $(X+Y)/d-t\leq Y/d$ . So, the second sum is bounded by

$$ Y\sum_{d\leq X}\sum_{X/d<t\leq(X+Y)/d}|\lambda_{C}(at^{2})|\ll c^{\omega(a)}Y^{2}\log(X)^{c}, $$

where $c$ is the bound on the prime values of $|\lambda_{C}(p)|$ .

Thus, we know that

$$ \sum_{d\leq X}\mu(d)\sum_{t\leq X/d}\lambda_{C}(at^{2})=Y^{-1}(S(X+Y)-S(X))\\
+O\left(|g_{a}(1)|XY^{-1}\left|\sum_{X\leq d\leq X+Y}\mu(d)\right|\right)+O\left(c^{\omega(a)}Y\log(X)^{c}\right). $$

Applying (6.2), we have that

$$ \sum_{d\leq X}\mu(d)\sum_{t\leq X/d}\lambda_{C}(at^{2})\ll\sup_{\alpha\leq\Re(s)\leq\sigma}|g_{a}(s)|\cdot Y^{-1}X^{2}\log(X)^{-99c}\\
+|g_{a}(1)|\cdot Y^{-1}X\left|\sum_{X\leq d\leq X+Y}\mu(d)\right|+c^{\omega(a)}Y\log(X)^{c}. $$

We take $Y=X\log(X)^{-42c}.$ We also note that by definition of $g_{a}(s)$ , we know that

$$ \sup_{\alpha\leq\Re(s)\leq\sigma}|g_{a}(s)|\ll(c+1)^{\omega(a)}. $$

This gives us that

$$ \sum_{d\leq X}\mu(d)\sum_{t\leq X/d}\lambda_{C}(at^{2})\ll(c+1)^{\omega(a)}X\log(X)^{-40c}. $$

∎

Finally, let us return to our original sum. Let us consider the non-short interval version for simplicity, but as in Lemma 6.2 and Lemma 6.3, the above can be modified for our slightly-short intervals. We consider the sum:

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|u|,|v|\leq B^{1/2}\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{t\leq B/\max(|u|,|v|)^{2}}\sum_{d\mid t}\mu(d)\lambda_{\Xi}\left(\frac{t^{2}F(u,v)}{d^{2}}\right). $$

At this point, we use the fact that if $\Xi$ is induced from a class group character, then $c=1$ . Moreover, we can calculate that

$$ \sup_{\alpha\leq\Re(s)<\sigma}|g_{p}(1)|\ll\begin{cases}1+p^{-\alpha},&\chi(p)=1,\\
0,&\chi(p)=-1.\end{cases} $$

We note that we can assume that $\alpha>1/2$ in the computations above, as this was the lower bound for the zero-free region. Thus, the bounds in the proof of Lemma 6.5 give us a more precise upper bound:

$$ \ll\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq B^{1/2}}\frac{B\log(B/\max(|u|,|v|)^{2})^{-40}}{\max(|u|,|v|)^{2}}\cdot(1\star\chi)(F(u,v))\cdot\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\mid F(u,v)\\
\chi(p)=1\end{subarray}}(1+p^{-2/3}). $$

Now, let us split $[0,B^{1/2}]$ into dyadic regions indexed by $B_{i}$ . The diagonal contribution is clearly the largest above, so we have the upper bound

$$ \sum_{B_{i}}\frac{B}{B_{i}^{2}}\log(B/B_{i}^{2})^{-40}\sum_{|u|,|v|\sim B_{i}}(1\star\chi)(F(u,v))\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\mid F(u,v)\\
\chi(p)=1\end{subarray}}(1+p^{-2/3})\\
\ll B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}\sum_{B_{i}}\log(B/B_{i}^{2})^{-40}\leq B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}\sum_{n=1}^{\log(B)}n^{-40}\ll B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}. $$

Compared to the main term of $\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}$ , this is negligible. We end this section by remarking that the process of changing the order of summation in Lemma 6.2 produces a weaker error term due to the extra factor of $\epsilon(B)$ , but this process can be similarly done with this perspective.

## 7. The cuspidal contribution – the Grössen case

In this section, we will prove Proposition 5.10. Let us recall the definition of $A(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h,\psi)$ (as defined in 5.12):

$$ A(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h,\psi)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}\sigma(F(u,v),\Psi^{h}\psi;\overline{\mathfrak{t}}), $$

where we have defined $\sigma(n,\psi;t)$ as

$$ \sigma(n,\psi;\mathfrak{t}):=\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{a})=n\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{t})=1\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{a})\right|. $$

Recall also that $\psi$ is any class group character and that $h\geq 1$ . Moreover, $\Psi$ (defined in Definition 3.2) is a Hecke Grössencharacter of infinite order.

Now, $\sigma(n;\Psi^{h}\psi,\overline{\mathfrak{t}})$ is a multiplicative, non-negative function, and bounded by $d(n)$ . Thus, we know that by Theorem 3.11,

$$ \displaystyle A(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h,\psi) \displaystyle\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\sum_{(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)}\sigma(F(u,v);\Psi^{h}\psi,\overline{\mathfrak{t}}) \displaystyle\ll L^{2}\sum_{N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B}\frac{B}{N(\mathfrak{t})}\prod_{i=1}^{r}\prod_{p\ll B/t}\left(1+\frac{\varrho_{f_{i}}(p)(\sigma(p;\Psi^{h}\psi,\overline{\mathfrak{t}})-1)}{p}\right). $$

Here we have used the observation that for all but finitely many primes, $\frac{\varrho_{F}(p)}{p^{2}}=\frac{\varrho_{f}(p)}{p}+O(p^{-2}).$ From now on, let us fix an irreducible factor $g(z)=f_{i}(z)$ ; we study

$$ \prod_{p\ll B/t}\left(1+\frac{\varrho_{g}(p)(\sigma(p;\xi,\overline{\mathfrak{t}})-1)}{p}\right), $$

where we take $\xi=\Psi^{h}\psi.$

We note that $\sigma(p;\xi,\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=0$ if $\chi(p)=-1$ , as in that case there are no prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}$ such that $N(\mathfrak{p})=p$ . Additionally, we know that $t$ is product of primes that split in $K$ , so we must have that $\gcd(t,p)=1$ for any $p$ such that $\chi(p)=-1.$ Motivated by these choices, we can split the above product as:

$$ \prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\ll B/t\\
\chi(p)=-1\end{subarray}}\left(1-\frac{\varrho_{g}(p)}{p}\right)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\ll B/t\\
\chi(p)=1\\
\gcd(p,t)=1\end{subarray}}\left(1+\frac{\varrho_{g}(p)(\sigma(p;\xi,\overline{\mathfrak{t}})-1)}{p}\right)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\ll B/t\\
p\mid t\end{subarray}}\left(1+\frac{\varrho_{g}(p)(\sigma(p;\xi,\overline{\mathfrak{t}})-1)}{p}\right). $$

Consider the primes $p$ such that $p\mid t$ . In this case

$$ \sigma(p;\xi,\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{p})=p\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{p},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\xi(\mathfrak{p})\right|=|\xi(\mathfrak{p})|=1. $$

Here we have used that since $p\mid t$ and $\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1$ , we must have that exactly one of the primes $\mathfrak{p}$ above $p$ satisfies $\gcd(\mathfrak{p},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1$ . So, the contribution from these primes is given by:

$$ \prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\ll B/t\\
p\mid t\end{subarray}}\left(1+\frac{\varrho_{g}(p)(\sigma(p;\xi,\overline{\mathfrak{t}})-1)}{p}\right)=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\ll B/t\\
p\mid t\end{subarray}}1=1. $$

Next, we consider the primes $p$ satisfying that $\chi(p)=1$ and $p\nmid t$ . Since $\gcd(p,t)=1$ , we know that

$$ \sigma(p;\xi,\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=\sigma(p;\xi,1)=|\xi(\mathfrak{p})+\overline{\xi}(\mathfrak{p})|=2|\cos(\theta_{p})|, $$

where $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime over $p$ and $\theta_{p}\in[0,2\pi]$ is an angle. By the following identity on cosine,

$$ 2|\cos(\theta)|\leq\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\cos(2\theta), $$

we know that

$$ \sigma(p;\xi,\overline{\mathfrak{t}})\leq\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{4}(\xi(\mathfrak{p})^{2}+\overline{\xi}(\mathfrak{p})^{2}). $$

Thus, we can rewrite the second product as

$$ \prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\ll B/t\\
\chi(p)=1\\
\gcd(p,t)=1\end{subarray}}\left(1+\frac{\varrho_{g}(p)(\sigma(p;\xi,\overline{\mathfrak{t}})-1)}{p}\right)\ll\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\ll B/t\\
\chi(p)=1\end{subarray}}\left(1+\frac{3\varrho_{g}(p)}{2p}+\sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})=p}\frac{\varrho_{g}(p)\xi(\mathfrak{p})^{2}}{N(\mathfrak{p})}-\frac{\varrho_{g}(p)}{p}\right). $$

The above analysis tells us that (7.1) can be simplified to the following expression:

$$ \prod_{p\ll B/t}\left(1+\frac{\varrho_{g}(p)(\sigma(p;\xi,\overline{\mathfrak{t}})-1)}{p}\right)\ll\exp\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\ll B/t\end{subarray}}\frac{-\varrho_{g}(p)}{p}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\ll B/t\\
\chi(p)=1\end{subarray}}\frac{3\varrho_{g}(p)}{2p}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\ll B/t\\
N(\mathfrak{p})=p\end{subarray}}\frac{\varrho_{g}(N(\mathfrak{p}))\xi^{2}(\mathfrak{p})}{N(\mathfrak{p})}\right). $$

In the third summation above, we observe that for all but finitely many primes, the existence of a prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ satisfying that $N(\mathfrak{p})=p$ implies that $\chi(p)=1$ .

Since $g(z)$ is irreducible, we have that

$$ \sum_{p\ll B/t}\frac{\varrho_{g}(p)}{p}=\log\log(B/t)+O(1). $$

On the other hand,

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\ll B/t\\
\chi(p)=1\end{subarray}}\frac{3\varrho_{g}(p)}{2p}=\frac{3}{4}\log\log(B/t)+\frac{3}{4}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{\sqrt{-\Delta}\in\mathbb{Q}[z]/g(z)}\cdot\log\log(B/t)+O(1). $$

The above follows from rewriting the above sum as

$$ \sum_{p\ll B/t}\frac{3\varrho_{g}(p)}{4p}+\sum_{p\ll B/t}\frac{3\chi(p)\varrho_{g}(p)}{4p} $$

and using Corollary 3.16 to evaluate the second sum.

It remains to handle the final sum in (7.2). We observe that if $\sqrt{-\Delta}\not\in\mathbb{Q}[z]/g(z)$ , then

$$ \varrho_{g}(p)=\#\{\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K_{g}}:N_{K_{g}/K}(\mathfrak{P})=\mathfrak{p}\} $$

for any prime $\mathfrak{p}$ over $p$ . Otherwise, $K\subset\mathbb{Q}[z]/g(z)$ and since $[K:\mathbb{Q}]=2$ , we have that

$$ \varrho_{g}(p)=2\cdot\#\{\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K_{g}}:N_{K_{g}/K}(\mathfrak{P})=\mathfrak{p}\} $$

for any prime $\mathfrak{p}$ over $p$ . Therefore, we can rewrite this sum as

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{p})\ll B/t}\frac{\varrho_{g}(N(\mathfrak{p}))\xi^{2}(\mathfrak{p})}{N(\mathfrak{p})}\ll\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K_{g}}\\
N(\mathfrak{P})\ll B/t\end{subarray}}\frac{\xi^{2}(N_{K_{g}/K}(\mathfrak{P}))}{N(\mathfrak{P})}+O(1). $$

Here the factor of $O(1)$ comes from a sum over primes $\mathfrak{P}$ such that $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{P})=p^{e}$ for $e>1$ .

We consider the character $\xi^{2}\circ N_{K_{g}/K}$ on $K_{g}$ ; this will be a Hecke character. Since $\Psi$ has infinite order, we can see that since $h\geq 1$ , $\Psi^{2h}\psi^{2}\circ N_{K_{g}/K}$ is a nontrivial Hecke character. We can also view $\xi^{2}\circ N_{K_{g}/K}$ as the base change of $\xi^{2}$ to $K_{g}$ . Since $\xi^{2}\circ N_{K_{g}/K}$ is a nontrivial Hecke character on $K_{g}$ , the prime ideal theorem with Grössencharacters ([36, Theorem 5.13]) states the following: for some constant $c>0$ ,

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})\leq X}\Lambda(\mathfrak{a})\Psi^{h}(\mathfrak{a})\psi(\mathfrak{a})\ll X\exp\left(-c\frac{\log(X)}{\sqrt{\log(X)}+\log(h)}\right)\log(xh)^{4}. $$

Taking $X=B/t$ and $h\leq\log(B)^{5}$ , we consequently have that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K_{g}}\\
N(\mathfrak{P})\ll B/t\end{subarray}}\frac{\xi^{2}(\mathfrak{P})}{N(\mathfrak{P})}=o(\log\log(B/t)). $$

Consequently, we have that

$$ \prod_{p\ll B/t}\left(1+\frac{\varrho_{g}(p)(\sigma(p;\xi,\overline{\mathfrak{t}})-1)}{p}\right)\ll\exp\left((-\frac{1}{4}+\frac{3}{4}(\varrho_{\Delta,g}-2))\cdot\log\log(X)+O(1)+o(\log\log(B/t)\right)\\
\ll\log(B/t)^{\varrho_{\Delta,g}-2-1/5}. $$

Finally, we sum over ideals $\mathfrak{t}$ :

$$ A(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h,\psi)\ll L^{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\ll B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\frac{B}{N(\mathfrak{t})}\cdot\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2-1/5}\ll L^{2}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1-1/5}. $$

This completes the proof of Proposition 5.9.∎

#### Example 7.1 (A counterexample when $\xi$ has finite order).

In this example, we show an example of when the bound of Proposition 5.10 fails for a character of finite order. Let $\Delta=23$ and thus $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-23})$ . Take $f(z)=z^{3}-z-1$ . Then $f(z)$ generates the Hilbert class field of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-23})$ , which has class group $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ . Let $\mathfrak{p}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K}$ be a prime ideal such that $N(\mathfrak{p})\mid F(u,v)$ for some $(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ . Consider $\textrm{Frob}_{\mathfrak{p}}\in\text{Gal}(K_{f}/K)\cong\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ . We note that

$$ \#\{\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K_{f}}:N(\mathfrak{P})=\mathfrak{p}\}=\textrm{Tr}(\textrm{Frob}_{\mathfrak{p}})=\begin{cases}3,&\textrm{Frob}_{\mathfrak{p}}=1\\
0,&\textrm{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

In other words, $\mathfrak{p}$ splits in $K_{f}$ if and only if $\mathfrak{p}$ is a principal ideal. However, if $N(\mathfrak{p})\mid F(u,v)$ , then we must be in the first case since then $\#\{\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_{K_{f}}:N(\mathfrak{P})=\mathfrak{p}\}>0$ ; in conclusion, for any prime $\mathfrak{p}$ such that $N(\mathfrak{p})\mid F(u,v)$ , $\mathfrak{p}$ is a principal ideal. Thus, we have that for any class group character $\psi$ ,

$$ \sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)}\psi(\mathfrak{a})=\sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)}1. $$

In this case, we get that

$$ \sum_{(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)}\sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)}\psi(\mathfrak{a})=\sum_{(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)}\sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)}1, $$

is exactly the same as the contribution from the Eisenstein part (when $\psi=1$ , since if the class group is $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ there are no other genus characters).

#### Remark 7.2.

We observe that in order for our argument above for Proposition 5.10 to achieve a polylogarithmic savings, it suffices for $\xi^{2}\circ N_{K_{g}/K}$ to be nontrivial for every irreducible factor $g(z)$ . If $\xi$ has infinite order, this is immediate. For most pairs $(\Delta,f(z))$ , the above condition also holds for $\xi$ of finite order. Let $H$ be the Hilbert class field of $K$ . The base change of a class group character $\xi^{2}$ to $K_{g}$ will also be nontrivial if $K_{g}\cap H=K.$

#### Remark 7.3.

As mentioned in §5.6, we can also interpret $A(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);h,\psi)$ as a correlation sum of Fourier coefficients of cusp forms along polynomial values. Let $\Xi$ be a cuspdial automorphic representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$ . We can use the argument above to study

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}\lambda_{\Xi}(p(n)) $$

for $p(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ a polynomial. Again, our problem reduces to analytic properties of the base change of $\text{sym}^{2}(\Xi)$ ; in particular, one hopes that it is cuspidal. This problem will be studied further in forthcoming work.

## 8. The Eisenstein contribution

For the next four sections, we will work towards the proof of Proposition 5.11. Recall from (5.5) that we define

$$ M_{q_{1},q_{2}}(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L))=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{k})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{k},\overline{\mathfrak{k}})=1\end{subarray}}\mu(\mathfrak{k})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/k\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t}\mathfrak{k},\overline{\mathfrak{t}\mathfrak{k}})=1\end{subarray}}S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);q_{1},q_{2},t,k), $$

where we define

$$ S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);q_{1},q_{2},t,k)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(x,y)\in(B/kt)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(x,y)=1\end{subarray}}\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(F(x,y)/k). $$

We proceed to analyze $S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);q_{1},q_{2},t,k)$ in this section and in §11 we resume the summation over $\mathfrak{k}$ and $\mathfrak{t}$ . Let us record our final goal for $S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);q_{1},q_{2},t,k):$

#### Proposition 8.1.

Let $F(x,y)$ be a squarefree binary form of degree $\leq 4$ and $L\gg\log(B)^{-10^{-10}}.$ Then we have that for $t$ and $k$ satisfying $tk\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)}),$ the following holds:

$$ S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);q_{1},q_{2},t,k)=\frac{BL^{2}}{tk^{3}}\cdot C_{q_{1},q_{2},f,k}(B/tk)\cdot\left(1+O\left(\log(B)^{-10^{-7}}\right)\right)\\
+O\left(\frac{64^{\omega(k)}\log(k)B}{tk^{3/2}}\cdot\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2-10^{-7}}+\frac{B^{3/4}}{(tk)^{3/4}}\cdot\left(L+(4\deg(F))^{\omega(k)}\nu_{1}(k)^{1/2}\right)\cdot\log(B)^{-10^{-7}}\right), $$

where $C_{q_{1},q_{2},f,k}(B/tk)$ is an expression that depends on the factorization of $F(x,y)$ . Additionally, for a fixed value of $k$ , there exists a constant $c_{q_{1},q_{2},f,k}$ such that

$$ C_{q_{1},q_{2},f,k}(B/tk)=c_{q_{1},q_{2},f,k}\log(B/tk)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}. $$

#### Remark 8.2.

At this stage the proof is essentially a combination of the proofs provided by de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum in [25] (for irreducible quartics and products of two irreducible quadratics) and by Heath-Brown in [33] (for the product of four linear factors) for $\Delta=1$ . In essence, we have reduced ourselves to case when $K$ has class number one.

First, we must apply a few necessary reductions to put the sum in a more malleable form. We recall our abusive notation that lets $-\Delta$ denote the modulus of the character $\chi$ , and is given explicitly by

$$ -\Delta:=\begin{cases}4\Delta,&\Delta>0,\\
-\Delta,&\Delta<0.\end{cases} $$

### 8.1. Multiplicativity of $\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}$

We recall from (5.6) that when $(n,-\Delta)=1$ ,

$$ \varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(n)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\mid n\end{subarray}}\chi_{q_{1}}(d)\chi_{q_{2}}(n/d). $$

This function is multiplicative, but not totally multiplicative. We would like to write:

$$ \varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(F(x,y))\approx\prod_{i=1}^{n}\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(F_{i}(x,y)), $$

but the above relation is not quite true. Instead, we can use the following multiplicativity relation.

#### Lemma 8.3.

Let $n$ and $m$ be integers coprime to $-\Delta$ . Then

$$ \varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(nm)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\mid\gcd(m,n)\end{subarray}}\mu(c)\chi(c)\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(n/c)\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(m/c). $$

#### Proof.

Since $\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}$ is multiplicative, it suffices to check this property on prime powers. Let $p$ be a prime. So, we can assume that $\gcd(p,-\Delta)=1.$ Then expanding the definition, we have that

$$ \varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(p^{e+f})=\sum_{i=0}^{e+f}\chi_{q_{1}}(p)^{i}\chi_{q_{2}}(p)^{e+f-i}. $$

On the other hand, we have that

$$ \varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(p^{e})\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(p^{f})=\sum_{i=0}^{e+f}\#\{k\leq e,\ell\leq f:k+\ell=i\}\cdot\chi_{q_{1}}(p)^{i}\chi_{q_{2}}(p)^{e+f-i}. $$

Now, because $\chi(p)=\chi_{q_{1}}(p)\chi_{q_{2}}(p)$ , the following equality is true:

$$ \varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(p^{e})\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(p^{f})-\chi(p)\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(p^{e-1})\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(p^{f-1})=\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(p^{e+f}). $$

∎

Thus, if $\gcd(F(x,y)/k,-\Delta)=1$ , we can write:

$$ \varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(F(x,y)/k)=\sum_{\mathbf{c}}\mu(\mathbf{c})\chi(\mathbf{c})\prod_{i=1}^{r}\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(F_{i}(x,y)/k_{i}c_{i}), $$

where $k=k_{1}...k_{r}$ and $c_{i}k_{i}\mid F_{i}(x,y)$ for each $i$ , and $\mathbf{c}$ is given by tuples of products of integers dividing $\gcd(F_{i}(x,y),F_{j}(x,y))$ for $i\neq j.$ These breakdowns depend on the factorization of $F(x,y)$ (for instance, if $F(x,y)$ is irreducible then there is no need for the above sum). We write down these decompositions explicitly in §11.1.

Moreover, since we will take $\gcd(x,y)=1$ , we have that $\gcd(F_{i}(x,y),F_{j}(x,y))=\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})$ , the resultant of $F_{i}$ and $F_{j}$ , for $i\neq j$ . Note that $\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})$ is a finite constant only depending on our polynomial $F(x,y)$ . Furthermore, this restricts the sum above to those $\mathbf{c}$ satisfying that $c_{i}\mid\prod_{i\neq j}\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})$ . This fact also allows us to determine that $k$ decomposes into finitely many combinations $k_{1}\ldots k_{r}$ where $k_{i}\mid F_{i}(x,y)$ – we choose one without loss of generality and write it as $\mathbf{k}=(k_{1},...,k_{r}).$ Plugging the above into (8.1), we get that:

$$ S(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L);q_{1},q_{2},t,k)=\sum_{\mathbf{c}}\mu(\mathbf{c})\chi(\mathbf{c})S(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{k}), $$

where we define:

$$ S(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{k}):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(x,y)\in(B/kt)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(x,y)=1\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(F_{i}(x,y)/c_{i}k_{i}) $$

### 8.2. Interpretation $\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}$ as $(1\star\chi)$

Next, we would like to make precise our claim that

$$ \varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(n)\approx(1\star\chi)(n). $$

As we have alluded to before, these two functions are morally equivalent.

First, we make the observation that if $n$ satisfies that $p\mid n\implies p\mid-\Delta$ , then

$$ \varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(n)=\sum_{N(\mathfrak{a})=n}\chi_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathfrak{a})=\chi_{q_{1}}(p_{q_{2}}(n))\chi_{q_{2}}(p_{q_{1}}(n))\mathbf{1}_{\exists\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=n}. $$

Since $\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(n)$ is multiplicative, we can always write

$$ \varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(n)=\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(p_{-\Delta}(n))\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(p_{\neg-\Delta}(n))=(\chi_{q_{1}}(p_{q_{2}}(n))\chi_{q_{2}}(p_{q_{1}}(n))\mathbf{1}_{\exists\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=p_{-\Delta}(n)})\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(p_{\neg-\Delta}(n)). $$

Recall that $\chi_{q_{1}}\chi_{q_{2}}=\chi$ and that these are quadratic characters. For $\gcd(n,-\Delta)=1$ , we have the relation:

$$ \displaystyle\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(n) \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\mid n\end{subarray}}\chi_{q_{1}}(n/d)\chi_{q_{2}}(d)=\sum_{d\mid n}\chi_{q_{1}}(n)\chi_{q_{1}}\chi_{q_{2}}(d) \displaystyle=\chi_{q_{1}}(n)\sum_{d\mid n}\chi(d)=\chi_{q_{1}}(n)(1\star\chi)(p_{\neg-\Delta}(n)). $$

We can thus reexpress (8.3) as:

$$ S(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{k})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(x,y)\in(B/tk)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(x,y)=1\\
k_{i}c_{i}\mid F_{i}(x,y)\end{subarray}}\epsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(p_{-\Delta}(F(x,y)/kc))\chi_{q_{1}}(p_{\neg-\Delta}(F(x,y)/kc))\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1\star\chi)(p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(x,y)/k_{i}c_{i}))\\
=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\ll(B/tk)^{2}\\
p\mid n\implies p\mid-\Delta\end{subarray}}\chi_{q_{1}}(p_{q_{2}}(n))\chi_{q_{2}}(p_{q_{1}}(n))\mathbf{1}_{\exists\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=n}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{i}\bmod-\Delta\\
\gcd(a_{i},-\Delta)=1\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}\chi_{q_{1}}(a_{i})\\
\times\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(x,y)\in(B/tk)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(x,y)=1\\
k_{i}c_{i}\mid F_{i}(x,y)\\
p_{-\Delta}(F(x,y)/kc)=n\\
p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(x,y)/k_{i}c_{i})\equiv a_{i}\bmod-\Delta\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1\star\chi)(p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(x,y)/k_{i}c_{i})). $$

Note that since $k=N(\mathfrak{k})$ where $\gcd(\mathfrak{k},\overline{\mathfrak{k}})=1$ , we must have that $\gcd(k,-\Delta)=1$ .

Let us bound away the contribution from the large $n$ .

#### Lemma 8.4.

Let $F(x,y)$ be a squarefree binary form of degree $\leq 4$ . Define for $n$ such that $p\mid n\implies p\mid-\Delta$ and a vector of residues $\mathbf{a}$ mod $-\Delta$ :

$$ U(n,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{k}):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(x,y)\in(B/tk)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
k_{i}c_{i}\mid F_{i}(x,y)\\
p_{-\Delta}(F(x,y)/c)=n\\
p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(x,y)/k_{i}c_{i})\equiv a_{i}\bmod-\Delta\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1\star\chi)(p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(x,y)/k_{i}c_{i})). $$

Then we have that

$$ U(n,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{k})\ll_{\Delta,f}\frac{BL^{2}\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}(8\deg(F))^{\omega(k)}}{tk^{2}n}. $$

#### Proof.

Note that since $(1\star\chi)(n)$ is a non-negative function,

$$ U(n,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{k})\leq\sum_{n=n_{1}...n_{r}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(x,y)\in(B/tk)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
k_{i}n_{i}\mid F_{i}(x,y)\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1\star\chi)(F_{i}(x,y)/k_{i}c_{i}). $$

Here, we have used the fact that $(1\star\chi)(dp_{\neg u}(n)))=(1\star\chi)(p_{\neg u}(n))$ for any $d$ satisfying that if $p\mid d$ then $p\mid-\Delta$ . We apply Theorem 3.11, we have that the inner sum above is bounded by

$$ \frac{BL^{2}}{tk}\cdot\log(B/tk)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{r}\frac{(8\deg(F))^{\omega(n_{i}k_{i})}}{n_{i}k_{i}}\ll\frac{BL^{2}\log(B/tk)^{\varrho_{\Delta,Q}-2}(8\deg(F))^{\omega(k)}}{tk^{2}n}. $$

Here we have used Corollary 3.16 and that $\omega(n_{i})\leq\omega(\Delta)$ for any value of $n_{i}$ . ∎

Consequently, we can bound the contribution from $n>N$ :

$$ \sum_{n>N}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\bmod-\Delta}U(n,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{k})\ll\frac{BL^{2}\log(B/tk)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}(8\deg(F))^{\omega(k)}}{tk^{2}}\cdot\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n>N\\
p\mid n\implies p\mid-\Delta\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{n}. $$

Since the sum over $n$ satisfying that $p\mid n\implies p\mid-\Delta$ is a geometric series, we can see that

$$ \sum_{n>N}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\bmod-\Delta}U(n,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{k})\ll\frac{BL^{2}\log(B/tk)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}(8\deg(F))^{\omega(k)}}{Ntk^{2}}. $$

For $N=\log(B/tk)^{10^{-7}},$ this error term is sufficient for Propositon 5.11. So, from now on we can assume that $n\leq\log(B/tk)^{10^{-7}}\ll\log(B)^{10^{-7}}$ (since $tk\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})$ ).

#### Remark 8.5.

Since we assume that $n\leq\log(B)^{10^{-7}}$ still grows as $B\rightarrow\infty$ , we must be somewhat careful in tracking the dependency of future bounds on $n$ . However, $n$ is still quite small, so we can allow for any reasonable polynomial dependency on $n$ .

Finally, let us define a new function for a fixed $n$ and tuple $\mathbf{a}$ satisfying that $\gcd(a_{i},-\Delta)=1$ for all $i$ :

$$ S(n,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{k})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(x,y)\in(B/tk)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
\gcd(x,y)=1\\
k_{i}c_{i}\mid F_{i}(x,y)\\
p_{q_{i}}(F(x,y)/c)=n_{i}\\
p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(x,y)/k_{i}c_{i})\equiv a_{i}\bmod-\Delta\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1\star\chi)(p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(x,y)/k_{i}c_{i})). $$

### 8.3. Removing the $\gcd$ condition

Now, we will remove the condition that $\gcd(x,y)=1$ using Möbius inversion. In particular, we know that

$$ S(n,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{k})=\sum_{b\leq(B/tk)^{1/2}}\mu(b)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(x,y)\in(B/tk)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
b\mid x,y\\
k_{i}c_{i}\mid F_{i}(x,y)\\
p_{q_{i}}(F(x,y)/c)=n_{i}\\
p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(x,y)/k_{i}c_{i})\equiv a_{i}\bmod-\Delta\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1\star\chi)(p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(x,y)/k_{i}c_{i})). $$

We can bound away the contribution given by large values of $b$ :

#### Lemma 8.6.

Let $F(x,y)$ be a squarefree binary form of degree $\leq 4$ . Define for a fixed $b$ :

$$ U(n,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{k};b):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(x,y)\in(B/kt)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
b\mid x,y\\
k_{i}c_{i}\mid F_{i}(x,y)\\
p_{q_{i}}(F(x,y)/c)=n_{i}\\
p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(x,y)/k_{i}c_{i})\equiv a_{i}\bmod-\Delta\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1\star\chi)(p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(x,y)/k_{i}c_{i})). $$

Then for any $B\geq X\gg 1$ , we have that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}X\leq b\ll(B/kt)^{1/2}\end{subarray}}\mu^{2}(b)U(n,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{k};b)\ll_{\Delta,F}\frac{BL^{2}\log(B/kt)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}(8\deg(F))^{\omega(k)}}{Xtk^{2}}. $$

#### Proof.

Again, by the nonnegativity of $(1\star\chi)(n)$ , we have that

$$ U(n,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{k};b)\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(x,y)\in b^{-1}(B/tk)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1\star\chi)(b^{\deg(F_{i})}F_{i}(x,y)/k_{i}c_{i}). $$

Now we apply Lemma 8.3 to separate the contribution from $b^{\deg(F_{i})}$ and $F_{i}(x,y)/k_{i}c_{i}$ :

$$ \sum_{e_{i}\mid b}\mu(e_{i})\chi(e_{i})\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1\star\chi)(b^{\deg(F_{i})}/e_{i})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(x,y)\in b^{-1}(B/tk)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
e_{i}\mid F_{i}(x,y)\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1\star\chi)(F_{i}(x,y)/k_{i}c_{i}e_{i}). $$

After using Theorem 3.11, we have that the above is bounded by

$$ \sum_{e_{i}\mid b}\mu^{2}(e_{i})\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1\star\chi)(b^{\deg(F_{i})}/e_{i})\cdot\frac{BL^{2}\log(B/tk)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}(8\deg(F))^{\omega(k)}}{b^{2}tk^{2}}\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{r}\frac{(8\deg(F))^{\omega(e_{i})}}{e_{i}}. $$

Summing over $b\geq X$ , we get the expression

$$ \frac{BL^{2}\log(B/tk)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}(8\deg(F))^{\omega(k)}}{tk^{2}}\sum_{b\geq X}\frac{\mu^{2}(b)}{b^{2}}\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{r}\sum_{e_{i}\mid b}\mu^{2}(e_{i})(1\star\chi)(b^{\deg(F_{i})}/e_{i})\cdot\frac{(8\deg(F))^{\omega(e_{i})}}{e_{i}}\\
\ll\frac{BL^{2}\log(B/tk)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}\deg(F)^{\omega(k)}}{tk^{2}}\sum_{b\geq X}\mu^{2}(b)\cdot\frac{a_{b}}{b^{2}}, $$

where we define:

$$ a_{b}:=\prod_{i=1}^{r}\prod_{p\mid b}\left(1+\frac{8\deg(F)\cdot(1\star\chi)(b^{\deg(F_{i})}/p)}{p}\right). $$

This function $a_{b}$ is multiplicative in $b$ , so we relate this sum to a Dirichlet series with an Euler product expansion. If we consider the singular series:

$$ \gamma(s):=\sum_{b=1}^{\infty}\mu^{2}(b)\cdot\frac{a_{b}}{b^{s}}=\prod_{p}\left(1+p^{-s}\prod_{i=1}^{r}\prod_{p\mid b}\left(1+\frac{8\deg(F)\cdot(1\star\chi)(b^{\deg(F_{i})}/p)}{p}\right)\right)\\
