Observe that $\#\{\mathfrak{k}:N(\mathfrak{t})=k\}\ll 2^{\omega(k)}.$ On the other hand, we have that

$$ \sum_{k\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})}\frac{64^{\omega(k)}\nu_{1}(k)^{1/2}}{k}\cdot\#\{\mathfrak{k}:N(\mathfrak{k})=k\}\\
\leq\left(\sum_{k\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})}\frac{1}{k}\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_{k\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})}\frac{\nu_{1}(k)C_{2}^{\omega(k)}}{k}\right), $$

where $C_{2}=2^{14}$ . The first term above is bounded by $\log(B)^{1/2}.$ Expanding out the second term, we have

$$ \sum_{k\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})}\frac{\nu_{1}(k)C_{2}^{\omega(k)}}{k}\leq\sum_{k\leq B}\frac{C_{2}^{\omega(k)}}{k}\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal{U}(k)}\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}(\Lambda(\alpha))}. $$

Since we know that

$$ \sum_{k\leq B}\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal{U}(k)}\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}(\Lambda(\alpha))}\ll\sum_{0\neq|\mathbf{v}|\leq\sqrt{B}}\frac{\#\{k\leq B:k\mid F(\mathbf{v})\}}{|\mathbf{v}|}\ll\sqrt{B}\log(B), $$

by partial summation the second term is bounded absolutely. In summary, we have that

$$ \sum_{k\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})}\frac{64^{\omega(k)}\nu_{1}(k)^{1/2}}{k}\cdot\#\{\mathfrak{k}:N(\mathfrak{k})=k\}\ll\log(B)^{1/2}. $$

Thus, this final error term is again upper bounded by $B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1-10^{-7}}.$ For all of the error terms above, we recall that $L\gg\log(B)^{-10^{-10}}.$

It remains to analyze the main term by expanding the definition of $C_{q_{1},q_{2},f,N(\mathfrak{k})}$ :

$$ BL^{2}\cdot\sum_{c_{ij}\mid\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})}\frac{\mu(\mathbf{c})\chi(\mathbf{c})}{c^{2}}\cdot\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathbf{c})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{k})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{k},\overline{\mathfrak{k}})=1\end{subarray}}\frac{\mu(\mathfrak{k})}{N(\mathfrak{k})^{3}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/k\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{t})}V(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{k},D). $$

Here we use $\mu(\mathbf{c})\chi(\mathbf{c})$ to denote the appropriate product depending on the factorization of $F(x,y)$ (as written down explicitly in §11.1). Let us expand out the definition of $V(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{k},D)$ and change the order of summation (using $\mathfrak{t}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{t}\mathfrak{k}$ ):

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{k})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{k},\overline{\mathfrak{k}})=1\end{subarray}}\frac{\mu(\mathfrak{k})}{N(\mathfrak{k})^{3}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t})\leq B/k\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{t})}V(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{k},D)\\
=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t}^{\prime})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t}^{\prime},\overline{\mathfrak{t}^{\prime}})=1\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{t}^{\prime})}\sum_{\mathfrak{k}\mid\mathfrak{t}^{\prime}}\frac{\mu(\mathfrak{k})}{N(\mathfrak{k})^{2}}\sum_{\mathbf{d}\leq(B/N(\mathfrak{t})^{\prime})^{\deg(F)/4}}\frac{\chi(d)\varrho_{F}^{*}(\mathbf{c}\mathbf{k}\mathbf{d})}{d^{2}}\prod_{p\mid ckd}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}. $$

Note that since $k=N(\mathfrak{k})\mid t=N(\mathfrak{t})$ , we know that if $p\mid k$ then $\chi(p)=1$ ; hence, $\chi(k)=1$ .

Let us consider the multiple Dirichlet series:

$$ \xi(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,\mathbf{c}):=\sum_{\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1}\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{t})^{s_{1}}}\sum_{\mathfrak{k}\mid\mathfrak{t}}\frac{\mu(\mathfrak{k})}{N(\mathfrak{k})^{2}}\sum_{\mathbf{d}}\frac{\chi(d)\varrho_{F}^{*}(\mathbf{c}\mathbf{k}\mathbf{d})}{d^{2s_{2}}}\prod_{p\mid ckd}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}. $$

We want to establish what the analytic behavior of this series looks like at $(s_{1},s_{2})=(1,1)$ . Since the series converges in the region $\Re(s_{1}),\Re(s_{2})>1$ , in this regime we have the Euler product:

$$ \xi(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,\mathbf{c})=\prod_{p\nmid-\Delta}L_{p}(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,\mathbf{c}), $$

where if $p\nmid\prod_{i\neq j}\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})$ , we define the local Euler factors $L_{p}(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,\mathbf{c})$ as:

$$ 1+(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\left(\frac{\chi(p)+1}{p^{s_{1}}}\left(1-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}\right)+\frac{\chi(p)\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2s_{2}}}+\frac{\chi(p)+1}{p^{s_{1}+2s_{2}}}\left(\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{2})}{p^{2}}\right)+\ldots\right). $$

Observe that since $\gcd(c,p)=1$ , the above local factors are independent of $\mathbf{c}$ . Here we have also used that if $p\nmid\prod_{i\neq j}\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})$ , then

$$ \varrho_{F}^{*}((p,1,\dots,1))+\dots+\varrho_{F}^{*}((1,\dots,p))=\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)=\#\{(x,y)\bmod p:\gcd(x,y,p)=1,p\mid F(x,y)\}. $$

Now, if $p\mid\prod_{i\neq j}\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})$ , then the expression for $L_{p}(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,\mathbf{c})$ is more complicated; however, this is a finite product and so we can consider this (for now) an absolute constant:

$$ \gamma(F,\chi,\mathbf{c}):=\prod_{p\mid\prod_{i\neq j}\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})}L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,\mathbf{c}). $$

Inspecting these local factors further, it becomes evident that the analytic behavior of $\xi(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,\mathbf{c})$ at $s_{1}=1$ , $s_{2}=2$ matches that of:

$$ \zeta_{K}(s_{1})\cdot\prod_{p}\left(1+\frac{\chi(p)\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2s_{2}}}\right). $$

Note that to conclude the above statement, we have used that $\varrho_{F}^{*}(n)\ll_{F}4^{\omega(n)}n$ to state that the difference between $\xi(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,\mathbf{c})$ and the above product converges absolutely for $\Re(s_{1}),\Re(s_{2})>1-\delta$ . At $s_{1}=1$ , we know that $\zeta_{K}(s_{1})$ has a simple pole.

On the other hand, we can see that

$$ \xi^{*}(s;F,\chi)=\prod_{p}\left(1+\frac{\chi(p)\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2s_{2}}}\right) $$

will share the same behavior at $s_{2}=1$ as $\xi(s;F,\chi)$ , which is the same behavior as that of the $L$ -function

$$ L(s;F,\chi)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}L(s;f_{i}\times\chi)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\subset\mathbb{Q}[z]/f_{i}(z)}\left(1-\frac{\chi(N(\mathfrak{p}))}{N(\mathfrak{p})^{s_{2}}}\right)^{-1}. $$

In particular, it will have a pole of order $\#\{1\leq i\leq r:K\subset\mathbb{Q}[z]/f_{i}(z)\}=\rho_{\Delta,f}-2$ at $s_{2}=1.$ This follows from Lemma 3.15 and its corollary.

With these two facts in hand, we can now return to our sum:

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{t}^{\prime})\leq B/\exp(\sqrt{\log(B)})\\
\gcd(\mathfrak{t}^{\prime},\overline{\mathfrak{t}^{\prime}})=1\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{t}^{\prime})}\sum_{\mathfrak{k}\mid\mathfrak{t}^{\prime}}\frac{\mu(\mathfrak{k})}{N(\mathfrak{k})^{2}}\sum_{\mathbf{d}\leq(B/N(\mathfrak{t})^{\prime})^{\deg(F)/4}}\frac{\chi(d)\varrho_{F}^{*}(\mathbf{c}\mathbf{k}\mathbf{d})}{d^{2}}\prod_{p\mid ckd}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1} $$

Indeed, since $\xi(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,\mathbf{c})$ has a simple pole at $s_{1}=1$ and a pole of order $\rho_{\Delta,f}-2$ at $s_{2}=2$ , this sum can be evaluated as:

$$ \gamma(F,\chi,\mathbf{c})\cdot C^{\prime}_{F,\chi,\mathbf{c}}\cdot\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}+O_{F,\chi,\mathbf{c}}(\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}). $$

Finally, we can evaluate our main term (11.8):

$$ BL^{2}\sum_{c_{ij}\mid\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})}\frac{\mu(\mathbf{c})\chi(\mathbf{c})}{c^{2}}\cdot\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathbf{c})\left(\gamma(F,\chi,\mathbf{c})\cdot C^{\prime}_{F,\chi,\mathbf{c}}\cdot\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}+O_{F,\chi,\mathbf{c}}(\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}\right). $$

Since the sum over $c_{ij}\mid\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})$ is finite, we can set

$$ C_{q_{1},q_{2},f}=\sum_{c_{ij}\mid\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})}\frac{\mu(\mathbf{c})\chi(\mathbf{c})}{c^{2}}\cdot\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathbf{c})\cdot\gamma(F,\chi,\mathbf{c})\cdot C^{\prime}_{F,\chi,\mathbf{c}}, $$

and complete the proof of Proposition 5.11.

∎

## 12. Analysis of the leading constant

Finally, we want to establish that our leading constant if $c_{\Delta,f}$ is zero then there is a local or Brauer-Manin obstruction to rational points on $X_{\Delta,f}$ . We can see from the reductions of section §5 that it suffices to classify when

$$ \sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}C_{q_{1},q_{2},f}=0. $$

In particular, we want to deduce exactly when the following expression is zero:

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{c}}\frac{\mu(\mathbf{c})\chi(\mathbf{c})}{c^{2}}\cdot\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathbf{c})\textrm{Res}_{s_{1}=1}\textrm{Res}_{s_{2}=1}\xi(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,\mathbf{c}), $$

where $\xi(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,\mathbf{c})$ is the series defined in (11.9). Here we use $\textrm{Res}_{s=1}$ to denote the first nonzero coefficient in the Laurent series expansion at $s=1$ . We will begin our analysis gradually by starting with the combinatorially simplest case: when $f(z)$ is irreducible. In this case, it is known by [10] that $X_{\Delta,f}$ satisfies the Hasse principle; we aim for the stronger result that if there are no local obstructions to $X_{\Delta,f}$ then there are $\asymp B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2}$ rational points of height at most $B$ .

Second, we introduce the auxiliary varieties that are inherent to our analysis – this comes to the sum over $c_{ij}$ . These varieties also appear in the finite and effective computation of [9] and [12] for determining if $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset.$ In this subsection, we also establish that if $f(z)$ has a linear factor then there exists an auxiliary variety containing a rational point.

Finally, we will classify when $c_{\Delta,f}=0$ by handling the cases when $f(z)$ factorizes. This will include the case when $f(z)$ factorizes as a product of two quadratics – the only scenario when the Hasse principle may fail.

### 12.1. The irreducible case

Let $f(z)$ be an irreducible polynomial. Then there are no torsors $c$ involved and our expression (12.1) becomes:

$$ \sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(1)\cdot\textrm{Res}_{s_{1}=1}\textrm{Res}_{s_{2}=1}\xi(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,1). $$

In Lemma 12.11, we find that if

$$ \bigtriangledown(1)=\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(1)=0 $$

then for some $p\mid-\Delta$ , $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})\neq\emptyset.$ In other words, $\bigtriangledown(1)$ detects the local obstructions for primes dividing $-\Delta$ .

So, we consider

$$ \textrm{Res}_{s_{1}=1,s_{2}=1}\xi(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,1)=\textrm{Res}_{s_{1}=1,s_{2}=1}\sum_{\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1}\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{t})^{s_{1}}}\sum_{\mathfrak{k}\mid\mathfrak{t}}\frac{\mu(\mathfrak{k})}{N(\mathfrak{k})^{2}}\sum_{d}\frac{\chi(d)\varrho_{F}^{*}(kd)}{d^{2s_{2}}}\prod_{p\mid kd}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}. $$

Let us define the local factor for $p\nmid-\Delta$ :

$$ L_{p}(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,1)=1+(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\cdot\left(\frac{\chi(p)+1}{p^{s_{1}}}\left(1-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}\right)+\frac{\chi(p)\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2s_{2}}}+\ldots\right). $$

It suffices to show a uniform lower bound on

$$ (1-p^{-1})^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,1). $$

Here we have recalled that $\xi(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,1)$ has a simple pole near $s_{1}=1$ and a pole of order $\rho_{\Delta,f}-2$ at $s_{2}=2.$

First, observe that since $\rho_{F}^{*}(n)\leq 4^{\omega(n)}n$ , for $p\gg 1$ we have a uniform lower bound on $L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,1)$ given by the geometric series:

$$ (1-p^{-1})^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}\left(1-\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{p}+\frac{16}{p^{2}}-+\frac{2\cdot(4p-8)}{p^{3}}+\dots\right)\right). $$

In other words, for $p\gg 1$ , the above expression is uniformly bounded below by some constant $c^{\prime}>0$ . With this bound in hand, it suffices to show that for any prime $p\nmid-\Delta$ , we have that $L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,1)\neq 0.$

For any exponent $e$ , we know definitionally that

$$ \varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{e})-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{e+1})}{p^{2}}\geq 0, $$

as any element satisfying $p^{e+1}\mid F(x,y)$ must satisfy that $p^{e}\mid F(x,y)$ . Further, we know that

$$ (p^{2}-1)-\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)\geq 0, $$

since the count $\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)$ excludes when $(x,y)=(0,0)\bmod p$ . Together, this tells us that if $\chi(p)=1$ , then $L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,1)>0$ , as it is the sum of 1 and only nonnegative terms. Indeed, we do not expect any local obstructions to occur when $\chi(p)=1$ .

If $\chi(p)=-1$ , then (since $\chi(p)+1=0$ and the terms dependent on $s_{1}$ disappear) we see that

$$ L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,1)=\left(1-(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}\right)+(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\left(\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{2})}{p^{4}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{3})}{p^{6}}\right)+\dots $$

Using the grouping indicated above, we again see that this term must be nonnegative. If $L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,1)=0$ , then we must additionally have that

$$ \varrho_{F}^{*}(p)=p^{2}-1,\quad\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{2k})=\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{2k+1})}{p^{2}},\forall k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}. $$

The left (right) equality holds if and only if $p$ divides all values of $F(x,y)$ ( $p^{2k+1}$ divides all values of $F(x,y)$ ). In other words, for some $k\geq 1$ , we have that $p^{2k-1}\mid F(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$ , but there are no solutions to $F(x,y)\equiv 0\bmod p^{2k}$ with $\gcd(x,y,p)=1$ . Since $\chi(p)=-1$ , this tells us that there are no nontrivial solutions to the equation

$$ x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=F(x,y)\bmod p^{2k}, $$

and thus there must be a local obstruction, i.e. $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})=\emptyset.$

Thus, we have proved the following result.

#### Proposition 12.1.

Let $f(z)$ be irreducible. Then if the leading constant $c_{\Delta,f}$ is zero then there is a local obstruction for $X_{\Delta,f}$ . Consequently, if there are no local obstructions, then $c_{\Delta,f}\neq 0$ and hence $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset$ . Thus, the Hasse principle holds for $X_{\Delta,f}.$

### 12.2. Descent and auxiliary varieties

To analyze (12.1) when $f(z)$ factorizes, we must first introduce the auxiliary varieties $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}$ (defined in (1.2)). Fortunately, these auxiliary varieties are well-studied and appear as crucial objects in Colliot-Thélène, Coray, and Sansuc’s work on the Brauer-Manin obstruction and descent. Specifically, in a sequence of papers [8, 13], Colliot-Thélène and Sansuc established the method of descent. In our proof, we would like to use the fibrations discussed by Colliot-Thélène, Coray, and Sansuc in [9] when $f(z)$ factorizes as the product of two irreducible quadratics. It is of note that in the proof of [12, Proposition 3] it is established that a similar set of auxiliary surfaces are intimately tied to these questions; observe that in [12, Proposition 3], these varieties are denoted as $W_{g}$ and take into account extra homogenization when $f(z)$ has an odd degree irreducible factor.

Let us recall from (1.2) the definition of our auxiliary varieties:

$$ X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}=\{(z,(x_{i},y_{i})_{i=1}^{r}:x_{i}^{2}+\Delta y_{i}^{2}=\alpha_{i}f_{i}(z)\neq 0\}. $$

In the next subsection, we describe how $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}$ relates to $X_{\Delta,f}$ in many ways. Most importantly is the following consequence of Harari’s formal lemma [32, Corollary 2.6.1] (see also [14, Theorem 13.4.3] and the example [14, p. 343]) and was demonstrated to the author by Colliot-Thélène in [16]. In [9] and [12], certain cases are also shown under certain degree parity conditions.

#### Theorem 12.2 (Colliot-Thélène [16]).

Assume that $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q}_{v})\neq\emptyset$ for every place $v$ and there is no Brauer-Manin obstruction to the Hasse principle for $X_{\Delta,f}$ . Then there exists an $(\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r})\in(\mathbb{Q}^{\times})^{r}$ satisfying $\alpha_{1}\dots\alpha_{r}=1$ , $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q}_{v})\neq\emptyset$ for all places $v$ .

#### Proof.

By assumption, let $(x_{v},y_{v},z_{v})\in X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})^{\textrm{Br}(X)}$ ; we can furthermore assume that $(x_{v},y_{v},z_{v})\in X^{*}_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$ . Let $U_{\Delta,f}$ denote the smooth compactification of $X^{*}_{\Delta,f}$ and hence $U_{\Delta,f}\subset X_{\Delta,f}$ . Then let $S$ denote the finite set of places of $\mathbb{Q}$ such that

$$ S:=\{v:\exists\gamma\in\textrm{Br}(U_{\Delta,f}),\gamma(x_{v},y_{v},z_{v})\neq 0\}. $$

Let $\beta_{i}=(-\Delta,f_{i})\in\textrm{Br}(U_{\Delta,f})$ denote an element of the Brauer group of $U_{\Delta,f}$ , for each $i=1,\ldots,r-1$ . Then Harari’s formal lemma [14, Theorem 13.4.3] gives an extension of $(x_{v},y_{v},z_{v})_{v\in S}$ to an adelic point $(M_{v})_{v\in\mathscr{P}\cup\{\infty\}}$ such that

$$ \sum_{v\in\mathscr{P}\cup\{\infty\}}\beta_{i}(M_{v})=0,\forall i=1,\ldots,r-1. $$

Note that Harari’s formal lemma specifically applies to those $\beta_{i}\in\textrm{Br}(U_{\Delta,f})\backslash\textrm{Br}(X_{\Delta,f})$ ; however, this equality trivially holds for any element of $\textrm{Br}(X_{\Delta,f})$ since $(x_{v},y_{v},z_{v})\in X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})^{\textrm{Br}(X)}.$

Next, we consider the exact sequence

$$ 1\rightarrow\mathbb{Q}^{\times}/N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(K^{\times})\rightarrow\oplus_{v\in\mathscr{P}\cup\{\infty\}}\mathbb{Q}_{v}^{\times}/N_{K_{v}/\mathbb{Q}_{v}}(K_{v}^{\times})\xrightarrow{\gamma}\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow 1. $$

Consider for $i\in\{1,\ldots,r-1\}$ the map

$$ (M_{v})\mapsto(f_{i}(z_{v}))\in\oplus_{v\in\mathscr{P}\cup\{\infty\}}\mathbb{Q}_{v}^{\times}/N_{K_{v}/\mathbb{Q}_{v}}(K_{v}^{\times}). $$

Since we know that

$$ \gamma((f_{i}(z_{v}))_{v})=\sum_{v\in\mathscr{P}\cup\{\infty\}}\beta_{i}(M_{v})=0\in\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}, $$

there must exist an element $\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{Q}^{\times}$ such that

$$ f_{i}(z_{v})=\alpha_{i}N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(x_{i}+y_{i}\sqrt{-\Delta})\neq 0. $$

Furthermore, the above holds simultaneously for all $\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{r-1}$ , so we must have that the auxiliary variety

$$ \begin{array}[]{c}x_{1}^{2}+\Delta y_{1}^{2}=\alpha_{1}f_{1}(z)\neq 0\\
\vdots\\
x_{r-1}^{2}+\Delta y_{r-1}^{2}=\alpha_{r-1}f_{r-1}(z)\neq 0\\
x_{r}^{2}+\Delta y_{r}^{2}=(\alpha_{1}\cdots\alpha_{r-1})^{-1}f_{r}(z)\neq 0\end{array} $$

contains an adelic point; in other words, for $\alpha_{r}=(\alpha_{1}\cdots\alpha_{r-1})^{-1}$ , we have that $(M_{v})_{v\in\mathscr{P}\cup\{\infty\}}\in X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}}).$ ∎

#### Remark 12.3.

We note that for any point $(z,(x_{i},y_{i})_{i=1}^{r})\in X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q})$ , we can create a point in $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})$ given by

$$ x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}(x_{i}+y_{i}\sqrt{-\Delta}),\textrm{ }z=z. $$

Thus, if the family of varieties $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}$ satisfies the Hasse principle, Theorem 12.2 gives that the Brauer-Manin obstruction is the only possible obstruction to the Hasse principle. In fact, this is exactly the approach Colliot-Thélène, Coray, and Sansuc [9] used to prove that when $f=f_{1}(z)f_{2}(z)$ is the product of two irreducible quadratics the only possible obstruction to the Hasse principle is the Brauer-Manin obstruction. Moreover, in [12, Proposition 3 and 4], Colliot-Thélène and Sansuc used this strategy with a variation of the auxiliary varieties to prove that under the assumption of Schinzel’s Hypothesis H, the only possible obstruction to the Hasse principle for Châtelet surfaces is the Brauer-Manin obstruction.

However, in the resolution of the question of the Hasse principle for Châtelet surfaces, Colliot-Thélène, Sansuc, and Swinnerton-Dyer [10][11], use a different parameterization of the rational points on $X_{\Delta,f}$ – this parameterization is given by torsors. This allows them to approach the hardest case, when $f(z)$ is irreducible, which is circuitous with the auxiliary varieties above. Fortunately for us, this case when $f(z)$ is irreducible is actually the clearest example for our argument, as demonstrated in the previous subsection.

Next, we make some more observations on connections between rational points on $X_{\Delta,f}$ and those on $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}.$

#### Lemma 12.4.

Assume that $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset$ . Then there exists $(\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r})\in(\mathbb{Q}^{\times})^{r}$ such that

$$ X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset. $$

#### Proof.

First note that if $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset$ , then $X_{\Delta,f}$ must be unirational (see [11, Proposition 9.8.(iii)] and [17, Theorem A]) and hence we have that $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})$ is Zariski-dense; so, $X^{*}_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset.$ Assume that for some $(x_{0},y_{0},z_{0})\in\mathbb{Q}$ we have that $x_{0}^{2}+\Delta y_{0}^{2}=f(z_{0})\neq 0$ . Then set $\alpha_{i}=f_{i}(z_{0})\neq 0$ for each $i$ and consider

$$ x_{i}^{2}+\Delta y_{i}^{2}=\alpha_{i}f_{i}(z). $$

This variety clearly has a rational point at $z=z_{0}$ for each $i$ . Thus, $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset.$ ∎

For the remainder of the section, we aim to prove the following proposition:

#### Proposition 12.5.

Let $\Delta\in\mathbb{Z}$ be a squarefree integer satisfying that $\sqrt{-\Delta}\not\in\mathbb{Q}$ . Let $f(z)\in\mathbb{Z}[z]$ be a separable polynomial of degree 3 or 4. Let $X_{\Delta,f}$ be the corresponding Châtelet surface. Then as $B\rightarrow\infty,$

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},B)=c_{\Delta,f}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}+O(B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1-10^{-10}}) $$

with $c_{\Delta,f}$ nonzero if there exists an $(\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r})\in(\mathbb{Q}^{\times})^{r}$ such that $\alpha_{1}\dots\alpha_{r}=1$ and $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q}_{v})\neq\emptyset$ for all places $v$ .

By Theorem 12.2, this tells us that $c_{\Delta,f}=0$ if and only if there is either a local or Brauer-Manin obstruction to rational points on $X_{\Delta,f}.$

#### 12.2.1. Finite classes of torsors

Now, we show that we actually only need to consider a finite set of values $(\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r})$ to understand $X_{\Delta,f}$ . In [12, Proposition 3], it is shown that one must only look at a finite set of values $(\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r})$ that belong to the kernels of certain natural maps. This sentiment of restricting to a finite set of representatives $(\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r})$ is repeated in the lemma below, but first we shall homogenize our varieties.

Let us fix a tuple $(\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r})\in\mathbb{Q}^{r}$ satisfying $\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{r}=1.$ We observe that we can instead look at the integral points on the homogenization of these variety $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}$ :

$$ Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}:=\{x_{i}^{2}+\Delta y_{i}^{2}=\alpha_{i}t_{i}^{2}F_{i}(u,v)\neq 0,\gcd(x_{i},y_{i},t_{i})=\gcd(u,v)=1,\forall i\}. $$

A version of this reduction is described explicitly by de la Bretèche and Browning in the derivation of [21, Lemma 4.2] for $\Delta=1$ . Next, we note that if $\alpha_{i}=\alpha_{i}^{\prime}\beta_{i}$ , where $\beta_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}$ and satisfies that $\beta_{i}=b_{i}^{2}$ , i.e. $\beta_{i}$ is a square, then we have that

$$ X_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}^{*}\cong X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1}^{\prime},...,\alpha_{r}^{\prime}}. $$

By the equivalence of these varieties, we can assume that $\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}$ are squarefree. We can also assume that $f_{1},\dots,f_{r}$ all satisfy that the coefficients of $f_{i}$ are at most divisible by a squarefree integer. Moreover, we also know that the product of all of the $\alpha_{i}$ is a square.

Further, if $\alpha_{i}=\alpha_{i}^{\prime}p_{i}$ for $\chi(p_{i})=1$ , then we fix some representative $c_{g_{i}}$ for the class group element $g_{i}=[\mathfrak{p}_{i}]\in C$ . If $\gamma_{i}=N(c_{g_{i}})$ , then we also have that

$$ X_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}^{*}\cong X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1}^{\prime}\gamma_{1},...,\alpha_{r}^{\prime}\gamma_{r}}. $$

So, we can assume, up to some fixed elements depending on the class group $C$ , that $\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}$ satisfy that if $p\mid\alpha_{i}$ then $\chi(p)=-1$ . We assume that $N(c_{[1]})=1$ .

#### Lemma 12.6.

Let $\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}\in\mathbb{Z}$ be squarefree and assume that if $p\mid\alpha_{i}$ then either $\chi(p)=-1$ or $p$ divides some norm of a fixed set of class group representatives. Moreover, assume that $\alpha_{1}\dots\alpha_{r}$ is a square. If $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset$ , then

$$ \alpha_{i}\mid\prod_{j\neq i}\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j}). $$

#### Proof.

Let $((x_{i},y_{i},t_{i}),u,v)$ be a point on $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}$ . Since $p\mid\alpha_{i}$ implies that $\chi(p)=-1$ or $p$ divides the norm of a nontrivial class group representative, we must have that $\alpha_{i}\mid F_{i}(u,v)$ for each $i$ in order for the equation

$$ x_{i}^{2}+\Delta y_{i}^{2}=\alpha_{i}t_{i}^{2}F_{i}(u,v)\neq 0 $$

to be solvable. Let us assume that $\alpha_{i}$ has the following prime factorization:

$$ \alpha_{i}=\prod_{\chi(p)=-1}p^{e_{p,i}}, $$

with $e_{p,i}\in\{0,1\}.$ Since the product of all of the $\alpha_{i}$ must be a square, we must have that

$$ e_{p,i}=\sum_{j\neq i}e_{p,i,j} $$

where $p^{e_{p,i,j}}\mid\gcd(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}).$ Then we also have that $p^{e_{p,i,j}}\mid F_{j}(u,v)$ as well. Since $\gcd(u,v)=1$ , this implies that $p^{e_{p,i,j}}\mid\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})$ . Since this holds for every pair $i$ and $j$ and all prime factors of $\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}$ , we have that

$$ \alpha_{i}\mid\prod_{j\neq i}\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j}). $$

∎

#### Remark 12.7.

We note that if there is some $b_{i}$ that divides all of the coefficients of $F_{i}$ , then $b_{i}\mid\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})$ for any $j\neq i$ . This is analogous to tracking the primes that divide the coefficients of $f(z)$ when $f(z)$ is irreducible in the case described above.

From Lemma 12.6, we see that it suffices to consider a finite set of tuples $(\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r})$ in order to prove Proposition 12.5. In particular, we can restrict ourselves to those $\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}$ that are squarefree and divide the pairwise resultants. These line up with the tuples $\mathbf{c}$ that we sum over in (12.1).

#### 12.2.2. Possible local obstructions

First, we want to determine for which primes $p$ we can have the possibility of local obstructions for $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}.$

#### Lemma 12.8.

Fix $\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}\in\mathbb{Z}$ as in Lemma 12.6. Let $\ell$ be a finite prime. Then the following are equivalent:

- (1) $Y_{\Delta,f_{1},\dots,f_{r},\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{r}}^{*}(\mathbb{Q}_{\ell})\neq\emptyset$ ,

- (2) There exists a solution to

$$ x_{i}^{2}+\Delta y_{i}^{2}=\alpha_{i}F_{i}(u,v),\forall i=1,\dots,r $$

over $\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}$ with $\gcd(u,v,\ell)=1$ .

Further, if $\ell\mid\prod_{i=1}^{r}\alpha_{i}$ and $\chi(\ell)=1$ then $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},\dots,f_{r},\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q}_{\ell})\neq\emptyset$ . If $\chi(\ell)=-1$ and $\ell^{e_{i}}\|\alpha_{i}$ , then $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q}_{\ell})\neq\emptyset$ if and only if

$$ \#\{(u,v)\in\mathbb{F}_{\ell}:\ell^{e_{i}\bmod 2}\mid F_{i}(u,v),\gcd(u,v,\ell)=1\}>0. $$

#### Remark 12.9.

By our assumptions on $\alpha_{i}$ , we have that $e_{i}\in\{0,1\}.$

#### Proof.

First, let us start with the equation

$$ x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=c. $$

For $\ell\nmid c(-\Delta)$ , there will always be solutions over $\mathbb{Q}_{\ell}$ by the Lang-Weil theorem and Hensel’s Lemma; hence there is no chance of a local obstruction at these places.

Consider if $\ell\mid c$ and $\gcd(\ell,-\Delta)=1$ . Now, if $\chi(\ell)=-1$ , we know that there can only be a solution to $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=c$ if $c=\ell^{2e}m,$ for some $e\geq 1$ and $\gcd(m,\ell)=1$ . On the other hand, if $\chi(\ell)=1$ , $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}$ factorizes as a product of linear factors mod $\ell$ . Thus, there is a nonzero solution to $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=c\bmod\ell$ , and by Hensel’s lemma this can be lifted to a solution in $\mathbb{Q}_{\ell}$ .

Now, we return to the original variety $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}.$ Now, we return to the original variety $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}.$ The first part of the lemma statement is follows from the definition of $Y_{\Delta,f_{1},\dots,f_{r},\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{r}}^{*}$ . Let $\ell\mid\prod_{i=1}^{r}\alpha_{i}$ . If $\chi(\ell)=1$ , then since $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}$ factors as a product of linear products mod $\ell$ , by a combination of Lang-Weil and Hensel’s Lemma there will always be a solution over $\mathbb{Q}_{\ell}$ .

So, we can assume from now on that $\chi(\ell)=-1$ . Let $e_{i}$ be the power such that $\ell^{e_{i}}\|\alpha_{i}$ . We can see that $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q}_{\ell})\neq\emptyset$ if and only if there is a point $(u,v)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}^{2}$ with $\gcd(u,v,\ell)=1$ such that $\ell^{e_{i}\bmod 2}\mid F_{i}(u,v)$ (as we need an even power of $\ell$ to divide $\alpha_{i}F_{i}(u,v)$ ). In other words, we must have that

$$ \#\{(u,v)\in\mathbb{F}_{\ell}:\ell^{e_{i}\bmod 2}\mid F_{i}(u,v),\gcd(u,v,\ell)=1\}>0. $$

This is in fact sufficient because from such a point with $\ell^{e_{i}\bmod 2}\mid F_{i}(u,v)$ , we can build a solution in $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q}_{\ell})$ .

∎

### 12.3. Computing the constant

Let us return to analyzing (12.1) in the general case when $f(z)$ factorizes; in this section, we prove Proposition 12.5. First, let us fix a $\mathbf{c}$ and define the local factor at a prime $p\nmid-\Delta$ as $L_{p}(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,\mathbf{c})$ ; when $p\mid-\Delta$ , we use the convention that $L_{p}(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,\mathbf{c})=1.$ We recall that we are looking at the expression:

$$ \sum_{c_{ij}\mid\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})}\frac{\mu(\mathbf{c})\chi(\mathbf{c})}{c^{2}}\left(\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathbf{c})\right)\times\textrm{Res}_{s_{1}=1}\textrm{Res}_{s_{2}=2}\prod_{p\mid c}L_{p}(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,\mathbf{c})\prod_{p\nmid c}L_{p}(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,\mathbf{c}). $$

Define $R=\prod_{i\neq j}\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})$ and for any prime $p\mid R$ , $\mathbf{c}_{p}$ the vector containing the $p$ -parts of $\mathbf{c}$ . Additionally, define

$$ \bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c}):=\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathbf{c}). $$

Then we can rearrange the above expression as:

$$ \textrm{Res}_{s_{1}=1}\textrm{Res}_{s_{2}=1}\prod_{p\nmid R}L_{p}(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,1)\times\left(\sum_{c_{ij}\mid\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})}\frac{\mu(\mathbf{c})\chi(\mathbf{c})}{c^{2}}\bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c})\times\left(\prod_{p\mid R}L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,\mathbf{c}_{p})\right)\right). $$

To understand the above expression better, our plan is as follows: first, we will analyze the product over primes $p\nmid R$ ; this reduces our computation to the finite sum over $\mathbf{c}$ . Second, we will determine when $\bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c})=0$ (and this will in turn end up telling us if there is a local obstruction at $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},\dots,f_{r},\mathbf{c}}(\mathbb{Q}_{\ell})$ for any $\ell\mid-\Delta$ ). Third, we must look at this sum over $\mathbf{c}$ and determine when there can be perfect cancellation (which will correspond to local obstructions for primes dividing $c$ ).

#### Lemma 12.10.

Let $R=\prod_{i\neq j}\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})$ . Then, if

$$ \textrm{Res}_{s_{1}=1}\textrm{Res}_{s_{2}=1}\prod_{p\nmid R}L_{p}(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,1)=0, $$

then for some prime $p\nmid R(-\Delta)$ with $\chi(p)=-1$ , $Y_{f_{1},\dots,f_{r},\mathbf{c}}^{*}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})=\emptyset.$

#### Proof.

For $p\nmid R$ , we have the following expression for $L_{p}(s_{1},s_{2};F,\chi,1):$

$$ 1+(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\left(\frac{\chi(p)+1}{p^{s_{1}}}\left(1-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}\right)+\frac{\chi(p)\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2s_{2}}}+\frac{\chi(p)+1}{p^{s_{1}+2s_{2}}}\left(\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{2})}{p^{2}}\right)+\dots\right) $$

In other words, this is the factor that appeared in the case when $F$ is irreducible. Let us repeat the proof for completion.

Note that it suffices to show a uniform lower bound on $L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,1)$ for $p\nmid R$ . Indeed when $p\gg 1$ , there is a uniform lower bound given by the geometric series (as $\varrho_{F}*(n)\leq 4^{\omega(n)}n$ )

$$ (1-p^{-1})^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}\left(1-\frac{4}{p}+\frac{16}{p^{2}}-+\frac{2\cdot(4p-8)}{p^{3}}+\dots\right). $$

In other words, for $p\gg 1$ , the above expression is uniformly bounded below by some constant $c^{\prime}>0$ . With this bound in hand, it suffices to classify when we have that $L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,1)=0$ for some $p\nmid R(-\Delta).$

Since $\varrho_{F}^{*}(n)<n^{2}$ (as to exclude the from the count when $(x,y)\equiv 0\bmod n$ ), we know that

$$ 1-(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}>0. $$

Additionally, we have that for any exponenet $e$ ,

$$ \varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{e})-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{e+1})}{p^{2}}\geq 0, $$

as any element satisfying $p^{e+1}\mid F(x,y)$ must satisfy that $p^{e}\mid F(x,y)$ . Together, these two facts give that $L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,1)>0$ for any prime $p$ such that $\chi(p)=1$ , as the local factor is a sum of $1$ with exclusively nonnegative terms.

If $\chi(p)=-1$ , then the term depending on $s_{1}$ disappears and we see that

$$ L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,1)=\left(1-(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}\right)+(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\left(\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{2})}{p^{4}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{3})}{p^{6}}\right)+\dots $$

Using the grouping indicated above, we again see that this term must be nonnegative. If $L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,1)=0$ , then we must additionally have that

$$ \varrho_{F}^{*}(p)=p^{2}-1,\quad\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{2k})=\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{2k+1})}{p^{2}},\forall k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}. $$

The left (right) equality holds if and only if $p$ divides all values of $F(x,y)$ ( $p^{2k+1}$ divides all values of $F(x,y)$ ). In other words, for some $k\geq 1$ , we have that $p^{2k-1}\mid F(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$ , but there are no solutions to $F(x,y)\equiv 0\bmod p^{2k}$ with $\gcd(x,y,p)=1$ . Since $\chi(p)=-1$ , this tells us that there are no nontrivial solutions to the equation

$$ x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=F(x,y)\bmod p^{2k}, $$

and thus there must be a local obstruction, i.e. $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})=\emptyset.$ ∎

Next, we want to understand when $\bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c})$ can be zero (and when it can be negative).

#### Lemma 12.11.

Let $\mathbf{c}$ be a fixed vector satisfying $\gcd(c_{i},-\Delta)=1$ for each $i=1,\dots,r$ . Then

$$ \bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c}):=\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathbf{c})\geq 0. $$

Additionally, $\bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c})=0$ implies that there exists $\ell\mid-\Delta$ such that $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\mathbf{c}}(\mathbb{Q}_{\ell})=\emptyset.$

#### Proof.

Let us expand out the definition of $\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathbf{c})$ :

$$ \sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(\mathbf{c})=\\
\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}\sum_{p\mid n\implies p\mid\Delta}\frac{\chi_{q_{1}}(p_{q_{2}}(n))\chi_{q_{2}}(p_{q_{1}}(n))\mathbf{1}_{\exists\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=n}}{n^{2}(-\Delta)^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{a}\bmod-\Delta\\
\gcd(a_{i},-\Delta)=1\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1+\chi(a_{i}))\chi_{q_{1}}(a)\varrho_{F}^{*}(n,\mathbf{c}\mathbf{a})\\
=\sum_{p\mid n\implies p\mid-\Delta}\frac{1}{n^{2}(-\Delta)^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{a}\bmod-\Delta\\
\gcd(a_{i},-\Delta)=1\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1+\chi(a_{i}))\varrho_{F}^{*}(n,\mathbf{c}\mathbf{a})\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}\chi_{q_{1}}(p_{q_{2}}(n))\chi_{q_{2}}(p_{q_{1}}(n))\chi_{q_{1}}(a)\mathbf{1}_{\exists\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=n}. $$

Observe that if $n$ satisfies that $p\mid n\implies p\mid-\Delta$ , then we have that

$$ \varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(n)=\chi_{q_{1}}(p_{q_{2}}(n))\chi_{q_{2}}(p_{q_{1}}(n))\mathbf{1}_{\exists\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=n}. $$

In particular, if $p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(u,v)/c_{i})\equiv a_{i}\bmod-\Delta$ and that $p_{-\Delta}(F(u,v))=n$ , then we know that

$$ \varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(F(u,v)/c)=\chi_{q_{1}}(p_{q_{2}}(n))\chi_{q_{2}}(p_{q_{1}}(n))\chi_{q_{1}}(a)(1\star\chi)(F(u,v)/cp_{-\Delta}(F(u,v))). $$

Thus, we can rewrite the above expression as:

$$ \bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c})=\sum_{p\mid n\implies p\mid-\Delta}\frac{1}{n^{2}(-\Delta)^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{a}\bmod-\Delta\\
\gcd(a_{i},-\Delta)=1\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1+\chi(a_{i}))\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}u,v\bmod n(-\Delta)\\
\gcd(u,v,-\Delta)=1\\
p_{-\Delta}(F(u,v))=n\\
p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(u,v)/c_{i})\equiv a_{i}\bmod-\Delta\end{subarray}}\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}\frac{\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(F(u,v)/c)}{(1\star\chi)(F(u,v)/c)}. $$

We recall that

$$ \sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}\varepsilon_{q_{1},q_{2}}(n)=r_{[1]\mathcal{G}}(n)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N(\mathfrak{a})=n\\
[\mathfrak{a}]\in[1]\mathcal{G}\end{subarray}}1\geq 0, $$

where $[1]\mathcal{G}$ denotes that $[\mathfrak{a}]$ sits in the identity coset of $C/\mathcal{G}$ , where $\mathcal{G}$ denotes the genus subgroup. Moreover, $r_{\mathcal{G}}(n)=0$ if $(1\star\chi)(n)=0$ , so the above expression is well-defined and non-negative. This completes the proof that $\bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c})\geq 0.$

Let us determine when $\bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c})$ is zero. We inspect (12.7) further:

$$ \bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c})=\sum_{p\mid n\implies p\mid-\Delta}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{\exists\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=n}}{n^{2}(-\Delta)^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{a}\bmod-\Delta\\
\gcd(a_{i},-\Delta)=1\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1+\chi(a_{i}))\\
\times\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}u,v\bmod n(-\Delta)\\
\gcd(u,v,-\Delta)=1\\
p_{-\Delta}(F(u,v))=n\\
p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(u,v)/c_{i})\equiv a_{i}\bmod-\Delta\end{subarray}}\delta_{F(u,v)/c}\mathbf{1}_{\exists\mathfrak{a}\in[1]\mathcal{G},N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)/c}, $$

where $\delta_{F(u,v)/c}>0$ is some positive constant. We immediately see that for $\bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c})=0$ , a few events could occur:

- (1) When $n$ satisfies that $p\mid n\implies p\mid-\Delta$ and that $\exists\mathfrak{a},N(\mathfrak{a})=n$ , for all $\mathbf{a}$ such that $\varrho_{F}^{*}(n,\mathbf{c}\mathbf{a})\neq 0$ , there exists some $i$ such that $\chi(a_{i})=-1$ .

- (2) When $n$ satisfies that $p\mid n\implies p\mid-\Delta$ and that $\exists\mathfrak{a},N(\mathfrak{a})=n$ , for all $\mathbf{a}\bmod\Delta$ satisfying that $\chi(a_{i})=1$ for all $i$ , for all $(u,v)\bmod n(-\Delta)$ such that $\gcd(u,v,-\Delta)=1$ , $p_{-\Delta}(F(u,v))=n$ and $p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(u,v)/c_{i})\equiv a_{i}\bmod-\Delta$ , there does not exist an ideal $\mathfrak{a}\in[1]\mathcal{G}$ satisfying that $N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)/c.$ As $[1]\mathcal{G}$ is the set of quadratic form with discriminant $-\Delta$ that are locally equivalent to $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}$ , this implies that

$$ X_{u,v,c}:=\{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=F(u,v)/c\} $$

has no solution over $\mathbb{Q}$ , and since this is a quadratic form, this implies that $X_{u,v,c}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})=\emptyset.$

Let us compare these events to the condition laid out in Lemma 12.8; in particular, we want to show that both events (1) and (2) above lead to the conclusion that there does not exist a solution to

$$ x_{i}^{2}+\Delta y_{i}^{2}=c_{i}F_{i}(u,v),\forall i=1,\dots,r, $$

over $\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}$ with $\gcd(u,v,\ell)=1$ for some $\ell\mid-\Delta$ .

We prove the contrapositive. Assume that there exists a solution $((x_{i},y_{i})_{i=1}^{r},u,v)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}$ with $\gcd(u,v,\ell)=1$ for each $\ell\mid-\Delta$ . Let $\ell^{e_{i}}\|F_{i}(u,v)$ for each $i=1,\dots,r$ and set

$$ n=\prod_{\ell\mid-\Delta}\ell^{e_{i}}. $$

Then there is a solution to

$$ x_{i}^{2}+\Delta y_{i}^{2}=c_{i}F_{i}(u,v)\bmod n(-\Delta),\forall i=1,\dots,r, $$

satisfying that $\gcd(u,v,-\Delta)=1$ and $p_{-\Delta}(F(u,v))=n$ . This implies a solution to

$$ x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=cF(u,v)\bmod n(-\Delta) $$

with $\gcd(u,v,-\Delta)=1$ . Consequently, since the only possible local obstructions to $X_{u,v,c}$ lie at the primes dividing $-\Delta$ , we know that there exists an ideal $\mathfrak{a}\in[1]\mathcal{G}$ satisfying $N(\mathfrak{a})=F(u,v)/c$ , and hence an ideal $\mathfrak{a}^{\prime}\mid\mathfrak{a}$ satisfying $N(\mathfrak{a})=n$ . Set $a_{i}=p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(u,v)/c_{i})\bmod-\Delta$ . If we can show that $\chi(a_{i})=1$ for each $i$ , then we know that events (1) and (2) both cannot occur.

Since we know that there exists $(x_{i},y_{i})\bmod n(-\Delta)$ such that

$$ x_{i}^{2}+\Delta y_{i}^{2}=c_{i}F_{i}(u,v)\bmod n(-\Delta), $$

we must have that for each $i=1,\dots,r$ , $\chi(p_{\neg-\Delta}(c_{i}F_{i}(u,v)))=1$ . Since $\gcd(c_{i},-\Delta)=1$ , we therefore have that

$$ \chi(p_{\neg-\Delta}(c_{i}F_{i}(u,v)))=\chi(p_{\neg-\Delta}(F_{i}(u,v)/c_{i}))=\chi(a_{i})=1. $$

Thus, $\chi(a_{i})=1$ for each $i$ and events (1) and (2) cannot occur. Consequently, we know that $\bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c})=0$ implies that there is a local obstruction at some prime $\ell\mid-\Delta$ .

∎

Having completed the above lemmas, we return to (12.6); recall that we are tasked with determining when the following expression is zero:

$$ \left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c_{ij}\mid\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})\\
p\mid c\implies\chi(p)=-1\\
\mu^{2}(\mathbf{c})=1\end{subarray}}\frac{\bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c})}{c^{2}}\cdot\prod_{p\mid c}L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,\mathbf{c}_{p})\right)\times\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c_{ij}^{\prime}\mid\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})\\
p\mid c^{\prime}\implies\chi(p)=1\end{subarray}}\frac{\mu(\mathbf{c}^{\prime})}{c^{\prime 2}}\prod_{p\mid c^{\prime}}L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,\mathbf{c}_{p})\right). $$

We split this into two lemmas.

#### Lemma 12.13.

If the following expression is nonzero

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c_{ij}^{\prime}\mid\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})\\
p\mid c^{\prime}\implies\chi(p)=1\end{subarray}}\frac{\mu(\mathbf{c}^{\prime})}{c^{\prime 2}}\prod_{p\mid c^{\prime}}L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,\mathbf{c}_{p}). $$

#### Lemma 12.14.

If the following expression is zero

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c_{ij}\mid\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})\\
p\mid c\implies\chi(p)=-1\\
\mu^{2}(\mathbf{c})=1\end{subarray}}\frac{\bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c})}{c^{2}}\cdot\prod_{p\mid c}L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,\mathbf{c}_{p}), $$

then for all $\mathbf{c}$ counted above, $Y_{\Delta,f_{1},\dots,f_{r},\mathbf{c}}^{*}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})=\emptyset;$ in other words, there is a local obstruction.

With these two lemmas in hand, in addition to Lemma 12.6, Lemma 12.10 and Theorem 12.2, this completes the proof of the statement of Theorem 1.3. In other words, this guarantees that if $c_{\Delta,f}=0$ then there is a local or Brauer-Manin obstruction to rational points on $X_{\Delta,f}$ .

#### Proof of Lemma 12.13.

Let $p\mid R$ be a prime satisfying that $\chi(p)=1$ . Fix for now a vector $\mathbf{c}$ in our summation. Assume that $\mathbf{c}_{p}=(p^{e_{i}})_{i=1}^{r}$ . Then we can expand out the local $L$ -function factor (here, we recall that $\mathbf{k}$ is a vector of length $r$ where exactly one entry is given by $p$ and all other entries are $1$ and we have a choice of decomposing $k$ such that $k_{i}\mid F_{i}(x,y)$ ; so, without loss of generality we choose that entry to be the first):

$$ L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,\mathbf{c}_{p})=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{2}{p^{n}}\left(\sum_{i_{j}\geq e_{j}}\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{i_{1}},\dots,p^{i_{r}}))}{p^{2(i_{1}+\dots+i_{r})}}-\sum_{i_{j}\geq e_{j}}\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{i_{1}+1},\dots,p^{i_{r}}))}{p^{2(i_{1}+\dots+i_{r}+1)}}\right)\\
=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{2}{p^{n}}\cdot\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i_{j}\geq e_{j}\\
j\geq 2\end{subarray}}\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{e_{1}},p^{i_{2}},\dots,p^{i_{r}}))}{p^{2(e_{1}+i_{2}+\dots+i_{r})}}. $$

Thus, we can write our summand as:

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c_{ij}\mid\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})\\
p\mid c\implies\chi(p)=1\end{subarray}}\frac{\mu(\mathbf{c})}{c^{2}}\prod_{p\mid c}L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,\mathbf{c}_{p})\\
=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\mid R\\
\chi(p)=1\end{subarray}}\frac{2}{(1-p^{-1})(1-p^{-2})}\times\sum_{e_{j}\leq\max_{i\neq j}\mathbf{1}_{p\mid\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})}}\prod_{j=1}^{r}\frac{(-1)^{e_{j}}}{p^{2e_{j}}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}f_{j}\geq e_{j}\\
j\geq 2\end{subarray}}\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{e_{1}},p^{f_{2}},\dots,p^{f_{r}}))}{p^{2(e_{1}+f_{2}+\dots+f_{r})}}. $$

Let $\mathcal{I}_{p}$ denote the indices $j$ for which $p\nmid\prod_{i\neq j}\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})$ . Then by inclusion-exclusion, the sum above collapses to:

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\in\mathcal{I}_{p}\setminus\{1\}\\
f_{j}\geq 0\end{subarray}}\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((1,\dots,p^{f_{r}})}{p^{2(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{p}}f_{j})}}-\mathbf{1}_{1\not\in\mathcal{I}_{p}}\cdot\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\in\mathcal{I}_{p}\setminus\{1\}\\
f_{j}\geq 0\end{subarray}}\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p,\dots,p^{f_{r}}))}{p^{2(1+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{p}}f_{j})}}. $$

Now if $1\in\mathcal{I}_{p}$ , then it is clear that this factor is strictly positive, as the summands are nonnegative and $\varrho_{F}^{*}((1,1,\dots,1))=1$ . So, it remains to check when $1\not\in\mathcal{I}_{p}$ . Then we note that for any fixed set of $f_{j}$ , we have that definitionally,

$$ \frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((1,\dots,p^{f_{r}}))}{p^{2(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{j}}f_{j})}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p,\dots,p^{f_{r}}))}{p^{2(1+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{p}}f_{j})}}\geq 0. $$

Thus, the summands are all nonnegative. Further, the summands are strictly positive unless $p\mid F_{1}$ . In this case, for each $j>1$ we must have that $p\mid\textrm{Res}(F_{1},F_{j})\mid\prod_{i\neq j}\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})$ ; we also that that $p\mid\prod_{i\neq 1}\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{1})$ as well. Hence $\mathcal{I}_{p}=\emptyset$ . So, the above expression becomes:

$$ \varrho_{F}^{*}((1,\dots,1))-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p,1,\dots,1))}{p^{2}}=1-\frac{p^{2}-1}{p^{2}}>0, $$

which is strictly positive. Here, we have used that if $p\mid F_{1}$ , then $\varrho_{F}^{*}((p,1,\dots,1))=p^{2}-1$ , since we require $\gcd(u,v,p)=1$ in the count. ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 12.14.

First, let us fix a vector $\mathbf{c}$ and a prime $p\mid c$ such that $\chi(p)=-1$ . Let us notate that $\mathbf{c}_{p}=(p^{e_{i}})_{i=1}^{r}$ . We consider the local factor:

$$ L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,\mathbf{c}_{p})=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\sum_{i_{j}\geq 0}\frac{\chi(p)^{i_{1}+\dots+i_{r}}\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{i_{1}+e_{1}},\dots,p^{i_{r}+e_{r}}))}{p^{2(i_{1}+\dots+i_{r})}}. $$

We now claim that if $\mathbf{c}$ satisfies that $\mu^{2}(\mathbf{c})=1$ and if $p\mid c$ then $\chi(p)=-1$ , then the following expression is nonnegative:

$$ c^{-2}\prod_{p\mid c}L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,\mathbf{c}_{p})=\prod_{p\mid c}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\left(\sum_{i_{j}\geq 0}\frac{(-1)^{(i_{1}+\dots+i_{r})}\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{i_{1}+e_{1}},\dots,p^{i_{r}+e_{r}}))}{p^{2(i_{1}+\dots+i_{r}+e_{1}+\dots+e_{r})}}\right). $$

We note that we can write this sum as

$$ \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{e_{1}+2i},p^{e_{2}},\dots,p^{e_{r}}))}{p^{2(e_{1}+2i+\dots+e_{r})}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{e_{1}+2i+1},p^{e_{2}},\dots,p^{e_{r}}))}{p^{2(e_{1}+2i+1+\dots+e_{r})}}\right)\\
-\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{e_{1}+2i},p^{e_{2}+1},\dots,p^{e_{r}}))}{p^{2(e_{1}+2i+e_{2}+1+\dots+e_{r})}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{e_{1}+2i+1},p^{e_{2}+1},\dots,p^{e_{r}}))}{p^{2(e_{1}+2i+1+e_{2}+1+\dots+e_{r})}}\right)\\
+\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{e_{1}+2i},p^{e_{2}+2},\dots,p^{e_{r}}))}{p^{2(e_{1}+2i+e_{2}+2+\dots+e_{r})}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{e_{1}+2i+1},p^{e_{2}+2},\dots,p^{e_{r}}))}{p^{2(e_{1}+2i+1+e_{2}+2+\dots+e_{r})}}\right)-\ldots $$

We now make a few observations: (1) Each of these summands is nonnegative; in particular

$$ \frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{i_{1}},p^{i_{2}},\dots,p^{i_{r}}))}{p^{2(i_{1}+\dots+i_{r})}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{i_{1}+1},p^{i_{2}},\dots,p^{i_{r}}))}{p^{2(i_{1}+1+\dots+i_{r})}}\geq 0. $$

This relation comes from the definition of $\varrho_{F}^{*}$ , for if $p^{i_{1}+1}\mid F_{1}$ then $p^{i_{1}}\mid F_{1}$ . (2) We also have the relation that for any tuple $(i_{1},\dots,i_{r})$ , the following inequality holds:

$$ \frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{i_{1}},p^{i_{2}},\dots,p^{i_{r}}))}{p^{2(i_{1}+\dots+i_{r})}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{i_{1}+1},p^{i_{2}},\dots,p^{i_{r}}))}{p^{2(i_{1}+1+\dots+i_{r})}}\\
\geq\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{i_{1}},p^{i_{2}+1},\dots,p^{i_{r}}))}{p^{2(i_{1}+i_{2}+1+\dots+i_{r})}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{i_{1}+1},p^{i_{2}+1},\dots,p^{i_{r}}))}{p^{2(i_{1}+1+i_{2}+1+\dots+i_{r})}}. $$

This relation comes from the fact that one of the conditions counted in $\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{i_{1}},\dots,p^{i_{r}}))$ is that $p^{i_{j}}\mid F_{j}(u,v)$ , which is an independent condition for each $j$ . Finally we make the observation that (1) and (2) hold irregardless of which indices we choose to compare (in other words, it did not need to be the first and second tuple).

Together, this gives us that

$$ \sum_{i_{j}\geq 0}\frac{(-1)^{(i_{1}+\dots+i_{r})}\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{i_{1}+e_{1}},\dots,p^{i_{r}+e_{r}}))}{p^{2(i_{1}+\dots+i_{r}+e_{1}+\dots+e_{r})}}\geq 0 $$

and hence the claim is shown.

Returning to our original expression:

$$ \textrm{NS}:=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c_{ij}\mid\textrm{Res}(F_{i},F_{j})\\
p\mid c\implies\chi(p)=-1\\
\mu^{2}(\mathbf{c})=1\end{subarray}}\frac{\bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c})}{c^{2}}\cdot\prod_{p\mid c}L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,\mathbf{c}_{p}), $$

we can see that for NS to be zero, we must have that for every $\mathbf{c}$ vector counted, either $\bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c})=0$ or that

$$ c^{-2}\prod_{p\mid c}L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,\mathbf{c}_{p})=0. $$

In Lemma 12.11, we saw that if $\bigtriangledown(\mathbf{c})=0$ , then there exists some $\ell\mid-\Delta$ such that there is a local obstruction, i.e. $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},\dots,f_{r},\mathbf{c}}(\mathbb{Q}_{\ell})=\emptyset.$ So, to conclude this lemma, we need to show that if the product of local factors is zero, then for some $p\mid c$ we have that $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},\dots,f_{r},\mathbf{c}}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})=\emptyset$ .

Let $p\mid c$ and $\chi(p)=-1$ . It suffices to show that if $L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,\mathbf{c}_{p})=0$ then $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},\dots,f_{r},\mathbf{c}}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})=\emptyset$ . If $\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{e_{1}},\dots,p^{e_{r}}))=0$ , then clearly $L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,\mathbf{c}_{p})=0$ . Since $\mu^{2}(\mathbf{c})=1$ , we know that $e_{j}\in\{0,1\}$ for each $j\in\{1,\dots,r\}$ , and that $e_{j}=1$ for some index $j$ (as $p\mid c$ ), so by Lemma 12.8 would imply that $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},\dots,f_{r},\mathbf{c}_{p}}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})=\emptyset.$

So from now on assume that $\varrho_{F}^{*}((p^{e_{1}},\dots,p^{e_{r}}))>0$ and that $L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,\mathbf{c}_{p})=0$ . We note that in both observations (1) and (2) above, equality holds if and only if $p^{i_{1}+1}\mid F_{1}$ in the first case and $p^{i_{2}+1}\mid F_{2}$ in the second, or if all terms in the expressions are zero. Hence, if $L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,\mathbf{c}_{p})=0$ , then for some $j\in\{1,\dots,r\}$ and for some $i\geq 0$ we have that $p^{e_{j}+2i+1}\mid F_{j}$ and that there are no $(u,v)\bmod p^{e_{j}+2i+2}$ such that $\gcd(u,v,p)=1$ and $F_{j}(u,v)\equiv 0\bmod p^{e_{j}+2i+2}$ . Consider then the equation:

$$ x_{j}^{2}+\Delta y_{j}^{2}=c_{j}F_{j}(u,v), $$

over $\mathbb{Q}_{p}$ . We can see that this implies that $v_{p}(c_{j}F_{j}(u,v))=p^{2e_{j}+2i+1}$ for all $(u,v)\in\mathbb{Q}_{p}$ , which by the argument of Lemma 12.8, gives us again that $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},\dots,f_{r},\mathbf{c}}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})=\emptyset.$

∎

Thus, if $c_{\Delta,f}=0$ then for all of the $\mathbf{c}$ above from Lemma 12.6, $Y^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\mathbf{c}}(\mathbb{Q}_{\ell})=\emptyset$ for some place $\ell$ . This completes the proof of Proposition 12.5, and thus Theorem 1.3. ∎

## Appendix A A special case of the leading constant

Assume that $\Delta>0$ is an odd prime. Further, let us assume that $f(x)$ is an irreducible quartic that remains irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta}).$ Our goal for this appendix to relate the leading constant to Peyre’s constant in this particular case. For $\Delta=1$ , this was previously completed in [25]. We would like to remind the reader at this point of our abusive notation: since $\Delta>0$ , we use $-\Delta$ to denote the modulus of $\chi_{-\Delta}$ , which is truly of size $4\Delta$ .

In this case, we have the following expression for our leading constant:

$$ c_{\Delta,f}=\frac{2|\mathcal{U}|}{|\mathcal{C}|}\left(\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(1)\right)\prod_{p\nmid-\Delta}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)\cdot\textrm{Res}_{s_{1}=1}\xi(s_{1},1;F,\chi,1), $$

where $\xi(s_{1},1;F,\chi,1)$ was defined in 11.9 as:

$$ \xi(s_{1},1;F,\chi,1)=\sum_{\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1}\frac{1}{N(\mathfrak{t})^{s_{1}}}\sum_{\mathfrak{k}\mid\mathfrak{t}}\frac{\mu(\mathfrak{k})}{N(\mathfrak{k})^{2}}\sum_{d}\frac{\chi(d)\varrho_{F}^{*}(kd)}{d^{2}}\prod_{p\mid kd}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}. $$

Before manipulating the intimidating expression above, let us first recall the definition of Peyre’s constant in this case. Peyre’s prediction for the leading constant in Manin’s conjecture in this case is given by $\omega_{\infty}\prod_{p<\infty}w_{p}$ , where $\omega_{p}$ and $\omega_{\infty}$ are the Hardy-Littlewood densities. At the real place, one can show that the archimedean denisty $\omega_{\infty}$ is equivalent to the following limit:

$$ \omega_{\infty}=\lim_{\delta\rightarrow 0}\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\frac{\text{vol}\{|x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}-t^{2}F(u,v)|<\epsilon/2:|tu^{2}|,|tv^{2}|\leq 1,\delta^{-1}<|t|\leq 1,x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}\leq\nu_{\Delta,f}^{2}\}}{\epsilon\log(1/\delta)} $$

It is also possible to express $\omega_{\infty}$ in terms of a singular integral; the expression above will have a clean and simple evaluation in terms of $\Delta$ and $f(z)$ later on. The $p$ -adic densities $\omega_{p}$ are defined as follows:

$$ \omega_{p}=\lim_{v\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{p^{4v}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v,x,y,t)\in(\mathbb{Z}/p^{v}\mathbb{Z})^{5}\\
u^{2}+\Delta v^{2}=t^{2}F(x,y)\bmod p^{v}\\
p\nmid(x,y)\\
p\nmid(u,v,t)\end{subarray}}1. $$

The goal of this section is to prove the following proposition.

#### Proposition A.1.

Let $\Delta>0$ be an odd prime and let $f(z)$ be an irreducible quartic that remains irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ . Then,

$$ c_{\Delta,f}=\frac{1}{4}\omega_{\infty}\prod_{p<\infty}\omega_{p}. $$

#### Remark A.2.

We point out that our original expression in (1.1) is that

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},B):=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\#\Big\{((x,y),(u,v),t)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{+}:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)\\
\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1,\max(|tu^{2}|,|tv^{2}|,\|x\pm y\sqrt{-\Delta}\|)\leq\nu_{\Delta,f}B\Big\}. $$

So, this factor of $1/4$ is expected since we do not restrict $t$ to be nonnegative when we compute the archimedean density.

We start the proof by first analyzing the Dirichlet series $\xi(s_{1},1;F,\chi,1)$ further. It will turn out that this Dirichlet series contains the local densities for all primes not dividing $-\Delta$ (i.e. $p\neq\Delta,2$ ); additionally, we see $L(1,\chi)$ appear as part of the expression.

#### Lemma A.3.

Let $\Delta>0$ be an odd prime and let $f(z)$ be an irreducible quartic that remains irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ . Then,

$$ \textrm{Res}_{s_{1}=1}\xi(s_{1},1;F,\chi,1)=L(1,\chi)\prod_{p\mid-\Delta}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)\prod_{p\nmid-\Delta}\omega_{p}\cdot\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}. $$

#### Proof.

Let us first define the following Dirichlet series for $\Re(s)>1$ :

$$ L_{\not\square,K}(s)=\sum_{\gcd(\mathfrak{t},\overline{\mathfrak{t}})=1}N(\mathfrak{t})^{-s}=\prod_{p}\left(1+(\chi(p)+1)(p^{-s}+p^{-2s}+\ldots)\right). $$

This series will have a simple pole at $s=1$ ; this can be seen by nice relation:

$$ L_{\not\square,K}(s)=\zeta_{K}(s)\zeta(2s)^{-1}. $$

Let us compute the residue of $L_{\not\square,K}(s)$ at $s=1$ :

$$ \displaystyle\textrm{Res}_{s=1}L_{\not\square,K}(s) \displaystyle=\lim_{s\rightarrow 1^{+}}\zeta(s)^{-1}L_{\not\square,K}(s) \displaystyle=\lim_{s\rightarrow 1^{+}}\prod_{p\mid-\Delta}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{s}}\right)\prod_{p\nmid-\Delta}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{s}}\right)\left(1+\frac{\chi(p)+1}{p^{s}(1-p^{-s})}\right) \displaystyle=\prod_{p\mid-\Delta}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)\lim_{s\rightarrow 1^{+}}\prod_{p\nmid-\Delta}\left(1+\frac{\chi(p)}{p^{s}}\right) \displaystyle=\prod_{p\mid-\Delta}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)\prod_{p\nmid-\Delta}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)L(1,\chi). $$

Now, we return to our original Dirichlet series $\xi(s_{1},1;F,\chi,1)$ , which also has a simple pole at $s=1$ . We can see that

$$ \displaystyle\textrm{Res}_{s=1}\xi(s,1;F,\chi,1) \displaystyle=\textrm{Res}_{s=1}L_{\not\square,K}(s)\cdot\lim_{s\rightarrow 1^{+}}L_{\not\square,K}(s)^{-1}\xi(s,1;F,\chi,1) \displaystyle=\textrm{Res}_{s=1}L_{\not\square,K}(s)\cdot\prod_{p\nmid-\Delta}\left(1+\frac{\chi(p)+1}{p-1}\right)^{-1}L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,1), $$

where $L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,1)$ are the local factors given by:

$$ L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,1)=1+\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{\chi(p)\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}+\frac{\chi(p)^{2}\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{2})}{p^{4}}+\dots\right)\\
+\frac{\chi(p)+1}{p}\left(1+\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{\chi(p)\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}+\frac{\chi(p)^{2}\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{2})}{p^{4}}+\dots-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}-\frac{\chi(p)\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{2})}{p^{4}}-\dots\right)\right)\\
+\frac{\chi(p)+1}{p^{2}}\left(1+\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{\chi(p)\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}+\frac{\chi(p)^{2}\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{2})}{p^{4}}+\dots-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}-\frac{\chi(p)\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{2})}{p^{4}}-\dots\right)\right)+\dots{} $$

For simplicity, let us define:

$$ \ell_{p}:=\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{\chi(p)\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}+\frac{\chi(p)^{2}\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{2})}{p^{4}}+\dots\right). $$

Then we can write these local factors as:

$$ \displaystyle L_{p}(1,1;F,\chi,1) \displaystyle=1+\ell_{p}+\frac{\chi(p)+1}{p}\left(1+\ell_{p}-\chi(p)\ell_{p}\right)+\frac{\chi(p)+1}{p^{2}}\left(1+\ell_{p}-\chi(p)\ell_{p}\right)+\dots \displaystyle=1+\ell_{p}+\frac{(\chi(p)+1)(1+(1-\chi(p))\ell_{p})}{p-1} \displaystyle=\begin{cases}1+\ell_{p},&\chi(p)=-1,\\
1+\ell_{p}+\frac{\chi(p)+1}{p-1},&\chi(p)=1.\end{cases} $$

Thus, we can evaluate further our residue as:

$$ \textrm{Res}_{s=1}L_{\not\square,K}(s)\cdot\prod_{\chi(p)=-1}(1+\ell_{p})\prod_{\chi(p)=-1}\left(1+\ell_{p}\cdot\left(1+\frac{\chi(p)+1}{p-1}\right)^{-1}\right). $$

It now behooves us to split into the cases when $\chi(p)=1$ and $\chi(p)=-1$ .

We start with the simpler case: fix a prime $p$ such that $\chi(p)=-1.$ Then our local factor is given by

$$ 1+\ell_{p}=\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}+\frac{\chi(p)\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}+\frac{\chi(p)^{2}\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{2})}{p^{4}}+\dots\right). $$

On the other hand, we have that

$$ \omega_{p}=\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)\lim_{v\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{p^{3v}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=F(u,v)\\
p\nmid(u,v)\end{subarray}}1. $$

We split our sum by the value $\gamma$ such that $v_{p}(F(u,v))=\gamma$ , i.e. we count

$$ \lim_{v\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{p^{3v}}\sum_{\gamma=0}^{v}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=F(u,v)\\
p\nmid(u,v)\\
p^{\gamma}\|F(u,v)\end{subarray}}1=\sum_{\gamma=0}^{\infty}\frac{\#\{(x,y,u,v)\bmod p^{\gamma+1}:p\nmid(u,v),p^{\gamma}\|F(u,v),x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=F(u,v)\}}{p^{3(\gamma+1)}}. $$

Since $\chi(p)=-1$ , we note that if $\gamma$ is odd, then this count is zero, i.e. there will be no solutions to $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=F(u,v)$ for $p^{\gamma}\|F(u,v)$ . So, it suffices to consider $\gamma$ even. Let $\gamma>0$ . In that case, we see that:

$$ \#\{(x,y,u,v)\bmod p^{\gamma+1}:p\nmid(u,v),p^{\gamma}\|F(u,v),x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=F(u,v)\}\\
=\sum_{\gcd(a,p)=1}\#\{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}\equiv p^{\gamma}a\bmod p^{\gamma+1}\}\cdot\#\{u,v:p\nmid(u,v),F(u,v)\equiv p^{\gamma}a\bmod p^{\gamma+1}\}\\
=(p+1)\left(p^{\gamma/2}\right)^{2}\cdot\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}u,v\bmod p^{\gamma+1}\\
p\nmid(u,v)\\
p^{\gamma}\mid F(u,v)\end{subarray}}1-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}u,v\bmod p^{\gamma+1}\\
p\nmid(u,v)\\
p^{\gamma+1}\mid F(u,v)\end{subarray}}1\right)=(p+1)p^{\gamma}\left(p^{2}\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma})-\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma+1})\right). $$

Here we have used that there will always be $(p+1)$ solutions to $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}\equiv a\bmod p$ for $\gcd(a,p)=1$ . Note that if $\gamma=0$ , then we have similarly that

$$ \#\{(x,y,u,v)\bmod p:p\nmid(u,v),p^{\gamma}\|F(u,v),x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=F(u,v)\}=(p+1)(p^{2}-1-\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)). $$

Plugging the above expression in, we have that

$$ \lim_{v\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{p^{3v}}\sum_{\gamma=0}^{v}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=F(u,v)\\
p\nmid(u,v)\\
p^{\gamma}\|F(u,v)\end{subarray}}1=\frac{p+1}{p}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}+\sum_{\gamma=1}^{\infty}\cdot\left(\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma})}{p^{2\gamma}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma+1})}{p^{2(\gamma+1)}}\right)\right). $$

Thus, we can express the local density as:

$$ \omega_{p}=\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}+\frac{\chi(p)\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}+\frac{\chi(p)^{2}\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{2})}{p^{4}}+\dots\right). $$

(Recall that $\chi(p)=-1$ ). Hence, we have that

$$ 1+\ell_{p}=\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-2}\omega_{p}. $$

Let us now fix a prime $p$ such that $\chi(p)=1$ and inspect the local density further.

$$ \omega_{p}=\lim_{v\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{p^{4v}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v,x,y,t)\bmod p^{v}\\
x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)\\
p\nmid(u,v)\\
p\nmid(x,y,t)\end{subarray}}1. $$

We split up our sum by the values of $v_{p}(t)$ and $v_{p}(F(u,v))$ .

$$ \omega_{p}=\lim_{v\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{\gamma_{1}=0}^{v}\sum_{\gamma_{2}=0}^{v}\frac{\#\{(u,v,x,y,t)\bmod p^{v}:\begin{array}[]{c}x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v),p\nmid(u,v),p\nmid(x,y,t)\\
p^{\gamma_{1}}\|t,p^{\gamma_{2}}\|F(u,v)\end{array}\}}{p^{4v}}. $$

If $2\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}<v$ and $\gamma_{1}>0$ , then this count becomes:

$$ \sum_{\gcd(a,p)=1}\#\{(x,y):x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=p^{2\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}}a\bmod p^{v},\gcd(x,y,p)=1\}\\
\times\#\{(u,v,t):t^{2}F(u,v)\equiv p^{2\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}}a\bmod p^{v},p^{\gamma_{1}}\|t,p^{\gamma_{2}}\|F(u,v),\gcd(u,v,p)=1\}. $$

For any value of $a$ coprime to $p$ , we have that

$$ \#\{(x,y)\bmod p^{k+1}:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=p^{k}a\bmod p^{k+1},\gcd(x,y,p)=1\}=\begin{cases}p-1,&k=0,\\
2(p-1)p^{k},&k\geq 1.\end{cases}. $$

Notably, this expression is independent of $a$ . Thus, we have that since $\gamma_{1}>0$ ,

$$ 2(p-1)p^{v-1}\cdot\#\{(u,v,t)\bmod p^{v}:p^{\gamma_{1}}\|t,p^{\gamma_{2}}\|F(u,v),\gcd(u,v,p)=1\}\\
=2(p-1)p^{v-1}\cdot(p-1)p^{v-\gamma_{1}-1}\cdot\left(p^{2(v-\gamma_{2})}\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma_{2}})-p^{2(v-\gamma_{2}-1)}\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma_{2}+1})\right). $$

On the other hand, if $2\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}\geq v$ and $\gamma_{1}>0$ , then our count becomes

$$ \#\{(x,y)\bmod p^{v}:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}\equiv 0\bmod p^{v},\gcd(x,y,p)=1\}\\
\times\#\{(u,v,t)\bmod p^{v}:p^{\gamma_{1}}\|t,p^{\gamma_{2}}\|F(u,v),\gcd(u,v,p)=1\}. $$

Now, we count for $v>0$ :

$$ \#\{(x,y)\bmod p^{v}:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}\equiv 0\bmod p^{v},\gcd(x,y,p)=1\}=2(p-1)p^{v-1}. $$

So, we get that for $\gamma_{1}>0$ and $2\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}\geq v$ , the expression:

$$ 2(p-1)p^{v-1}\cdot(p-1)p^{v-\gamma_{1}-1}\cdot\left(p^{2(v-\gamma_{2})}\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma_{2}})-p^{2(v-\gamma_{2}-1)}\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma_{2}+1})\right). $$

Finally, if $\gamma_{1}=0$ , we evaluate that the count is equal to

$$ \begin{cases}(p-1)^{2}(p^{2}-1-\varrho_{F}^{*}(p))p^{4(v-1)},&\gamma_{2}=0,\\
(\gamma_{2}+1)(p-1)^{2}p^{2(v-1)}(p^{2(v-\gamma_{2}})\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma_{2}})-p^{2(v-\gamma_{2}-1)}\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma_{2}+1})),&\gamma_{2}>0.\end{cases} $$

Thus, we can now evaluate $\omega_{p}$ :

$$ \omega_{p}=\lim_{v\rightarrow\infty}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}\right)+\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{2}\sum_{\gamma_{2}=1}^{v-1}(\gamma_{2}+1)\left(\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma_{2}})}{p^{2\gamma_{2}}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma_{2}+1})}{p^{2(\gamma_{2}+1)}}\right)\\
+2\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{2}\sum_{\gamma_{1}=1}^{v/2}\frac{1}{p^{\gamma_{1}}}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}\right)+2\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}2\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}<v\\
\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}>0\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{p^{\gamma_{1}}}\left(\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma_{2}})}{p^{2\gamma_{2}}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma_{2}+1})}{p^{2(\gamma_{2}+1)}}\right)\\
+2\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{2}\sum_{\gamma_{1}\geq v/2}\frac{1}{p^{\gamma_{1}}}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}\right)+2\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}2\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}\geq v\\
\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}>0\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{p^{\gamma_{1}}}\left(\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma_{2}})}{p^{2\gamma_{2}}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma_{2}+1})}{p^{2(\gamma_{2}+1)}}\right). $$

Taking the limit as $v\rightarrow\infty,$ we get:

$$ \omega_{p}=\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}\right)+\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}+\sum_{\gamma_{2}=1}^{\infty}\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma_{2}})}{p^{2\gamma_{2}}}\right)\\
+\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{2}\cdot\frac{2}{p-1}\cdot\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}-\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}\right)+\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)\cdot\frac{2}{p-1}\cdot\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p)}{p^{2}}\\
=\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{2}\left(1+\frac{2}{p-1}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)+\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{2}\sum_{\gamma_{2}=1}^{\infty}\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma_{2}})}{p^{2\gamma_{2}}}. $$

It is time to return to the expression that we get for our local factor at $p$ when $\chi(p)=1$ ; that is

$$ 1+\ell_{p}\cdot\left(1+\frac{2}{p-1}\right)^{-1}. $$

Plugging in our definition of $\ell_{p}$ when $\chi(p)=1$ , we have:

$$ \left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}+\left(1+\frac{2}{p-1}\right)^{-1}\sum_{\gamma=1}^{\infty}\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma})}{p^{2\gamma}}\right)\\
=\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}\left(1+\frac{2}{p-1}\right)^{-1}\left(\left(1+\frac{2}{p-1}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)+\sum_{\gamma=1}^{\infty}\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(p^{\gamma})}{p^{2\gamma}}\right). $$

Thus, we have that

$$ 1+\ell_{p}\cdot\left(1+\frac{2}{p-1}\right)^{-1}=\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}\left(1+\frac{2}{p-1}\right)^{-1}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{-2}\omega_{p}. $$

Collecting our terms together ((A.3) and (A.4)), we achieve that

$$ \textrm{Res}_{s=1}\xi(s_{1},1;F,\chi,1)\\
=\textrm{Res}_{s=1}L_{\not\square,K}(s)\cdot\prod_{p\nmid-\Delta}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}\omega_{p}\cdot\prod_{\chi(p)=-1}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}\prod_{\chi(p)=1}\left(1+\frac{2}{p-1}\right)^{-1}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-2}. $$

Noting that this expression for $\chi(p)=1$ is equivalent to $(1-p^{-2})^{-1}$ , and plugging in the values of the residue at $s=1$ of $L_{\not\square,K}(s)$ , we get:

$$ \textrm{Res}_{s=1}\xi(s_{1},1;F,\chi,1)=\prod_{p\mid-\Delta}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)\prod_{p\nmid-\Delta}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)^{-1}L(1,\chi)\prod_{p\nmid-\Delta}\omega_{p}. $$

This completes the proof of the lemma.

∎

With Lemma A.3 in hand, we see that

$$ c_{\Delta,f}=\frac{2|\mathcal{U}|}{|\mathcal{C}|}L(1,\chi)\left(\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(1)\right)\prod_{p\mid-\Delta}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)\prod_{p\nmid-\Delta}\omega_{p}. $$

By Dirichlet’s class number formula, we know that since $\Delta>0$ ,

$$ L(1,\chi)=\frac{2\pi|\mathcal{C}|}{|\mathcal{U}|\sqrt{\Delta}}. $$

So, this leaves us with the following expression for $c_{\Delta,f}$ :

$$ c_{\Delta,f}=\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{\Delta}}\prod_{p\nmid-\Delta}\omega_{p}\times\left(\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=-\Delta}^{\prime}\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(1)\right)\prod_{p\mid-\Delta}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right). $$

It is now time to approach those primes dividing $-\Delta$ (i.e. $4\Delta$ ). Recall that we chose $\Delta$ to be itself an odd prime, so these are simply $2$ and $\Delta$ . Inspecting the sum over genus characters further, we see that if $\Delta\equiv 3\bmod 4$ , then we only sum over $q_{1}=1$ and $q_{2}=4\Delta$ . On the other hand, if $\Delta\equiv 1\bmod 4$ , then we sum over two pairs of $(q_{1},q_{2})$ : $(1,4\Delta)$ and $(4,\Delta)$ .

### A.1. $\Delta\equiv 3\bmod 4$

We review our definition of $\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(1)$ as in Definition 11.3:

$$ \bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(1)=\sum_{p\mid n\implies p\mid 4\Delta}\frac{\chi_{q_{1}}(p_{q_{2}}(n))\chi_{q_{2}}(p_{q_{1}}(n))\mathbf{1}_{\exists\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=n}}{n^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\bmod 4\Delta\\
\gcd(a,4\Delta)=1\end{subarray}}\frac{\chi_{q_{1}}(a)}{(4\Delta)^{2}}\times\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1+\chi(a_{i}))\varrho_{F}^{*}(n,\mathbf{a}), $$

where the local count is given by:

$$ \varrho_{F}^{*}(n,a)=\#\{\mathbf{x}\bmod 4n\Delta:\gcd(x,y,4\Delta)=1,p_{4\Delta}(F(x,y))=n,p_{\neg 4\Delta}(F(x,y))\equiv a_{i}\bmod 4\Delta\}. $$

For $(q_{1},q_{2})=(1,4\Delta)$ , this reduces to

$$ \sum_{p\mid n\implies p\mid 4\Delta}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{\exists\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=n}}{n^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{a}\bmod 4\Delta\\
\gcd(a,4\Delta)=1\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1+\chi(a_{i}))\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(n,\mathbf{a})}{(4\Delta)^{2}}. $$

Fix a value of $n$ . It is a straightforward computation to see when $\Delta\equiv 3\bmod 4$ , the following identity holds:

$$ \#\{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=na\bmod 4n\Delta\}=(1+\chi(a))\cdot 4n\Delta. $$

So, we can rewrite the above expression as:

$$ \sum_{p\mid n\implies p\mid 4\Delta}\mathbf{1}_{\exists\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=n}\cdot\frac{\#\left\{(u,v,x,y)\bmod 4n\Delta:\begin{array}[]{c}x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=F(u,v)\bmod 4n\Delta\\
\gcd(u,v,4\Delta)=1,p_{4\Delta}(F(u,v))=n\end{array}\right\}}{(4n\Delta)^{3}}. $$

From the Chinese remainder theorem, this can be rewritten as $w_{2}w_{\Delta}$ where

$$ w_{2}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mathbf{1}_{\exists\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=2^{k}}\frac{\#\left\{(u,v,x,y)\bmod 2^{k+2}:\begin{array}[]{c}x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=F(u,v)\bmod 2^{k+2}\\
\gcd(u,v,2)=1,v_{2}(F(u,v))=k\end{array}\right\}}{2^{3(k+2)}} $$

and we have that

$$ w_{\Delta}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\#\left\{(u,v,x,y)\bmod\Delta^{k+1}:\begin{array}[]{c}x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=F(u,v)\bmod\Delta^{k+1}\\
\gcd(u,v,\Delta)=1,v_{\Delta}(F(u,v))=k\end{array}\right\}}{\Delta^{3(k+1)}}. $$

Observe that if $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)$ and $\Delta\mid t$ , then automatically we have that $\Delta\mid x,y$ . So, we have that

$$ \displaystyle w_{\Delta} \displaystyle=\left(1-\frac{1}{\Delta}\right)^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\#\left\{(u,v,x,y)\bmod\Delta^{k+1}:\begin{array}[]{c}x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)\bmod\Delta^{k+1}\\
\gcd(u,v,\Delta)=1,\gcd(x,y,t,\Delta)=1,\\
v_{\Delta}(F(u,v))=k\end{array}\right\}}{\Delta^{4(k+1)}} \displaystyle=\left(1-\frac{1}{\Delta}\right)^{-1}\omega_{\Delta}. $$

So, it remains to relate $w_{2}$ to $\omega_{2}$ , the 2-adic density.

We now observe that if there does not exist an ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ such that $N(\mathfrak{a})=2^{k}$ , then there are no solutions to $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)$ with $v_{2}(F(u,v))=k$ over $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ . So, we have that $w_{2}$ is the $2$ -adic density of the variety given by $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=F(u,v)$ over $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ . However, since $\Delta\equiv 3\bmod 4$ , there do exist solutions to $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)$ with $2\mid t$ and $\gcd(x,y,t,2)=1$ . Indeed, after splitting by $\gamma$ such that $2^{\gamma}\|t$ , this gives us that

$$ \omega_{2}=w_{2}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\dots\right)=w_{2}. $$

In summary, we have that for $\Delta\equiv 3\bmod 4$ ,

$$ \prod_{p\mid 4\Delta}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=4\Delta}^{\prime}\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(1)=\frac{1}{2}\omega_{2}\omega_{\Delta}. $$

### A.2. $\Delta\equiv 1\bmod 4$

We must now range over two genus characters: when $(q_{1},q_{2})=(1,4\Delta)$ and $(4,\Delta)$ . By (A.5), our next step is to evaluate:

$$ \prod_{p\mid 4\Delta}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)\left(\bigtriangledown_{1,4\Delta}(1)+\bigtriangledown_{4,\Delta}(1)\right). $$

Expanding the definition of $\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(1)$ from Definition 11.3, we have that

$$ \bigtriangledown_{1,4\Delta}(1)+\bigtriangledown_{4,\Delta}(1)=\sum_{p\mid n\impliedby p\mid 4\Delta}\mathbf{1}_{\exists\mathfrak{a}:N(\mathfrak{a})=n}\sum_{\gcd(a,4\Delta)=1}\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(n,a)}{(4n\Delta)^{2}}\\
\times\left(1+\chi(a)+\chi_{4}(p_{\Delta}(n))\chi_{\Delta}(p_{2}(n))(\chi_{4}(a)+\chi_{\Delta}(a))\right). $$

Observe that since $\Delta\equiv 1\bmod 4$ , we know that $\chi_{4}(p_{\Delta}(n))=1$ . Additionally, since $\Delta\equiv 1\bmod 4$ , we have that there exists $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{a}^{\prime}$ such that $N(\mathfrak{a})=\Delta$ and $N(\mathfrak{a}^{\prime})=2$ . So, we can also remove the indicator function. This leaves us with the summation:

$$ \bigtriangledown_{1,4\Delta}(1)+\bigtriangledown_{4,\Delta}(1)=\sum_{p\mid n\impliedby p\mid 4\Delta}\sum_{\gcd(a,4\Delta)=1}\frac{\varrho_{F}^{*}(n,a)}{(4n\Delta)^{2}}\\
\times\left(1+\chi(a)+\chi_{\Delta}(p_{2}(n))(\chi_{4}(a)+\chi_{\Delta}(a))\right). $$

Next, we want to relate this bottom expression to the number of solutions to $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=na\bmod 4n\Delta$ .

#### Lemma A.4.

Assume that $p\mid n\implies p\mid 4\Delta$ and that $\gcd(a,4\Delta)=1$ . Then

$$ \#\{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=na\bmod 4n\Delta\}=\left(1+\chi(a)+\chi_{\Delta}(p_{2}(n))(\chi_{4}(a)+\chi_{\Delta}(a))\right)\cdot 4n\Delta. $$

#### Proof.

Assume that $n=2^{b}\Delta^{c}$ . Then by the Chinese remainder theorem, we want to understand the following counts:

$$ x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=2^{b}\Delta^{c}a\bmod\Delta^{c+1},\quad x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=2^{b}\Delta^{c}a\bmod 2^{b+2}. $$

In the first scenario, if $c=0$ , then there are exactly $(1+\left(\frac{2^{b}a}{\Delta}\right))\cdot\Delta^{c+1}=(1+\chi_{\Delta}(p_{2}(n))\chi_{\Delta}(a))\cdot\Delta^{c+1}$ such solutions to the equation. On the other hand, if $c>0$ , then $\Delta\mid x$ . Then, after a change of variables, we are left with the equation

$$ \Delta x^{2}+y^{2}=2^{b}\Delta^{c-1}a\bmod\Delta^{c} $$

and lifting such solutions to $\mathbb{Z}/\Delta^{c+1}\mathbb{Z}$ . We repeat the procedure and deduce that again there are $(1+\chi_{\Delta}(p_{2}(n))\chi_{\Delta}(a))\cdot\Delta^{c+1}$ such solutions.

On the other hand, since $\Delta$ is odd and $\gcd(a,4\Delta)=1$ , if $b=0$ then the number of solutions to

$$ x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}=\Delta^{c}a\bmod 4 $$

is given by $(1+\chi_{4}(\Delta^{c}a))\cdot 4.$ Now assume that $b>0$ . Observe that $1+\Delta\equiv 2\bmod 4$ , let us write $\delta$ such that $1+\Delta\equiv 2\delta\bmod 8.$ In other words, we can take $\delta=\frac{\Delta-1}{2}$ . Then if $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}\equiv 2^{b}\Delta^{c}a\bmod 2^{b+2}$ , we can consider

$$ x^{\prime}+y^{\prime}\sqrt{-\Delta}=\frac{x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}}{(1+\sqrt{-\Delta})^{2}}. $$

Observe that $x^{\prime 2}+\Delta y^{\prime 2}\equiv\delta^{b}\Delta^{c}a\bmod 2^{b+2}.$ Thus, we can count the number of solutions to $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}\equiv 2^{b}\Delta^{c}a\bmod 2^{b+2}$ as

$$ (1+\chi_{4}(a)\chi_{4}(\delta)^{b})\cdot 2^{b+2}. $$

Recall that $\Delta\equiv 1\bmod 4$ and so $\chi_{4}(\Delta)=1.$

We now claim that

$$ (1+\chi(a)+\chi_{\Delta}(p_{2}(n))(\chi_{4}(a)+\chi_{\Delta}(a)))\cdot 4n\Delta=(1+\chi_{\Delta}(p_{2}(n))\chi_{\Delta}(a))(1+\chi_{4}(a)\chi_{4}(\delta)^{b})\cdot 2^{b+2}\Delta^{c+1}. $$

To see this, we expand out the product on the right hand side:

$$ 1+\chi_{\Delta}(p_{2}(n))\chi_{\Delta}(a)+\chi_{4}(a)\chi_{4}(\delta)^{b}+\chi_{\Delta}(p_{2}(n)a)\chi_{4}(a)\chi_{4}(\delta)^{b}. $$

Comparing this with $1+\chi(a)+\chi_{\Delta}(p_{2}(n))(\chi_{4}(a)+\chi_{\Delta}(a))$ , we can see that it suffices to show that

$$ \chi(a)+\chi_{\Delta}(p_{2}(n))\chi_{4}(a)=\chi_{4}(a)\chi_{4}(\delta)^{b}+\chi_{\Delta}(p_{2}(n)a)\chi_{4}(a)\chi_{4}(\delta)^{b}. $$

At this point, recall that $\Delta\equiv 1\bmod 4$ and that

$$ \chi_{4}(\delta)=\left(\frac{2}{\Delta}\right)=\begin{cases}1,&\Delta\equiv 1\bmod 8,\\
-1,&\Delta\equiv 5\bmod 8.\end{cases} $$

Thus, we have that

$$ \chi_{4}(\delta^{b}\Delta^{c}a)=\left(\frac{2}{\Delta}\right)^{b}\left(\frac{a}{4}\right)=\chi_{\Delta}(p_{2}(n))\chi_{4}(a), $$

since by definition $\chi_{\Delta}(\cdot)=\left(\frac{\cdot}{\Delta}\right)$ and $p_{2}(n)=2^{b}$ . On the other hand,

$$ \chi_{\Delta}(p_{2}(n)a)\chi_{4}(a)\chi_{4}(\delta)^{b}=\left(\frac{2}{\Delta}\right)^{b}\chi_{\Delta}(a)\left(\frac{2}{\Delta}\right)^{b}\chi_{4}(a)=\chi(a). $$

Here we have recalled that $\chi=\chi_{4\Delta}.$

∎

With Lemma A.4 in hand, we can see that

$$ \bigtriangledown_{1,4\Delta}(1)+\bigtriangledown_{4,\Delta}(1)=\sum_{p\mid n\implies p\mid 4\Delta}\frac{\#\left\{(u,v,x,y)\bmod 4n\Delta:\begin{array}[]{c}x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=F(u,v)\bmod 4n\Delta\\
\gcd(u,v,4\Delta)=1,p_{4\Delta}(F(u,v))=n\end{array}\right\}}{(4n\Delta)^{3}}. $$

Now the computation follows in the same way as when $\Delta\equiv 3\bmod 4$ and we again achieve that when $\Delta\equiv 1\bmod 4$

$$ \prod_{p\mid 4\Delta}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)\sum_{q_{1}q_{2}=4\Delta}^{\prime}\bigtriangledown_{q_{1},q_{2}}(1)=\frac{1}{2}\omega_{2}\omega_{\Delta}. $$

### A.3. Evaluation at the real place

We now calculate $\omega_{\infty}$ : we use the volume formula for an ellipse of the shape $\{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}\leq a\}$ :

$$ \omega_{\infty}=\lim_{\delta\rightarrow 0}\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\log(1/\delta)^{-1}\epsilon^{-1}\int_{\delta<|t|\leq 1}\int_{|u|,|v|\leq|t|^{-1/2}}\text{vol}(\{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}\in t^{2}F(u,v)+[-\epsilon/2,\epsilon/2]\})dudvdt\\
=\lim_{\delta\rightarrow 0}\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\log(1/\delta)^{-1}\epsilon^{-1}\int_{|t|\leq 1}\int_{|u|,|v|\leq|t|^{-1/2}}\frac{\pi\epsilon}{\sqrt{\Delta}}dudvdt\\
=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\Delta}}\lim_{\delta\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{\log(1/\delta)}\int_{1/\delta<t\leq 1}\int_{|u|,|v|\leq t^{-1/2}}dudvdt=\frac{8\pi}{\sqrt{\Delta}}. $$

Putting together Lemma A.3 and our calculations from (A.6) and (A.7), we see that

$$ c_{\Delta,f}=\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{\Delta}}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\omega_{2}\omega_{\Delta}\prod_{p\nmid-\Delta}\omega_{p}=\frac{1}{4}\omega_{\infty}\prod_{p<\infty}\omega_{p}. $$

This completes the proof of Proposition A.1. ∎
